title: Anticoagulated melaena with an uncertain disposition
setting: Monitored bay in a UK district general emergency department
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient, identify immediate risks, arrange focused investigation and explain a safe plan and disposition.
materials_provided: Observations: pulse 104/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 36.5 C, SpO2 96% on air, NEWS2 1. Two episodes of melaena since yesterday and one brief collapse on standing. Medicines: apixaban 5 mg twice daily, ramipril and atorvastatin. Bloods: haemoglobin 89 g/L, platelets 182 x 10^9/L, creatinine 94 micromol/L, INR 1.1.
sp_role_script: You are 74-year-old Margaret, anxious and embarrassed by the black stool. Opening: 'I nearly fainted in the bathroom. Does the blood thinner mean I am bleeding inside?' If asked about amount, say there was a large black stool and you feel light-headed when standing. You have not vomited blood. You took your usual apixaban yesterday. Disclose previous peptic ulcer only if asked about stomach problems or prior bleeding. If asked about chest pain or breathlessness, say neither is present. You become tearful when discussing going home alone and want reassurance about who will look after you.

checklist.item: Recognises suspected upper gastrointestinal bleeding and treats the NEWS2 score as an underestimate because of the collapse and postural symptoms.
Asks about haematemesis, stool volume and frequency, syncope, prior ulcer or bleeding, alcohol, liver disease and adherence to apixaban.
Checks airway and breathing, pulse character, capillary refill, abdominal tenderness and signs of chronic liver disease before proposing investigation.
Requests large-bore intravenous access, repeat observations, full blood count, coagulation screen, renal and liver tests, group and save and a venous blood gas.
Does not transfuse solely because the haemoglobin is 89 g/L, and states that transfusion should follow symptoms, ongoing loss and a senior decision.
Explains that apixaban may need temporary review but will not be stopped permanently without the bleeding and specialist teams agreeing.
Requests urgent gastroenterology and critical care review and admits for monitored care and early endoscopy according to local major bleeding guidance.
Gives a clear closing plan covering observation, further tests, possible endoscopy, medication review and escalation if bleeding or dizziness worsens.

model_answer: I would introduce myself, check that Margaret is comfortable and take a focused history while the nurse repeats observations and places two large-bore cannulas. I need to establish whether she has haematemesis, ongoing melaena, abdominal pain, previous ulcers, liver disease, alcohol use or another bleeding source. Her apixaban, renal function and last dose matter, as does any antiplatelet use. The brief collapse and postural symptoms mean this is clinically significant bleeding even though the NEWS2 score is only 1. I would examine for shock, abdominal tenderness and chronic liver disease, then request full blood count, coagulation, renal and liver tests, group and save, and a venous blood gas. She needs a monitored bed and urgent senior emergency medicine review. I would discuss early gastroenterology input for endoscopy and critical care support according to local major bleeding guidance. I would not reverse apixaban automatically for a stable non-catastrophic bleed or transfuse for the haemoglobin value alone. The bleeding team and haematology should guide temporary withholding or reversal, with attention to thrombosis risk. I would explain that the likely source is above the bowel and that endoscopy may find and treat it. The safe disposition is admission for repeated observations, blood tests and specialist review. I would tell Margaret who will review her, what symptoms require immediate escalation and that the team will speak with her family about support at home.
references_provided: Local major gastrointestinal bleeding pathway and the patient's anticoagulation clinic letter.

title: Confusion in decompensated liver disease
setting: Clinical decisions unit in a UK teaching hospital emergency department
candidate_instructions: Assess the cause of confusion, perform a focused examination and present a prioritised investigation, treatment and admission plan.
materials_provided: Observations: pulse 96/min, BP 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 37.1 C, SpO2 98% on air, NEWS2 5, capillary glucose 7.8 mmol/L. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness. Notes: alcohol-related cirrhosis, ascites and previous variceal banding. Medicines: spironolactone, furosemide and lactulose, although recent adherence is unclear.
sp_role_script: You are Daniel, aged 52, brought by a neighbour because you are confused. Opening: 'I do not need a fuss. I just cannot get my words out.' Answer questions slowly. Hidden information: last alcohol was three days ago; you have tremor, sweats and saw insects on the wall last night; your neighbour found you on the floor but you did not lose consciousness. Disclose the fall only if asked about injury or events today. Admit poor sleep and poor eating when asked. If challenged kindly about alcohol, become defensive, then acknowledge drinking a bottle of spirits most days until three days ago.

checklist.item: Obtains collateral history about the time course of confusion, alcohol intake, last drink, falls, head injury, medication adherence and bowel frequency.
Treats hypoglycaemia, sepsis, hypoxia, drug toxicity, stroke and intracranial injury as reversible causes to exclude before labelling the confusion as hepatic encephalopathy.
Performs a focused neurological examination including GCS, pupils, focal signs, tremor, asterixis and evidence of autonomic withdrawal.
Examines for ascites, jaundice, bruising, injection marks and features of chronic liver disease, and checks for occult injury after the fall.
Requests full blood count, renal and liver profiles, clotting, ammonia if locally used, blood gas, lactate, glucose, blood cultures, urine testing and chest imaging where indicated.
Starts a locally approved pathway for alcohol withdrawal with symptom monitoring and benzodiazepine treatment rather than using a fixed sedative regimen.
States that parenteral thiamine should be given according to the local alcohol-related brain injury pathway and not delayed while waiting for a specialist review.
Discusses lactulose dosing, constipation, dehydration and electrolyte review, and avoids both over-diuresis and unsupported fluid overload.
Admits to a monitored ward bed, requests early hepatology and mental health or alcohol liaison input, and gives clear instructions for review and escalation.

model_answer: I would assess Daniel using an ABCDE approach while obtaining collateral history from his neighbour. Causes that must be excluded include hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, sepsis, stroke, head injury after the fall, medication toxicity, gastrointestinal bleeding and alcohol withdrawal. I would check his GCS and pupils, look for focal neurology, tremor and autonomic signs, and examine for asterixis, ascites, jaundice, bruising and signs of chronic liver disease. Hypoglycaemia is already excluded by the bedside glucose of 7.8 mmol/L, but I would still review the timing and reliability of measurements. I would request full blood count, renal and liver tests, clotting, blood gas, lactate, blood cultures and imaging determined by the examination. If ammonia is used locally, I would interpret it alongside the clinical picture rather than in isolation. Daniel has features of alcohol withdrawal after three days without alcohol, and possible hepatic encephalopathy. Both need active treatment. I would use the local symptom-triggered alcohol withdrawal pathway, give parenteral thiamine according to local policy and discuss lactulose after considering constipation and electrolytes. I would avoid admission under a vague label of confusion. He needs a monitored bed, repeated neurological observations, early hepatology input and alcohol liaison involvement. I would explain the provisional causes to Daniel and his neighbour, state that delirium can fluctuate, and arrange urgent senior review if his GCS falls, he develops fever, bleeding or focal neurological signs.
references_provided: Local alcohol withdrawal and decompensated liver disease pathways.

title: Late presentation after a paracetamol overdose
setting: Emergency department clinical area with access to the local poisons information resource
candidate_instructions: Demonstrate how you would assess and manage this overdose, including use of the local treatment chart and arrangement of a safe disposition.
materials_provided: Patient details: 24-year-old, weight 58 kg, ingested up to 20 paracetamol 500 mg tablets 14 hours ago, no co-ingestants, no vomiting. Observations are normal, capillary glucose 6.1 mmol/L, ALT 68 U/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L. Venous blood gas: pH 7.36, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L. A treatment chart and poisons information resource are available.
task_details: Talk through the actions you would take now, using the chart to decide whether treatment is needed and identifying what information is still required. Explain the observations and blood results and show how you would arrange urgent transfer or admission.

checklist.item: Obtains the time of ingestion, stated dose, weight, co-ingestants, vomiting, liver disease and medication history before using the poisons chart.
Recognises that treatment must not wait when the interval, dose or history is uncertain and acetylcysteine is indicated by the local pathway.
Checks the local treatment chart and any updated poisons advice rather than relying on a remembered nomogram line.
Requests repeat full blood count, renal and liver tests, clotting, electrolytes and glucose, and explains that ALT and clotting need serial review.
Arranges immediate senior and poisons advice for a late presentation with an abnormal ALT and starts treatment without avoidable delay.
Asks about intent, previous attempts, safeguarding concerns, access to medicines and a safe place to stay without sounding judgemental.
Requests urgent mental health or crisis assessment and does not treat medical clearance as a substitute for an assessment of suicide risk.
Explains the admission plan, monitoring, treatment duration and escalation triggers, and arranges appropriate transfer if the local unit cannot provide care.

model_answer: I would first confirm the time, possible dose, patient weight and whether she vomited or took anything else. The precise ingestion is uncertain, the presentation is late and the ALT is already mildly abnormal, so I would not delay treatment while trying to make the numbers fit a remembered chart. I would use the current local poisons chart and contact the poisons service, then start acetylcysteine according to the approved local regimen. The chart determines whether further measurement or a modified regimen is needed. I would request repeat liver tests, clotting, renal function, electrolytes and glucose, and monitor for hepatic injury or a coagulopathy. I would examine for any other injuries and establish baseline observations. The overdose is only one part of the assessment. I would ask about intent, a suicide plan, previous attempts, access to medicines, substances and social support. I would involve the crisis team urgently and discuss safeguarding with a senior clinician. The safe disposition is admission to a unit able to continue acetylcysteine and serial organ function monitoring, with escalation to hepatology or a liver unit if the liver injury progresses. I would explain each step back to the patient, check her understanding, and arrange close observation while she is in the emergency department. I would also check the local pathway for transfer and communicate the plan clearly to receiving staff.
references_provided: Current local paracetamol overdose chart and poisons information service.

title: Demand to leave while hypoxic
setting: Majors cubicle in a busy UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: De-escalate the situation, assess whether the patient can make the decision to leave, and negotiate a safe plan while arranging treatment.
materials_provided: Observations: pulse 112/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, temperature 38.3 C, SpO2 90% on air, NEWS2 9. Chest auscultation: widespread expiratory wheeze and reduced air entry at the right base. The patient has no known dementia and is normally independent.
sp_role_script: You are Paul, aged 46. You are frightened, breathing heavily and standing with your coat on. Opening: 'I am not staying. Give me tablets and oxygen for home.' You have a previous asthma admission and have been using a reliever inhaler more often. Hidden information: you are the sole carer for your father, you have no allocated work leave and you fear hospitals. Disclose these reasons only when asked what is worrying you or what makes leaving feel necessary. If the candidate explains risks calmly and offers a plan, soften and sit down. If they issue commands, raise your voice and move towards the curtain.

checklist.item: Uses a calm, non-judgemental opening, lowers the conflict, sits at the patient's level and asks what is driving the wish to leave.
Reassesses airway, breathing, speech, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation, chest sounds and mental state before discussing discharge.

Identifies that the patient is hypoxic and tachycardic and activates the emergency team response, requests senior review, continuous monitoring, oxygen to the appropriate target and urgent investigation.
Considers acute severe asthma and pneumonia and arranges chest radiograph, blood tests and treatment according to the relevant local pathway.
Explains clearly that taking oxygen home is not a safe treatment and that leaving now could allow respiratory failure to progress.
Assesses capacity by checking whether Paul can understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision, rather than equating an unwise choice with incapacity.
Responds to the carer duty by contacting the nurse in charge, social work or the local carer support route while urgent treatment continues.

If Paul has capacity and refuses, respects the refusal and does not treat the deteriorating clinical risk as authority to override it; documents the discussion, seeks urgent senior review, addresses his carer responsibilities and offers treatment, review and immediate-return advice.
Closes with a direct safety plan naming who will monitor him, what will happen next and which symptoms require an emergency call.

model_answer: I would keep my voice calm and introduce myself while the nurse brings oxygen and continuous monitoring. I would not block the exit or make promises about admission before I know what Paul fears. I would ask why leaving feels necessary and acknowledge his responsibility for his father and his fear of hospitals. At the same time I would assess him: he is hypoxic, tachycardic and working hard to breathe. I would listen to the chest, check speech and mental state, activate the emergency team response and request senior help, start oxygen to the appropriate target and arrange focused tests and treatment for acute severe asthma or pneumonia. I would explain that oxygen cannot safely be supplied for home use through the emergency department and that leaving with a saturation of 90% could lead to worsening respiratory failure. I would assess capacity under the Mental Capacity Act by testing understanding, retention, use of information and communication. An unwise decision alone does not prove incapacity. If Paul has capacity and refuses admission, I still need urgent senior review and a documented risk discussion. I would offer treatment while he stays, contact the team responsible for his father and arrange the safest possible follow-up. If Paul remains capacitous, I would respect his refusal of admission and treatment and would not use the Mental Capacity Act, security or restraint to override it. I would seek urgent senior review, offer treatment while he is willing to stay, address his responsibility for his father and give immediate-return advice. If his capacity changes, I would reassess the specific decision. If he then lacks capacity and immediate treatment is necessary to save life or prevent serious harm, I would use the section 5 Mental Capacity Act route and the least restrictive action, with a lawful basis for any deprivation of liberty. Mental Health Act powers would be considered only if the statutory mental disorder criteria are met. My closing plan would name the monitoring, treatment, review and exact symptoms that require urgent help.
references_provided: UK acute asthma and oxygen therapy information plus the trust Mental Capacity Act policy.

title: Wrong patient label on a pre-transfusion sample
setting: Emergency department medical handover room
candidate_instructions: Speak to the nurse who has brought you the laboratory call. Take immediate safety actions, explain how you will speak to the patient and set out the incident and learning response.
materials_provided: A 67-year-old patient with symptomatic anaemia is awaiting transfusion. The laboratory has found that her blood sample carries another patient's hospital number and date of birth. No unit has left the blood bank. The patient has not yet been told.
sp_role_script: You are Staff Nurse Aisha, tired and upset after a busy shift. Opening: 'The lab says the label is wrong. I took that sample. What happens now?' Hidden information: you labelled the tube in the treatment room while answering an emergency buzzer and did not check the wristband at the bedside. You are worried about being blamed. You want to know whether the patient is safe. If the candidate listens and asks for facts, explain your actions honestly. If confronted aggressively, become defensive and say nothing more.

checklist.item: Makes immediate patient safety the first priority by confirming that no blood component has been released and pausing the transfusion plan.
Listens to Aisha without blaming her, acknowledges the pressure she is under and asks for a calm factual sequence of events.
Requests a correctly labelled repeat group and save using full bedside identity checks, including asking the patient to state identifying details when possible.
Reviews whether the patient's anaemia is symptomatic enough to need urgent senior review while the repeat sample is processed.
Plans an honest duty-of-candour conversation with the patient, explaining what happened, that no blood was given and what safety checks are now in place.
Escalates to the nurse in charge and transfusion laboratory or site coordinator and starts or supports the local incident report promptly.
Identifies system factors such as interruption during labelling and separates learning from individual blame while still addressing unsafe practice.
Closes by telling Aisha what will happen next, offering senior support, and naming the review, documentation and follow-up actions.

model_answer: I would start by confirming that no unit has been collected or transfused and ask the laboratory to quarantine any associated request. Patient safety comes first. I would then ask Aisha to tell me what happened from start to finish. I would acknowledge that the department is busy and that she reported the problem promptly. The aim is not to blame her before the facts are known. I would send a repeat sample with a full bedside identity check, using the wristband and a second check rather than relying on a room label. I would contact the blood bank, tell the nurse in charge and review whether the patient needs urgent critical care or other treatment while we wait. I would speak to the patient with a senior colleague available. I would explain honestly that a sample was mislabelled, that no blood was transfused, that the error was found before harm and that we are repeating the tests safely. I would document that conversation. I would submit an incident report and ask the transfusion laboratory to review whether patient identification matched at every stage. The learning should address interruptions, labelling at the bedside and a clear stop-the-line rule. Aisha also needs support and a chance to contribute to the review. I would close by confirming the repeat sample result, the revised transfusion decision and who will follow up the incident.
references_provided: Trust blood transfusion policy, bedside identity-check standard and incident reporting procedure.

title: Teaching a junior doctor to assess a broad complex tachycardia
setting: Emergency department teaching room with a 12-lead ECG and monitor trace
candidate_instructions: Teach the junior doctor a safe structured approach to the ECG and the initial decisions. Use spoken explanation and a short teach-back; do not simply present a lecture.
materials_provided: Monitor and 12-lead ECG show a regular broad complex tachycardia at 178/min. The patient is alert with BP 104/66 mmHg and no chest pain. The trainee has read basic ECGs but has little experience of broad complex tachycardia.
sp_role_script: You are Dr Sam, an FY2 doctor who is keen but nervous. Opening: 'I know it is broad, but how do I decide if this is VT or something else?' Answer the candidate's questions in short sentences. You can identify rate, rhythm and QRS width after prompting, but you initially jump to adenosine because you think all tachycardias are treated the same way. Become more confident when the candidate uses questions, a repeated structure and a short practice attempt. At the end, explain back what you would do if the patient became unstable.

checklist.item: Checks Sam's prior knowledge and sets two or three specific learning points for the eight-minute teaching episode.
Teaches a repeatable sequence covering patient stability, rate, rhythm, QRS width, axis, morphology, prior ECG and reversible causes.
Explains that a broad complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise in this clinical setting.
Distinguishes assessment of an unstable patient requiring urgent synchronised cardioversion from assessment of a stable patient who needs senior review and investigation.
Explains why adenosine is not a safe diagnostic shortcut in an unstable patient and why it can be harmful in some broad complex rhythms.
Names the escalation route to the emergency medicine consultant and critical care team and states that treatment must match the local tachycardia algorithm.
Uses a short case-based question and asks Sam to apply the sequence to this ECG rather than only listening.
Uses teach-back to confirm the key points and gives one specific, achievable action for Sam's next supervised assessment.
Gives feedback in a supportive, specific way and closes by asking Sam to summarise the stability-based decision rule.

model_answer: I would begin by asking Sam what he already knows and what worries him about this ECG. I would agree three objectives: recognise instability, use a structure to describe the rhythm and choose a safe next action. I would start with the patient, not the tracing. If there is hypotension, ischaemic chest pain, heart failure, reduced consciousness or shock, the patient needs urgent synchronised cardioversion under the local tachycardia pathway and immediate senior and anaesthetic support. In this stable patient, I would guide Sam through rate, rhythm, QRS width, axis, morphology and comparison with an old ECG. I would reinforce that a regular broad complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise and that personal pattern recognition is not a safe exclusion rule. We would look for capture beats, fusion beats, extreme axis and AV dissociation while recognising their absence does not exclude VT. I would explain that adenosine is not a routine diagnostic test and should not delay definitive treatment in an unstable patient. I would ask Sam to apply the structure aloud, correct one unsafe step and then invite him to teach it back in two sentences. I would give feedback on what he did well, name one action to practise and tell him to call me before giving treatment to a future patient with broad QRS tachycardia. The teaching closes with a clear escalation rule, not a list of diagnoses.
references_provided: Local adult tachycardia algorithm and Resuscitation Council UK adult advanced life support guidance.

title: Peri-arrest anaphylaxis after intravenous antibiotic
setting: Resuscitation room in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Lead the first five minutes of resuscitation. State your assessments and orders aloud, allocate roles and escalate when needed.
materials_provided: A 64-year-old woman developed facial swelling, widespread urticaria and wheeze two minutes after intravenous antibiotics. Observations: pulse 128/min, BP 72/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 88% on 15 L oxygen, GCS 13, capillary refill 4 seconds. The airway is noisy and the voice is hoarse.
sp_role_script: You are the emergency nurse and team. Open with: 'She became swollen immediately after the antibiotic and is getting drowsy.' Follow clear closed-loop orders. If the candidate does not name a team leader, ask who is leading. Disclose stridor and difficulty swallowing when airway assessment is requested. The anaesthetic registrar is two minutes away. Critical care and the resuscitation consultant are available by phone.

checklist.item: States that they are leading, confirms the diagnosis of anaphylaxis and assigns roles for airway, circulation, drugs, timing and record keeping.
Assesses airway swelling and voice change, gives high-flow oxygen, applies monitoring and calls anaesthetics and critical care immediately.
Orders intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh using the appropriate adult dose and states the interval before reassessment and repeat.
Stops the likely trigger and states that intramuscular adrenaline is first line, with intravenous adrenaline reserved for a monitored, experienced team setting.
Positions the patient supine with legs elevated if breathing allows, starts rapid crystalloid resuscitation and reassesses perfusion after each bolus.
Calls for a difficult airway plan and prepares for early intubation while avoiding a delay caused by waiting for the swelling to resolve.
Allocates someone to document times, drugs, observations and investigations, including serial blood gases and mast cell tryptase samples according to local policy.
Uses closed-loop communication, asks for a time-out when priorities conflict and escalates to the consultant and intensive care team.
Closes with a post-stabilisation plan for monitored admission, allergen documentation, allergy referral and a clear handover.

model_answer: I would take leadership aloud, confirm anaphylaxis and state that the trigger antibiotic must stop. I would allocate the nurse to airway and observations, another to circulation and fluids, one to draw up drugs and one to record times. Oxygen goes on at high flow while anaesthetics and critical care are called now. This patient has airway swelling, hypotension and hypoxia, so this is life threatening. I would give 500 micrograms of adrenaline, which is 0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, intramuscularly into the anterolateral middle third of the thigh, reassess after 5 minutes and repeat if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist. Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for an experienced monitored team and must not be improvised outside the local protocol. I would position her supine with legs raised if she tolerates it, establish large-bore access and give rapid crystalloid boluses, checking perfusion and lung findings after each. The hoarse voice and stridor require an urgent difficult-airway plan. Anaesthesia should be present early and should prepare for intubation before complete obstruction. I would continue the local anaphylaxis algorithm, monitor continuously, and document every drug and time. Serial tryptase sampling may be arranged according to policy after the immediate resuscitation. Once stabilized, she needs intensive care or a high-dependency bed, allergy documentation and follow-up. I would hand over the suspected trigger, treatment sequence, response and remaining airway risk, then debrief the team and support staff after the patient is transferred.
references_provided: Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis guidance and trust difficult airway and anaphylaxis policies.

title: Unstable pelvic trauma after a motorcycle collision
setting: Major trauma resuscitation bay in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Lead the primary survey and damage-control resuscitation. State actions aloud, set priorities and make the transfer decision.
materials_provided: A 27-year-old motorcyclist is alert but pale after a high-speed collision. A pelvic binder is in place. Observations: pulse 136/min, BP 76/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 94% on 15 L oxygen, GCS 14, temperature 35.8 C. The abdomen is tender and the pelvis is clinically unstable. A pelvic x-ray shows a displaced ring injury. The major trauma centre is 25 minutes away.
sp_role_script: You are the trauma team. Open with: 'Pelvic binder is on from the road, he is getting more drowsy and we cannot find a radial pulse.' Follow clear orders and report when a task is complete. The blood bank can activate the major haemorrhage protocol immediately. The regional major trauma centre has an interventional radiology suite and accepts the patient. Point out if the candidate gives repeated large crystalloid boluses without activating blood products.

checklist.item: Declares leadership, assigns clear roles and uses a primary survey while bringing the trauma consultant and anaesthetist to the bedside.
Checks airway with cervical spine protection, confirms oxygenation and ventilation, then recognises decompensated shock in the circulation assessment.
Confirms the pelvic binder is at the level of the greater trochanters and avoids repeated pelvic springing or log rolls.
Activates the major haemorrhage protocol, requests blood products and tranexamic acid within the local major trauma pathway and limits avoidable crystalloid.
Requests large-bore access, blood gas, crossmatch, clotting and pelvic or abdominal imaging in a sequence that does not delay haemorrhage control.
Prioritises external haemorrhage control and early definitive haemostasis, with interventional radiology, surgery or transfer depending on the pathway.
Prevents hypothermia with active warming and warmed fluids, and states that damage-control resuscitation includes correcting calcium and clotting abnormalities.
Makes an explicit early decision to transfer to the major trauma centre and communicates the urgency and interventions required.
Gives a structured handover to the receiving team and briefs the team on priorities, contingencies and post-event debrief.

model_answer: I would take command, ask for silence when needed and appoint airway, circulation, procedures, drugs and scribe roles. This is a time-critical major trauma. The airway needs assessment with cervical spine protection while high-flow oxygen continues. Breathing is assessed quickly, then circulation shows decompensated shock. I would confirm the pelvic binder sits over the greater trochanters and avoid repeated pelvic examination. The major haemorrhage protocol must be activated now, with balanced blood products and tranexamic acid according to the local major trauma pathway. I would give only limited crystalloid while blood arrives and establish large-bore access. The patient also needs active warming, calcium and clotting replacement guided by the protocol and blood gas results. I would plan early haemorrhage control rather than relying on imaging alone. A displaced pelvic ring injury with this physiology raises concern for major retroperitoneal bleeding, and he may need interventional radiology or surgery at the major trauma centre. The centre accepts him and has interventional radiology, so I would arrange urgent transfer after essential stabilisation on scene and prereferral. I would not allow a CT scan at this hospital to delay haemostasis. The anaesthetic and trauma teams should prepare for transfer and possible deterioration. I would hand over mechanism, time, observations, treatment, response, imaging and outstanding needs, then debrief the team and notify the consultant in charge.
references_provided: Trust major haemorrhage and major trauma transfer pathways plus regional trauma network guidance.

title: Prolonged seizure with falling oxygen saturation
setting: Resuscitation bay in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Lead the immediate management of an adult in convulsive status epilepticus. State your orders, monitoring plan and escalation triggers.
materials_provided: A 39-year-old man has been seizing for 20 minutes. He has no known epilepsy and no wristband. Observations: pulse 142/min, BP 158/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 8/min and irregular, SpO2 87% on 15 L oxygen, temperature 38.1 C. Capillary glucose 3.1 mmol/L. Intraosseous access can be obtained if intravenous access fails.
sp_role_script: You are the resuscitation team. Open with: 'He has been fitting since the ambulance arrived and we cannot get a cannula.' Follow airway, circulation and drug orders clearly. Report the low glucose and shallow breathing when measured. The anaesthetic registrar and intensive care consultant are available immediately. If the candidate gives no airway plan, state that suction and a bag-mask are ready but no one has been assigned to use them.

checklist.item: Takes team leadership, assigns airway, access, medication, timing and history roles and asks for a time reference for seizure onset.
Opens the airway, suctions if needed, supports ventilation with a bag-mask and avoids forcing objects into the mouth.
Treats the capillary glucose of 3.1 mmol/L immediately according to the local pathway while continuing antiseizure treatment.
Orders a full benzodiazepine dose by the appropriate route and states the timing for reassessment and a repeat dose.
Obtains intravenous access or uses the local intraosseous route and prepares second-line antiseizure treatment without delay.
Calls anaesthetics and intensive care early and states that persistent seizure activity requires a controlled airway and second-line treatment.
Tests and treats reversible causes including glucose, sodium, calcium, hypoxia, infection, pregnancy and poisoning while protecting the patient.
Uses closed-loop communication and keeps a clear record of seizure duration, drugs, doses, route, response and adverse effects.
Plans post-ictal CT and neurology or critical care review according to the cause and response, with a named disposition and handover.

model_answer: I would take leadership and confirm the seizure started twenty minutes ago. The airway team opens the airway, suctions secretions and supports ventilation with a bag-mask while oxygen and capnography are applied. Someone records each drug and time. The capillary glucose is low, so I would treat it immediately using the local hypoglycaemia pathway while continuing seizure treatment. I would obtain intravenous access quickly and move to the local intraosseous route if it fails. Current status epilepticus guidance directs a full benzodiazepine dose by the appropriate route, followed by reassessment and a further dose if the seizure continues within the specified interval. I would not use an inadequate dose because access is difficult. Anaesthetics and intensive care are called now because the patient is hypoxic and may need a controlled airway and second-line antiseizure treatment. While the seizure continues, I would check temperature, blood gas, sodium, calcium, renal function, toxicology risk and pregnancy status where relevant. I would look for a reversible cause without interrupting airway support. Once the seizure is controlled, he needs close monitoring, a CT head and neurology or intensive care review according to the clinical picture. I would hand over the duration, treatment sequence, glucose correction and current airway plan. My disposition is a resuscitation or high-dependency area with a clear trigger for immediate anaesthetic review.
references_provided: Local status epilepticus algorithm and UK resuscitation guidance.

title: Posterior elbow dislocation with a weak radial pulse
setting: Minor injuries procedure room in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Assess the limb, plan analgesia and reduction, demonstrate the procedure on the model, and state the reassessment and post-reduction plan.
materials_provided: A 35-year-old fell from a ladder and holds the elbow flexed. The olecranon is displaced posteriorly. The hand is warm, capillary refill is 3 seconds, the radial pulse is weak and sensation is reduced in the thumb web space. X-ray confirms a posterior elbow dislocation without a visible fracture. A procedure model and splinting materials are available.
sp_role_script: You are the patient and procedure assistant. Opening: 'My fingers feel strange and the pain is awful.' Say the pain is 9 out of 10. Report worsening numbness when asked. Follow instructions clearly, remind the candidate to check the limb before and after the procedure, and state that you feel faint if the limb is left unsupported.
task_details: Demonstrate the positioning, traction and counter-traction you would use. Do not attempt the procedure without confirming the analgesia and sedation plan, senior support and pre-procedure neurovascular findings.

checklist.item: Records radial pulse, capillary refill, colour, motor function and sensory status before any procedure.
Recognises the weak pulse and altered sensation as a neurovascular emergency and requests immediate senior and orthopaedic or vascular advice.
Provides effective analgesia and chooses procedural sedation or another approved method after checking fasting status, comorbidities, allergies and monitoring needs.
Positions the patient safely, provides gentle longitudinal traction with counter-traction and avoids forceful leverage during reduction.
Repeats the full distal neurovascular examination immediately after reduction and compares it with the pre-procedure findings.
Arranges post-reduction imaging, a splint in a safe position and repeat neurovascular observations at set intervals.
States that persistent pulselessness or worsening neurological deficit after reduction requires urgent operative vascular or orthopaedic assessment.
Explains each step, obtains consent, warns about sedation risks and gives the patient clear instructions for reporting numbness, pain or colour change.
Closes with the definitive follow-up, plaster or splint plan and admission or transfer decision if the limb is not safely stable.

model_answer: I would first immobilise the arm in a comfortable position and record the radial pulse, capillary refill, colour, wrist and finger movement, and sensation. The weak radial pulse and reduced sensation in the thumb web space make this a neurovascular emergency, so I would call the emergency medicine consultant and seek immediate orthopaedic and vascular advice. I would give effective analgesia and use the local procedural sedation policy, checking allergies, fasting status, comorbidities and airway risk. The procedure is performed with monitoring and a trained assistant. I would position the elbow comfortably and apply gentle longitudinal traction with counter-traction while supporting the forearm, avoiding force or repeated attempts. After reduction I would repeat the entire neurovascular examination and document it immediately. The limb would be splinted in the approved position and re-imaged. If the pulse does not return or the neurological deficit worsens, the patient needs urgent specialist assessment and likely operative treatment. I would not discharge this patient from the emergency department on reassurance alone. The disposition depends on the post-reduction examination: admission or specialty transfer when there is persistent compromise, and structured fracture clinic follow-up when the limb is stable and perfusion is restored. I would explain the procedure, sedation risks and warning symptoms to the patient, then confirm the plan and observation schedule with the nursing team.
references_provided: Trust procedural sedation policy, elbow injury pathway and neurovascular observation chart.

title: A painful wrist with a normal first X-ray
setting: Minor injuries unit in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Take a focused history from the nurse practitioner, interpret the available findings and agree a safe plan for this patient.
materials_provided: A 29-year-old cyclist has central wrist pain after a fall on an outstretched hand. There is tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, pain on axial loading of the thumb and no visible deformity. Standard wrist radiographs are reported as no fracture. The patient wants to drive home after a long shift.
sp_role_script: You are Nurse Practitioner Chris, presenting the case. Opening: 'The X-ray is normal, so can she go?' Hidden information: she has severe pain when lifting a cup, there is no other focal tenderness and she is reliable with transport. You are unsure whether a thumb spica is needed. If asked about follow-up, explain that the local virtual fracture clinic accepts suspected scaphoid injuries and repeat imaging can be arranged there. Ask the candidate to state the advice you should give before she leaves.

checklist.item: Confirms the mechanism, hand dominance, occupation, ability to drive and whether there is other injury or prior wrist surgery.
Checks anatomical snuffbox tenderness, scaphoid tubercle tenderness, thumb axial loading and range of movement while examining nearby bones and the distal radius.
Recognises that a normal initial X-ray does not exclude a scaphoid fracture and avoids false reassurance.
States the value of early immobilisation for clinical suspicion and arranges follow-up or repeat imaging according to the local suspected scaphoid pathway.
Applies a properly fitted thumb spica splint or cast through the local pathway and explains the importance of not immobilising in a painful or unsafe position.
Explains why she should not assume the wrist is normal, and gives clear advice about pain, swelling, numbness or inability to use the hand.
Arranges a named review or imaging date and makes clear that the patient should not rely on an open return without a booking.
Asks Chris to teach back the plan and documents the examination, imaging limitation, immobilisation and follow-up.

model_answer: A normal first wrist X-ray does not rule out a scaphoid fracture. I would ask about the exact mechanism, hand dominance, work and driving needs, previous wrist injury and any other pain or loss of function. On examination I would check anatomical snuffbox tenderness, scaphoid tubercle tenderness and pain on axial thumb loading, then make sure the distal radius, carpus, ligaments and thumb base do not show a more obvious injury. If the history and examination remain suspicious, I would immobilise the wrist in a thumb spica according to the local pathway and provide effective analgesia. The patient should not be told that the wrist is normal. I would explain that some small fractures are not visible on the first set of images and that repeat imaging or specialist review is required. I would use the local virtual fracture clinic or suspected scaphoid pathway and give her a booking rather than an open return. She needs a follow-up plan that is clear even if the repeat X-ray is also normal, because clinical scaphoid injury may still need assessment. I would check that she has safe transport home and that her job does not require heavy lifting or use of the affected hand. I would ask Chris to explain the plan back, confirm the splint and follow-up are documented, and tell the patient which symptoms require urgent return.
references_provided: Local suspected scaphoid and virtual fracture clinic pathway.

title: A feverish child with a spreading rash
setting: Paediatric emergency department in a UK district general hospital
candidate_instructions: Assess the child with the parent, recognise the immediate threat, initiate treatment and explain the plan and escalation to the parent.
materials_provided: A 3-year-old is lethargic and clinging to a parent. Measured weight 15 kg. Observations: pulse 168/min, respiratory rate 44/min, BP 78/44 mmHg, temperature 39.6 C, SpO2 96% on air, capillary refill 4 seconds, local paediatric early warning score high. There is a non-blanching purple rash on the trunk. The child is alert to voice but difficult to rouse.
sp_role_script: You are the parent, frightened and holding the child. Opening: 'She was fine this morning and now she will not wake up properly. What is happening?' You have no relevant medical history to report and the child takes no regular medicines. If asked, say there is no known allergy. Answer only the questions asked and become more distressed when the rash is examined. You want to know why antibiotics and fluids are needed and whether the child will be transferred. Settle when the plan is explained in short, honest sentences.

checklist.item: Uses a paediatric ABCDE assessment, recognises shock and altered consciousness, starts oxygen because shock is present despite an SpO2 of 96%, and examines the rash and capillary refill without delaying treatment.
Treats suspected meningococcal sepsis as the working diagnosis and calls the paediatric consultant, anaesthetist, intensive care team and nurse in charge early.
Obtains intravenous or intraosseous access promptly while arranging blood gas, glucose, blood cultures, full blood count, clotting and other tests only if they will not delay antibiotics.

Gives broad-spectrum intravenous or intraosseous antibiotics from the current paediatric formulary and local sepsis pathway within 1 hour of identifying high-risk sepsis, taking cultures first only when this will not delay treatment.

Gives a glucose-free, sodium-containing crystalloid bolus of 10 mL/kg over less than 10 minutes, up to 250 mL, using the measured 15 kg weight and reducing the volume if cardiac or kidney disease is present; reassesses after the first bolus, gives a second only if there is no improvement, and alerts a consultant to attend in person if there is no improvement after the second.
Explains in plain words that the child may have a severe infection, why urgent antibiotics and fluids are being started and what the team is doing next.
Arranges a monitored bed and discusses transfer or retrieval early if the local hospital cannot provide paediatric intensive care.
Checks the child's weight or uses the measured length-based system, records drug doses and times, and uses closed-loop communication with the team.
Closes by naming the senior clinician, explaining contact tracing and public health arrangements, and offering the parent a clear update and support.

model_answer: I would start with a paediatric ABCDE assessment while keeping the parent close enough to comfort the child. The child is shocked, has a non-blanching rash and altered consciousness, so I would treat suspected meningococcal sepsis as the working diagnosis and call the paediatric consultant, anaesthetist, intensive care team and nurse in charge now. Because shock is present, I would start oxygen now despite the oxygen saturation of 96% on air and titrate it while I reassess airway, breathing and circulation. I would obtain intravenous access quickly and use the intraosseous route if access is delayed. Using the measured weight of 15 kg, I would give broad-spectrum antibiotics from the current paediatric formulary and local sepsis pathway within 1 hour of identifying high-risk sepsis; blood cultures must not delay them. I would give a glucose-free, sodium-containing crystalloid bolus of 10 mL/kg over less than 10 minutes, up to a maximum of 250 mL, which is 150 mL at this weight, with a smaller volume if cardiac or kidney disease is present. I would reassess perfusion, respiratory effort, liver size and mental state after the first bolus, give a second bolus only if there is no improvement, and alert a consultant to attend in person if there is no improvement after the second. I would also check glucose and blood gas and arrange the other sepsis investigations without interrupting treatment. The child needs continuous monitoring and a resuscitation bed. I would explain to the parent that this may be a severe bloodstream infection, that the rash is a warning sign and that treatment has started. I would say who is leading, what tests are running and when I will return. If paediatric intensive care is not available locally, I would contact the regional retrieval service early. I would document weights, doses, times and response, ask public health to advise on contact prophylaxis and ensure the parent has a named person to speak with.
references_provided: Current UK paediatric sepsis and meningitis pathways, paediatric formulary and local retrieval contact sheet.

title: Leading the department during a corridor surge
setting: Emergency department nurse in charge office during a UK winter surge
candidate_instructions: Act as the emergency department doctor in charge for the next ten minutes. Create a safe, prioritised plan and explain what you will escalate and how you will measure whether it worked.
materials_provided: There are 38 patients waiting, 11 ambulance handovers outstanding, four patients with chest pain not yet assessed and two patients in the waiting room with NEWS2 of 6 or above. There are no inpatient beds available. The paediatric area has one nurse and the resuscitation room is full.
sp_role_script: You are Nurse in Charge Priya. Opening: 'We cannot take another ambulance until someone is moved. Two waiting patients look worse and I have lost an hour of staffing.' You want a clear plan, not a list of ideal resources. If asked, say two corridor trolleys can be staffed, one discharge lounge bed may become available and the site manager has not yet escalated to the executive on call. Push back if the candidate suggests moving the sickest patients into the corridor without a monitoring and escalation plan.

checklist.item: Creates a rapid safety scan and prioritises the two high NEWS2 patients, the unassessed chest pains and ambulance handovers by clinical risk.
Runs a short huddle with explicit roles for triage, resuscitation, ambulance offload, flow and escalation.
Moves staff and space only with a named clinician, monitoring plan and clear trigger for return to a higher-care area.
Identifies patients who can safely use same-day emergency care, ambulatory pathways, discharge lounge or senior review to release capacity.
Escalates to the site manager, executive on call and relevant specialty teams using the trust escalation policy, with specific asks and a time to report back.
Gives the nursing team a clear safety message and acknowledges the pressure without promising resources that do not exist.
Allocates a runner or senior decision-maker to reassess waiting patients at fixed intervals and records deterioration actions.
Measures success using concrete indicators such as unseen high-risk patients, offload delays, resuscitations started and staff available, then sets a review time.
Closes with a clear handover to the next shift or site team and states which risks remain unresolved.

model_answer: I would start with a one-minute safety scan, not a bed meeting. The two patients with NEWS2 of 6 or above and the four unassessed chest pains are the first priorities. Priya and I would agree who is responsible for each group, who is available for resuscitation and who can reassess the waiting room at a fixed interval. I would move patients into corridor spaces only when a named clinician, monitoring and an escalation route are in place. I would not create a second area that cannot see deterioration. I would identify ambulatory or same-day emergency care patients, request senior specialty review where it can unlock a pathway, and ask the discharge lounge and site manager for concrete options. I would escalate to the executive on call now because the department is unable to meet safe standards with the current resources, and I would ask for staff, beds or ambulance diversion within the trust policy. I would tell the team what is known, what is not yet available and what each person must do if a patient deteriorates. I would record the decisions and use measures such as time to first assessment, high-risk waiting patients remaining unseen, ambulance offload delay and resuscitation capacity. We would review at a set time and adjust. At handover I would state the unresolved risks, the names of the most vulnerable patients and the escalation already made.
references_provided: Trust emergency department escalation policy, site capacity dashboard and ambulance handover procedure.

title: Managing care during a pathology system outage
setting: Emergency department coordination desk during an overnight digital systems failure
candidate_instructions: Lead the emergency department response to the outage. Decide what to keep open, what to pause and how to communicate and review risk.
materials_provided: The laboratory information system is offline and there is no estimate for restoration. Point-of-care blood gases, glucose and troponin devices are working. The blood bank can issue products using its downtime procedure. There are three patients on the sepsis pathway, one possible ectopic pregnancy and a trauma call inbound.
sp_role_script: You are Dr Lewis, the site coordinator. Opening: 'Pathology says it may be two hours, but they cannot promise anything. What do you want to do?' Hidden information: the blood bank downtime procedure works, the maternity unit can perform urgent ultrasound and the community same-day pathway cannot accept referrals while its own system is down. If asked, confirm the executive on call is available. Challenge any plan that relies on routine bloods being available or that silently allows low-risk pathways to continue without safety checks.

checklist.item: Declares a clear command role and creates a written downtime response with named leads for clinical care, laboratory communication and escalation.
Protects time-critical pathways for sepsis, major trauma and suspected ectopic pregnancy while stopping or modifying pathways that depend on unavailable results.
States that clinical assessment and point-of-care tests do not replace unavailable laboratory tests and that treatment must not be delayed by waiting for them.
Contacts the blood bank, radiology and on-call specialties to confirm which emergency services remain available and how urgent results will be communicated.
Briefs clinical teams with concrete limits, agreed alternatives and a route to escalate uncertainty rather than allowing individual workarounds.
Escalates capacity and clinical risk to the executive on call and agrees a trigger for ambulance diversion or mutual aid.
Sets a review interval and tracks high-risk patients, pending results, deteriorating patients and delays in definitive care.
Documents the downtime decisions, communications and risks, and assigns responsibility for reconciliation when systems return.
Closes with a structured handover and a plan to inform patients and staff about delays and revised pathways.

model_answer: I would take command and establish a written downtime board with a clinical lead, laboratory contact, flow lead and escalation contact. The immediate question is not whether the department is open; it is which care can be delivered safely. Sepsis, major trauma and the possible ectopic pregnancy remain time-critical. Point-of-care gases and glucose help, but they do not replace full laboratory tests. I would tell teams to start treatment when clinically indicated and not wait for a working system. The blood bank downtime procedure should be used and radiology contacted for the ectopic pathway. I would stop any low-risk pathway that depends on routine blood results, including parts of the same-day service that cannot accept referrals. I would brief staff on the concrete limits, the alternatives and the requirement to escalate uncertainty to a senior clinician. Dr Lewis and I would contact the executive on call and ask for support with staffing, capacity and mutual aid. I would set a review time and track every high-risk patient, pending sample and delay to definitive care. If the outage continues or the department cannot maintain standards, we would escalate to ambulance diversion under trust policy. I would document decisions and communications, then assign a team to reconcile results and records when the system returns. The handover would state known risks, patients awaiting urgent review and open actions.
references_provided: Trust laboratory downtime procedure, business continuity plan and emergency department escalation policy.

title: Critical appraisal of a prehospital airway trial
setting: Quiet appraisal room beside the emergency department
candidate_instructions: Discuss how you would examine the internal and external validity of the supplied practice paper and whether it should change local practice. Do not summarise the article and do not perform calculations.
materials_provided: A fictional practice abstract reported a multicentre cluster randomised trial comparing a supraglottic airway strategy with bag-mask ventilation before hospital arrival in 2,400 adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The primary outcome was survival at 30 days. Allocation concealment was unclear. There was substantial crossover, outcome assessors were not blinded and the confidence interval included no benefit. The trial ran in urban and rural ambulance services with different response times.
sp_role_script: You are an emergency medicine consultant examiner. Opening instruction: 'Start where you think the study can mislead us. I will ask you to separate what the study can tell us from what it cannot.' If the candidate begins by summarising the paper, redirect them to one source of bias or one threat to relevance. Ask how cluster effects, crossover and unblinded outcome assessment affect confidence. Later ask what they would need before changing the local airway strategy. Do not ask for a numerical result or a calculation.

checklist.item: Frames the question in PICO terms and identifies the intervention, comparator, population and primary outcome.
Identifies unclear allocation concealment, cluster-level effects and crossover as factors that could dilute or distort the estimated effect.
Explains why lack of blinding of outcome assessors matters, especially when the outcome and subsequent care may be influenced by knowledge of treatment.
Recognises that a confidence interval including no benefit does not justify claiming equivalence and considers the precision and certainty of the result.
Assesses whether the ambulance services, response times, staff training and cardiac arrest population resemble the local system.
Considers whether the trial measured a patient-important outcome and whether surrogate measures or post-randomisation care could change the interpretation.
Names other relevant evidence and guideline context and avoids basing a practice change on a single trial.
States a proportionate decision path involving the regional ambulance service, resuscitation leads, training and audit before implementation.
Explains uncertainty clearly to a non-research audience and separates evidence about the intervention from local operational feasibility.

model_answer: I would start with the question, population, comparator and outcome rather than recounting the abstract. The study addresses a practical prehospital decision in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. My first validity concern is that allocation concealment is unclear. A cluster design also means patients within one ambulance service are not independent, so I would want the analysis to account for clustering. The reported crossover matters because crews allocated to one strategy may have used another, which can dilute a true effect. Unblinded outcome assessment is a further concern, although 30-day survival is less subjective than many outcomes; subsequent hospital care could still differ if teams know the allocated airway strategy. The confidence interval including no benefit means the study does not establish equivalence, and I cannot call one strategy safely superior from this result. I would inspect randomisation, baseline service characteristics, missing data, adherence and the prespecified analysis. Externally, the mix of urban and rural services helps relevance, but response times and clinician skill may differ from my region. I would compare this trial with systematic review evidence and resuscitation guidance. I would not change practice from one paper. I would discuss it with the ambulance service and resuscitation leads, identify training and governance requirements, and decide whether a monitored pilot or audit is justified. I would communicate that the evidence remains uncertain and that local standard operating procedures should stay in place until a coordinated review is complete.
references_provided: Fictional peer-reviewed practice article extract, appraisal framework and current resuscitation guideline summary.

title: Written response to a morphine overdose error
setting: Emergency department governance office with thirty minutes of protected time
candidate_instructions: Write a concise clinical and governance response to the incident. Address immediate patient care, disclosure, contributing factors and a measurable improvement plan.
materials_provided: Timeline: a 58-year-old with renal impairment was prescribed morphine 2 mg for pain. A pre-filled 10 mg syringe was selected and the full amount was intended for administration. The patient was given oxygen and naloxone after becoming drowsy, recovered fully and remains under observation. The nurse reports that two similarly packaged syringes were stored together.
task_details: Write in plain English using headings: immediate actions, duty of candour, contributing factors and actions with measures. Include a just-culture approach, a named owner for each action and a review date. Do not write a disciplinary verdict before the facts are complete.

checklist.item: States immediate ABCDE monitoring, oxygen and naloxone use according to the opioid toxicity pathway, and repeated observation of respiration and consciousness.
Reviews the patient's renal function, other sedatives, allergies, prescribed dose and response, and records the medication and adverse event clearly.

Describes prompt notification to the patient with reasonable support, a true account of the known facts, details of further enquiries and an apology, then confirms that the in-person notification is recorded securely and followed by a written notification containing the account, enquiries, their results and an apology.
Reports the incident through the local system and escalates to the nurse in charge, pharmacy and the responsible consultant.
Separates the factual timeline from assumptions and identifies individual, task, equipment, environment and organisational contributory factors.
Adopts a just-culture approach, supports the staff involved and considers whether temporary restriction, supervision or retraining is proportionate.
Proposes at least three concrete systems actions such as syringe segregation, barcode scanning, high-alert labels and a second-check point.
Gives measurable outcome, process and balancing measures with a named owner and review date rather than broad statements such as improve safety.

States how learning will be shared, how the patient will be updated and which new harm information would require reconsideration under the trust's current PSIRF patient safety incident response policy and plan.

model_answer: Immediate actions: assess the patient using ABCDE, monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, consciousness and pain, and use oxygen and naloxone according to the local opioid toxicity pathway. Repeat observations because naloxone can wear off before morphine. Review renal impairment, other sedatives, allergies, the prescribed dose and the response to treatment, and document everything. Keep the patient under monitored observation and inform the consultant, nurse in charge and pharmacy. Duty of candour: speak to the patient promptly with a senior clinician present. Explain that the intended dose was lower, what overdose occurred, what treatment was given and what surveillance is needed. I would apologise that this happened. Record the discussion and give a route for questions or follow-up. I would make a secure record of the in-person notification and send the patient a written notification containing the factual account, details of the further enquiries, their results when available and an apology. Contributing factors: record the sequence without assuming blame. Consider look-alike syringes stored together, workspace interruptions, checking process, knowledge of high-alert medicines and whether the prescription and preparation interfaces supported the error. Staff support and a just-culture assessment should start early. Actions: separate strengths and use distinct high-alert labels; add a second-check or barcode point where the workflow allows; audit high-alert syringe storage and administration. Measures: track medication errors reported, near misses, compliance with storage checks and patient harm severity, with balancing measures for delays and workflow burden. Name owners and set monthly review dates. Share the findings at governance and team meetings, update the patient and return the case to the trust's patient safety incident response process for reconsideration if new harm information or wider system risk changes the required response.
references_provided: Trust incident reporting, duty of candour and high-alert medicines policies plus the opioid toxicity pathway.

title: Recurrent falls and a very slow pulse
setting: Monitored assessment bay in a UK teaching hospital emergency department
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient, interpret the ECG in context, review medicines and agree a safe investigation and disposition plan.
materials_provided: An 84-year-old woman has had two falls with brief loss of consciousness. Observations: pulse 38/min, BP 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.3 C, SpO2 97% on air, NEWS2 3. ECG shows complete heart block with a narrow-complex junctional escape rhythm at 38/min. Medicines include bisoprolol, diltiazem and digoxin, all started in the last eight weeks. Potassium is 4.6 mmol/L.
sp_role_script: You are 84-year-old Eileen. Opening: 'I blacked out while making tea and now I feel weak. Is it just my age?' Hidden information: you had no chest pain or aura before the falls, and you recovered within seconds. Your daughter thinks the tablets have made you more tired. Disclose the medicine review only when asked about recent changes, dizziness or fatigue. You become anxious about a machine or pacemaker and want to know whether you must stay. If the candidate explains each step and reassures you that monitoring will continue, agree to admission.

checklist.item: Clarifies the collapse mechanism, warning symptoms, injury, recovery, exertional symptoms and any history of syncope or structural heart disease.
Assesses perfusion, heart sounds, postural observations when safe and signs of heart failure while avoiding a repeat fall risk.
Recognises complete heart block as a potentially unstable rhythm and requests continuous monitoring and immediate senior and cardiology review.
Requests electrolytes, renal function, glucose, full blood count and digoxin level where indicated, and checks for reversible causes.
Withholds bisoprolol, diltiazem and digoxin immediately while obtaining urgent senior, cardiology and toxicology advice, then considers whether any can be restarted after specialist review.
Explains that the falls may be caused by a conduction problem and that discharge from the emergency department is unsafe before specialist assessment.

Admits to a monitored bed, arranges repeat ECG and rhythm review, uses atropine 500 micrograms IV for adverse features and repeats it every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg, avoids atropine if the high-degree block develops a wide QRS, considers glucagon because beta-blocker or calcium-channel-blocker toxicity may contribute, and sets clear triggers for temporary pacing or urgent resuscitation.
Closes with a structured referral to cardiology, medication review after rhythm control and a plan to discuss the pacing decision with Eileen and her family.

model_answer: I would assess Eileen with continuous monitoring already in place and avoid asking her to stand until the fall risk is clear. I need to know whether she had chest pain, palpitations, aura, injury, exertion or a prolonged recovery, and whether she has previous heart failure or sudden death in the family. Her pulse is only 38/min and the ECG shows complete heart block. Even though her blood pressure is acceptable now, this is an unstable conduction problem and can deteriorate without warning. I would call the emergency medicine consultant and cardiology registrar early. I would request electrolytes, renal function, glucose, full blood count and a digoxin level where indicated. Complete heart block can occur with myocardial ischaemia, electrolyte disturbance or drug toxicity. All three medicines can depress AV conduction, so I would withhold bisoprolol, diltiazem and digoxin immediately and obtain urgent senior, cardiology and toxicology advice before considering any future restart. I would give atropine 500 micrograms IV for adverse features and repeat it every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg, while avoiding atropine if the high-degree block develops a wide QRS. I would also consider glucagon because beta-blocker or calcium-channel-blocker toxicity may contribute. Eileen needs admission to a monitored area with repeated ECG review and direct access to the resuscitation team. I would explain that a pacemaker assessment may be needed and that the medicine review comes after immediate safety. I would involve her daughter with consent. I would arrange a cardiology plan before discharge, document the monitoring and escalation triggers, and provide a clear handover to the receiving team.
references_provided: Patient medicine list, ECG printout and local bradycardia referral pathway.

title: Agitation, sweating and jerking limbs
setting: Emergency department majors area in a UK district general hospital
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient and medication history, decide whether toxidrome features are present and set out the immediate treatment and escalation plan.
materials_provided: A 36-year-old woman is agitated, sweaty and unable to sit still. Observations: pulse 124/min, BP 156/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, temperature 38.4 C, SpO2 98% on air. She has continuous ankle clonus and increased lower-limb reflexes. Medicines: sertraline increased recently, tramadol for back pain and sumatriptan for migraine. No alcohol or recreational drug use is reported. Capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L.
sp_role_script: You are Dr Mina, the medical registrar who has asked the candidate to review the patient. Opening: 'She started sertraline and then took tramadol, and now she says her legs will not stop moving.' Hidden information: symptoms began within a day of the higher sertraline dose, she has not had a seizure, there is no headache or focal weakness, and she has normal skin turgor with no history of thyroid disease. If asked, give the exact medicines and timings. Press the candidate to distinguish serotonin toxicity from infection, an antipsychotic reaction or withdrawal.

checklist.item: Establishes the exact serotonergic medicines, recent dose change, timing, other drugs, alcohol and previous adverse reactions.
Checks temperature, muscle rigidity, clonus, deep tendon reflexes, pupil size, skin findings and neurological signs while protecting the patient from harm.
Recognises the combination of serotonergic drug exposure, agitation, autonomic instability, hyperthermia and clonus as probable serotonin toxicity.
Considers and excludes other causes including infection, delirium, stimulant toxicity, serotonin withdrawal, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and thyroid disease.
Stops all contributory serotonergic medicines immediately while concurrently obtaining poisons or toxicology and senior advice.
Requests focused investigations including blood gas, renal and liver function, electrolytes, glucose and infection tests while continuing clinical monitoring.
Provides calming care, reduces stimulation, uses cooling and a locally approved sedative strategy, and avoids a medication that worsens rigidity or hyperthermia.

Escalates urgently to critical care if the temperature is at least 39 C with rigidity, altered consciousness or cardiovascular instability, or if the temperature continues to rise despite active cooling.
Closes with a monitored admission plan, a precise medication reconciliation and referral to toxicology, pharmacy or mental health as appropriate.

model_answer: I would approach this as a potentially evolving toxidrome. Mina has given me a clear medication clue: a recent sertraline increase plus tramadol. I would confirm the timing, dose, any other serotonergic medicines, over-the-counter products, recreational drugs and previous reactions. I would examine for clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity, temperature, pupil changes, sweating and mental state. Agitation, autonomic instability and lower-limb clonus after serotonergic drugs strongly suggest serotonin toxicity, but I would still consider infection, delirium, stimulant toxicity, withdrawal, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and thyroid disease. I would stop the contributing medicines immediately while seeking senior and toxicology advice, and monitor continuously. I would request blood gas, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose and focused infection tests. Treatment is mainly supportive: a calm environment, cooling, fluids and careful use of a locally approved sedative. I would avoid using a medicine that could worsen rigidity or heat generation. If her temperature reaches at least 39 C with rigidity, altered consciousness or cardiovascular instability, or continues to rise despite active cooling, critical care needs to be involved urgently for closer monitoring and possibly a controlled airway and muscle relaxation. Once she is stable, she needs a monitored admission, pharmacy-led medication reconciliation and a plan for depression treatment that avoids the same combination. I would explain the provisional diagnosis to Mina, document the discontinued medicines and set clear parameters for escalation.
references_provided: Current medicines reconciliation record and regional poisons service contact.

title: Vomiting with modestly raised glucose on an SGLT2 inhibitor
setting: Clinical decisions area in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient, interpret the acid-base picture and outline initial treatment, monitoring and specialty referral.
materials_provided: A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes empagliflozin, metformin and ramipril. He has two days of vomiting and abdominal pain. Observations: pulse 108/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, temperature 36.8 C, SpO2 98% on air, NEWS2 4. Capillary glucose 11.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas: pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L. Capillary ketones 6.2 mmol/L.
sp_role_script: You are 48-year-old Omar. Opening: 'It cannot be a diabetic emergency because my sugar is only a little high.' Hidden information: you stopped eating yesterday, have been drinking little and your empagliflozin was continued despite vomiting. You take no insulin. Disclose abdominal discomfort and reduced urine output when asked. You fear needles but will cooperate when told why tests are urgent. If the candidate explains the diagnosis without blame, agree to treatment and ask what will happen to your diabetes medicines.

checklist.item: Clarifies fluid intake, vomiting, urine output, infection symptoms, missed medicines, insulin use, recent surgery and pregnancy status if relevant.
Recognises diabetic ketoacidosis in a patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor despite modest hyperglycaemia, because glucose may be normal or only mildly raised and must not be used alone to exclude DKA.
Interprets the acid-base results alongside ketones and electrolytes and does not dismiss DKA because of the relatively modest glucose.
Starts the local adult DKA pathway with appropriate crystalloid, insulin and glucose co-administration while avoiding a premature insulin stop as glucose falls.
Monitors potassium closely, interprets the initial value in the context of renal function and acidosis, and avoids insulin if the local safe threshold is not met.
Stops the SGLT2 inhibitor during the acute illness and reviews metformin and antihypertensive treatment with senior or specialty advice.
Searches for the precipitant with focused examination, urine testing, cultures and imaging when clinically indicated, and expects a negative infection screen result.
Explains the diagnosis, insulin and glucose plan, monitoring and expected duration in plain English and invites questions.
Admits to a monitored area, requests diabetes and critical care or renal review when indicated, and states escalation triggers for cerebral or cardiovascular deterioration.

model_answer: The glucose of 11.8 mmol/L is only modestly raised and does not exclude diabetic ketoacidosis. Empagliflozin can cause ketoacidosis with only modest hyperglycaemia, especially during dehydration, vomiting, infection or reduced food intake. His pH is 7.18 and ketones are high, so I would start the local adult DKA pathway immediately. I would check renal function, a full blood count, calcium and liver tests, look for infection or another precipitant, and review all medicines. Initial treatment includes 0.9% sodium chloride, a fixed-rate insulin infusion and, because the admission glucose is below 14 mmol/L, glucose 10% at 125 mL/hour from the outset so insulin can continue safely. I would not stop insulin just because the glucose becomes normal. The potassium is 5.1 mmol/L now, but insulin and fluids will move it into cells, so repeat testing and local thresholds are critical. Empagliflozin should be stopped during the acute illness, and metformin and ramipril need review in the context of renal function and dehydration. The patient needs frequent observations, hourly glucose and ketone checks, neurological monitoring and ECG monitoring when indicated. Because ketones 6.2 mmol/L and pulse 108/min meet JBDS severity criteria, I would request urgent consultant and diabetes review and consider high dependency care now, with immediate critical care escalation if he becomes unstable or develops a reduced conscious level. He needs admission to a monitored bed. I would explain why a modestly raised glucose can still mean DKA, answer his questions without blame and give a clear plan for medicines and follow-up after recovery.
references_provided: Local adult diabetic ketoacidosis protocol, current diabetes formulary and SGLT2 inhibitor safety information.
