title: Leaving after an overdose with a suicide plan
setting: Private assessment room in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Assess immediate risk, capacity and legal options, then negotiate the safest possible plan while arranging urgent senior and mental health input.
materials_provided: A 25-year-old woman has taken a mixed overdose and has now been assessed by the emergency medicine consultant and poisons service; all required treatment and observation are complete, and she is medically cleared for mental health assessment. She is now dressed and asking to leave. She says, 'I will not stay, and nothing you do will stop me.' She has no acute intoxication and no delirium. The crisis team is busy and the emergency mental health liaison service is available by telephone.
sp_role_script: You are 25-year-old Leah. Opening: 'I took some tablets because I wanted to die. I am finished talking now.' Hidden information: you wrote a goodbye message, have dispersed of some medicines and intend to return to an isolated flat where you have another supply. You reject help initially but will listen when the candidate is calm and direct. During the capacity assessment, Leah can repeat and explain the material facts, including the risk of death, treatment and alternatives; she can retain them during the discussion, compare the options and communicate a consistent choice. Her distress affects how she presents but does not prevent her from understanding or using the information. She continues to refuse admission. If the candidate assumes incapacity just because you are distressed, become more closed. Disclose the plan and supply only when asked specifically about immediate safety.

checklist.item: Speaks calmly, acknowledges the overdose and current distress, and asks about immediate safety rather than arguing about whether Leah must stay.
Ask about the intended outcome, a specific plan, access to lethal means, the goodbye message, previous attempts, substance use and a safe place to go.
Assesses decision-specific capacity under the Mental Capacity Act and does not equate distress, an unwise decision or refusal with incapacity.
Calls senior emergency medicine and mental health liaison urgently and agrees a definitive risk-management plan rather than leaving the patient unsupervised.
Explains honestly what the team can and cannot do, offers treatment and a safe holding plan, and avoids threats or coercive language.

If immediate serious risk remains, follows the local emergency pathway and current mental health law with senior support, including police or approved mental health professional involvement where appropriate.
Arranges observation, environmental safety, medication reconciliation and transfer or review according to the agreed risk plan.
Documents the risk assessment, capacity reasoning, discussions, who was contacted and why the chosen disposition is proportionate.
Closes by naming the responsible clinician, review time, communication with the crisis team and the plan if Leah tries to leave before review.

model_answer: I would sit down, introduce myself and acknowledge that Leah has had a very difficult night. I would not begin with a warning about detention. I would ask what happened, what she intended and whether she still has thoughts of ending her life. I need to know about a specific plan, method, access to tablets or other means, a goodbye note, previous attempts, use of alcohol or drugs and where she would go. Her statement suggests immediate risk, so senior emergency medicine staff and the mental health liaison team must be involved now. I would assess decision-specific capacity under the Mental Capacity Act by explaining the risks and options in simple words, checking whether she can understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision. Distress alone does not make her incapable, but severe distress may impair her ability to use the information. I would ask her to remain for a mental health assessment and explain what the team will offer while she waits. I would not make a threat or pretend I have powers I do not have. If she has capacity and still refuses, I would document the discussion and escalate immediately to senior clinicians and the approved mental health pathway. If her risk is immediate and serious, the team should use the current legal emergency route with police or an approved mental health professional where appropriate. She needs a safe environment, close observation, removal of harmful substances where possible and a named review clinician.
references_provided: Trust self-harm and Mental Capacity Act policies, current mental health law quick-reference sheet and emergency mental health liaison contact.

title: A colleague admits a paediatric dosing mistake
setting: Quiet corridor outside a paediatric emergency department
candidate_instructions: Speak with the trainee. Protect the patient, establish the facts, respond to the professional issue and agree the incident and support plan.
materials_provided: An FY2 doctor intended to give intravenous paracetamol 180 mg (15 mg/kg) to a 12 kg child but administered 1 g after selecting the adult dose at 10:15. The child is currently well and observations are normal. The trainee has told you privately and asks you not to report it because they are already distressed.
sp_role_script: You are Dr Ben, an FY2 doctor, tearful and overwhelmed. Opening: 'Please do not tell anyone. I have learned my lesson and I will never do it again.' Hidden information: the prescribed dose was paracetamol 180 mg intravenously, but you gave 1 g at 10:15 after selecting the adult dosing column. You were distracted by two other sick children and did not ask for a second check. The child has no liver disease and took no other paracetamol. You fear that a report will end your career. If the candidate reassures without acting, remain focused on secrecy. If the candidate is direct, calm and supportive, provide the full timeline and accept the need for an incident review.

checklist.item: Confirms the patient weight, drug, prescribed dose, administered dose, timing, formulation and other paracetamol exposure.
Prioritises assessment and observation of the child and seeks senior paediatric toxology or poisons advice according to the local pathway.
Responds to Ben with calm concern and makes clear that the safety issue and possible harm cannot be kept confidential.
Escalates to the paediatric consultant and nurse in charge and starts the local incident reporting process.
Plans a duty-of-candour conversation with the family, explaining what happened, the current condition, treatment plan and how they will be updated.
Obtains a factual statement promptly and separates the calculation error from contributing factors such as distraction, supervision and checking systems.
Uses a just-culture approach, supports Ben while setting proportionate limits on further unsupervised prescribing pending senior review.
Identifies concrete learning actions such as paediatric dose checking, independent second checks and distraction controls, with owners and measures.
Closes by telling Ben who will support him, what will happen next and when the family and team will receive an update.

model_answer: I would first check the child directly and ask Ben for the exact weight, prescribed dose, volume given, timing and any other paracetamol. The immediate priority is the child, not protecting confidentiality. I would tell the paediatric consultant and nurse in charge, review the observations and seek poisons advice or a paediatric toxicology review according to local guidance. The child may need liver tests and a treatment decision based on the actual dose and timing. I would then speak with Ben calmly. I would acknowledge that he reported the mistake and is distressed, while stating clearly that I cannot keep a potential patient harm confidential. He should provide a factual statement while events are fresh and should not alter records. I would ask the family to a private conversation with a senior clinician. We would explain what was given, what is known about the risk, what monitoring or treatment will occur and when we will return. I would use a just-culture approach. The report should examine the dosing column, distraction, second-check process and supervision, not just his calculation. Until the review is complete, I would arrange proportionate senior oversight for his prescribing. Ben also needs occupational health or postgraduate support. I would close by confirming his next contact, the child's review plan and who will share learning with the department.
references_provided: Local paediatric prescribing, incident reporting and duty-of-candour policies plus paediatric poisons contact.

title: Teaching an FY1 to escalate a deteriorating patient
setting: Emergency department seminar room beside a simulated ward telephone
candidate_instructions: Teach a new FY1 how to use SBAR for a deteriorating patient. Use a brief explanation, a short role-play and teach-back.
materials_provided: Scenario notes: an 81-year-old inpatient has become more breathless after fluids. Respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 90% on air, pulse 118/min, BP 92/54 mmHg, new confusion. The FY1 has not phoned a registrar independently before.
sp_role_script: You are Dr Hannah, a nervous FY1 starting her second week. Opening: 'I know something is wrong, but I freeze when I phone the registrar.' You can list the observations but tend to start with the patient's long medical history. Hidden information: you have not rehearsed a structured call and fear being told off. If the candidate gives you a clear framework, practise answering the phone as the registrar. End by saying back what you would state first, what you would request and when you would call back.

checklist.item: Checks Hannah's experience and asks her to identify the parts of an escalation call she finds difficult.
Sets two or three clear learning objectives, including a concise opening, the current problem and a specific request.
Explains each SBAR component with an emergency medicine example and distinguishes background from the current assessment.
Highlights the abnormal observations, the likely fluid overload or deterioration and the need for an immediate bedside review.
Corrects a history-led opening and helps Hannah practise a concise statement of the patient, problem and urgency.
Uses role-play to practise the call and gives specific feedback on clarity, confidence and the request for help.
Explains when to call again, how to escalate beyond the first responder and how to document the call and response.
Uses teach-back and asks Hannah to deliver the whole SBAR without prompts.
Closes with one achievable practice goal and an offer of supervised repetition before her next shift.

model_answer: I would begin by asking Hannah what usually happens when she calls for help and which part makes her freeze. I would set three aims: recognise a deteriorating patient, use SBAR in a short call and ask clearly for a bedside review. I would explain the structure with this case. Situation: an 81-year-old inpatient has become breathless with new confusion and rising oxygen needs. Background: brief relevant history only, such as why she is in hospital and what fluids she received. Assessment: the respiratory rate is 30/min, saturation is 90% on air, pulse is 118/min, blood pressure is 92/54 mmHg and she is newly confused. I would say that I am worried about respiratory deterioration or fluid overload. Recommendation: ask the registrar to attend now, state what treatment has already been started and agree a review time. Then we would role-play the call. I would interrupt gently if she begins with the entire past medical history and ask her to start again with the immediate threat. After the role-play, I would give specific feedback on what was clear and one change to make. I would remind her to document the call, the response and any disagreement, and to call again if the patient worsens. Finally, I would ask her to repeat the SBAR without prompts and agree to observe one real call after the teaching session.
references_provided: Local deteriorating patient escalation policy, SBAR pocket card and simulation scenario.

title: A missed dialysis session and a widening ECG
setting: Resuscitation room in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Lead the immediate treatment of a patient with severe hyperkalaemia. State priorities, medication orders and the plan for definitive potassium removal.
materials_provided: A 68-year-old man missed two dialysis sessions. He is weak and drowsy. Observations: pulse 42/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on air, GCS 14. ECG shows absent P waves, a broad QRS complex and a sine-wave pattern. Point-of-care potassium is 7.6 mmol/L. The renal registrar and intensive care team are available.
sp_role_script: You are the resuscitation team. Open with: 'His ECG is changing and he is becoming harder to rouse.' Report the potassium promptly if asked. Follow clear orders and confirm when drugs are drawn up. The renal registrar can arrange urgent dialysis and the intensive care consultant is coming. If the candidate delays myocardial protection while discussing dialysis, state that the monitor is becoming more unstable.

checklist.item: Takes leadership, states that this is a hyperkalaemic peri-arrest emergency and assigns monitoring, access, drug and documentation roles.
Calls for immediate senior, renal and critical care support and prepares the defibrillator and pacing or peri-arrest equipment.
Orders intravenous calcium for myocardial membrane protection without waiting for a repeat laboratory potassium.
Orders insulin with glucose according to the local protocol and arranges close glucose monitoring after treatment.
Adds an appropriate inhaled beta-agonist and considers sodium bicarbonate only in the specific acidotic context defined by local renal guidance.
Requests urgent renal replacement therapy and treats the patient as a time-critical transfer even if initial medication improves the ECG.
Reviews potassium-raising medicines, renal function, acid-base status and the cause while avoiding repeated calcium without reassessment.
Repeats ECG and potassium at the prescribed intervals, checks for hypoglycaemia and communicates changes clearly to the team.
Closes with a clear handover, definitive disposition and explicit triggers for immediate resuscitation.

model_answer: I would recognise a peri-arrest hyperkalaemic emergency and take leadership. The team applies continuous cardiac monitoring, obtains intravenous access and prepares the defibrillator while renal and intensive care support are called now. I would give intravenous calcium immediately for myocardial protection. The ECG is changing and treatment must not wait for a repeat laboratory result. Next, I would give insulin with glucose using the local adult protocol and monitor glucose closely, because hypoglycaemia can follow. A nebulised beta-agonist can be added as a temporary measure. Sodium bicarbonate is not routine and should be considered only in the specific context described by local renal guidance. These treatments shift potassium into cells; none removes it from the body. This patient needs urgent dialysis, so the renal registrar must arrange transfer or treatment in parallel. I would stop potassium-raising medicines after review, check renal function and acid-base status and look for the cause. The QRS and potassium need repeat testing at the protocol intervals, and I would reassess the monitor after every intervention. If he develops unstable bradycardia or another peri-arrest rhythm, the team follows the current resuscitation algorithm while definitive removal is arranged. I would give a structured handover with the ECG changes, potassium, drugs and timings, and confirm the dialysis plan.
references_provided: Local adult hyperkalaemia protocol, renal replacement referral pathway and peri-arrest algorithm.

title: Motorcyclist with worsening chest trauma
setting: Major trauma resuscitation bay in a UK emergency department
candidate_instructions: Lead the primary survey. State the immediate thoracic intervention, team priorities and definitive trauma plan.
materials_provided: A 31-year-old motorcyclist was thrown over the handlebars. Observations: pulse 138/min, BP 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 36/min, SpO2 82% on 15 L oxygen, GCS 12, trachea deviated to the left, reduced right-sided air entry and distended neck veins. A major trauma centre is 20 minutes away and accepts unstable patients.
sp_role_script: You are the trauma team. Open with: 'Right chest is silent, saturations are falling and he is harder to wake.' Follow clear orders and report when the chest is exposed. If the candidate asks for a chest X-ray before decompression, state that the patient is becoming peri-arrest. Thoracostomy equipment and a chest drain are ready. The anaesthetic registrar is at the bedside and the major trauma centre is waiting for a call.

checklist.item: Takes leadership, assigns airway, chest procedure, circulation, drugs and transfer roles, and calls the trauma consultant and anaesthetist.
Recognises tension pneumothorax from the mechanism, deviated trachea, absent breath sounds, shock and severe hypoxia.
Orders immediate pleural decompression by the locally approved thoracostomy technique without waiting for imaging.
Secures the airway with cervical spine protection and prepares for rapid sequence intubation only with a clear plan for the deteriorating chest and circulation.
Requests a chest drain after decompression and reassesses air entry, oxygenation, haemodynamics and the possibility of ongoing bleeding.
Activates major haemorrhage if indicated, obtains access and blood products, and avoids large fluid boluses that could worsen thoracic bleeding.
Searches for other life-threatening chest injuries including haemothorax, flail chest, cardiac injury and major vessel injury after the first intervention.
Uses closed-loop communication and keeps a procedural pause if the airway plan conflicts with immediate chest decompression.
Gives an early major trauma centre transfer request with the mechanism, physiology, interventions and estimated arrival time.

model_answer: This patient has a clinical tension pneumothorax and is peri-arrest. I would take leadership, tell the team the working diagnosis immediately and ask one clinician to decompress the chest using the locally approved thoracostomy technique. I would not wait for a chest X-ray. Oxygen continues while the right chest is exposed and monitoring is applied. Another team member prepares a chest drain and airway equipment. The anaesthetist needs to know that positive-pressure ventilation can worsen an untreated tension pneumothorax. I would secure the airway with cervical spine protection only after or alongside immediate decompression, using a clear shared plan rather than allowing two procedures to collide. After decompression, the team reassesses breath sounds, saturation, blood pressure and chest movement. The chest drain is placed next and connected safely. I would activate the major haemorrhage protocol if shock persists and arrange blood products while limiting unmeasured crystalloid. Once the first thoracic threat is controlled, I would look for haemothorax, flail segment, cardiac injury or ongoing bleeding and consider chest imaging only when it will change management. The major trauma centre should receive an early transfer request with the physiology and procedures. My disposition is direct transfer to the major trauma centre once the airway, chest and haemorrhage plan are secure, with a structured handover of times and responses.
references_provided: Trust major trauma and chest trauma pathways plus regional trauma network transfer guidance.

title: Postpartum sepsis with rising oxygen needs
setting: Resuscitation room in a UK emergency department with obstetric support available
candidate_instructions: Lead the initial resuscitation of a woman who is unwell after childbirth. State priorities, investigations and the obstetric and critical care escalation plan.
materials_provided: A 29-year-old woman is five days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. She has fever, vomiting and abdominal pain. Observations: pulse 136/min, BP 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, temperature 39.2 C, SpO2 91% on air, capillary refill 4 seconds, GCS 14. Blood gas shows lactate 5.4 mmol/L. The obstetric registrar and critical care team are available.
sp_role_script: You are the resuscitation team. Opening: 'She delivered five days ago, has a rash on her abdomen and is becoming confused.' Follow clear orders and report the observations when asked. If the candidate asks about vaginal loss, describe heavy, offensive lochia. If asked about the baby, say the baby is safe at home with a relative. Point out if the candidate fails to call obstetrics. The critical care team will come urgently once asked.

checklist.item: Takes leadership, assigns roles and calls the obstetric registrar, critical care and senior emergency medicine clinician early.
Recognises septic shock in a recently postpartum woman and considers uterine sepsis, retained products, wound infection and other obstetric sources.
Applies high-flow oxygen to the appropriate target, obtains monitoring and urgent intravenous access, and requests point-of-care blood gas and glucose.

Starts broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics from the current sepsis and obstetric pathway within 1 hour of identifying high-risk sepsis, taking cultures first only when this will not delay treatment.

Gives a 500 mL sodium-containing crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes within 1 hour of identifying high-risk sepsis, then reassesses perfusion, lungs and mental state; gives a second bolus only if there is no improvement and alerts a consultant to attend in person if there is no improvement after the second.
Requests blood cultures, full blood count, renal and liver tests, clotting, lactate and imaging or obstetric examination guided by the source.
Involves critical care for vasopressor support if perfusion does not improve, while minimising delay to antibiotics and source control.
Explains the current concern and treatment plan to the patient in short sentences and checks understanding while she is confused.
Closes with a monitored high-dependency disposition, obstetric source-control plan and structured team handover including the baby's safety.

model_answer: I would take leadership and say that this is suspected septic shock in a woman who gave birth five days ago. The team applies high-flow oxygen to the appropriate target, monitoring and large-bore intravenous access while obstetrics and critical care are called now. I would examine for uterine tenderness, heavy or offensive lochia, abdominal wall infection, breast infection and respiratory signs, but treatment must begin immediately. I would give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics from the current sepsis and obstetric pathway within 1 hour of identifying high-risk sepsis; blood cultures must not delay them. Because she has recently been pregnant and meets high-risk criteria with a lactate above 4 mmol/L and systolic pressure below 90 mmHg, I would also give a 500 mL sodium-containing crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes within 1 hour. I would reassess perfusion, respiratory status and mental state after the first bolus, give a second bolus only if there is no improvement, and alert a consultant to attend in person if there is no improvement after the second. I would request blood gas, lactate, full blood count, renal and liver tests, clotting and cultures. The obstetric team needs to assess for uterine sepsis, retained products or another source that may require urgent treatment. If her blood pressure remains inadequate after careful fluids, critical care should start vasopressor support according to the local pathway. She needs a high-dependency bed and continuous monitoring. I would explain to her what is happening while repeatedly checking orientation, and ask about the baby's care and safeguarding support. The disposition includes obstetric source control, intensive care review and a clear handover of antibiotics, fluids, lactate and the response to treatment.
references_provided: Current UK sepsis guidance, local maternity sepsis pathway and maternity early warning chart.

title: Open tibial fracture after a farm fall
setting: Emergency department procedure room in a rural UK hospital
candidate_instructions: Demonstrate the immediate wound, splinting, antibiotic and referral plan for this open fracture. State what you would document and how you would arrange transfer.
materials_provided: A 44-year-old farmer fell from a trailer. There is a 6 cm wound over the anterior tibia with exposed bone and mud contamination. Distal pulses are present, sensation is reduced over the first web space, and there is active bleeding controlled by direct pressure. X-ray shows a displaced tibial shaft fracture. The regional orthoplastic centre is 70 minutes away.
sp_role_script: You are the patient and procedure assistant. Opening: 'The bone came through and there is dirt everywhere. Am I going to lose my leg?' Report severe pain and state that your hand feels numb when asked. Remind the candidate to check pulses and sensation before and after splinting. If the candidate starts repeated wound cleaning without analgesia or a plan for theatre, say you cannot tolerate it.
task_details: Show how you would cover and splint the limb, state the initial medication considerations using local guidance, and give a clear handover to the receiving orthoplastic team.

checklist.item: Records the wound size, contamination, exposed bone, distal pulses, capillary refill, motor function and sensation before and after splinting.
Controls bleeding with direct pressure, removes visible loose debris without repeated aggressive irrigation and covers the wound with a sterile saline-soaked dressing.
Provides effective analgesia and applies a well-padded splint that stabilises the fracture without worsening the wound or neurovascular status.
Recognises that this highly contaminated open tibial fracture requires immediate surgical wound excision by the combined orthoplastic service and escalates without delay.

Gives intravenous prophylactic antibiotics immediately if not already given, without waiting for imaging, wound cleaning or transfer, after checking allergies and renal function, and completes tetanus risk assessment using the local open-fracture regimen.
Documents the time of injury, time of antibiotic, wound findings, neurovascular status and imaging, and arranges immediate transfer or local theatre according to the pathway.
Keeps the patient nil by mouth, arranges group and save, imaging and monitoring, and avoids unnecessary dressing changes before specialist review.
Explains the risk of infection and compartment syndrome, the need for surgery and the transfer plan in clear language.
Gives the receiving orthoplastic team a structured handover and names the person responsible for updating the patient and family.

model_answer: I would first control bleeding with direct pressure and give effective analgesia. I would examine the wound without probing it repeatedly, record its size and contamination, and document pulses, capillary refill, movement and sensation. The reduced sensation over the first web space is an important neurovascular finding. I would remove only loose debris and cover the wound with a sterile saline-soaked dressing. I would immobilise the leg with a well-padded splint in a safe position, then repeat the full neurovascular examination. The patient needs intravenous prophylactic antibiotics immediately, without waiting for imaging or transfer, with allergies, renal function and tetanus status checked and the local open-fracture regimen used. This is a high-energy open tibial fracture with heavy soil contamination, so I would call the senior emergency clinician and regional orthoplastic service immediately. Because this wound is highly contaminated, it requires immediate surgical wound excision. I would arrange direct transfer to the orthoplastic theatre pathway rather than plan delayed cleaning or debridement. I would not delay transfer for repeated cleaning or dressing changes. I would arrange group and save, appropriate imaging, nil-by-mouth status and close monitoring for compartment syndrome. The regional centre should receive an early call with the wound, neurovascular findings, fracture pattern and antibiotic time. If immediate transfer is not possible, the local orthopaedic and theatre teams need to agree a safe interim plan. I would explain the infection risk, nerve symptoms, operation and transfer in plain words, keep the patient informed and give a structured handover naming who will update the family.
references_provided: Local open fracture pathway, current antibiotic and tetanus guidance and orthoplastic transfer contact sheet.

title: A head injury while taking apixaban
setting: CT-ready major trauma area in a UK district general hospital
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient and carer concerns, arrange time-critical imaging and set out the neurosurgical and reversal plan without waiting for repeated observations.
materials_provided: A 79-year-old woman fell at home and hit her head. She vomited twice and has become more confused. Observations: pulse 88/min, BP 162/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on air, GCS 14, capillary glucose 6.4 mmol/L. She takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. CT is available now and the nearest neurosurgical unit is 45 minutes away. No focal weakness is present.
sp_role_script: You are the patient's son, sitting beside her. Opening: 'She said she felt fine at first, but she has been sick and keeps asking the same question.' Hidden information: she lives alone, has had a previous fall and took apixaban this morning. She has no known dementia and is usually fully independent. If asked, you can provide her medication list and baseline function. You are worried about bleeding and want to know whether the blood thinner antidote is needed. Do not disclose the repeated questions unless the candidate asks the son for a collateral history.

checklist.item: Obtains the mechanism, time of injury, loss of consciousness, vomiting, seizure, headache and baseline cognition from the son.
Assesses airway, breathing, circulation, GCS, pupils, focal neurology, scalp injury and cervical spine risk while protecting the airway.
Recognises that age, anticoagulation, vomiting and reduced GCS create a high risk of intracranial bleeding and requests immediate CT.
Does not wait for a second GCS observation or routine clotting results before urgent imaging, and arranges continuous neurological monitoring during transfer.
Contacts haematology and the regional neurosurgical team early and discusses reversal only with the imaging result and local major haemorrhage protocol.
Requests evidence of the last apixaban dose, renal function, full blood count and clotting in parallel with CT, and avoids assuming a normal routine test excludes drug effect.
Arranges repeat GCS and pupil checks, escalation for vomiting, headache or neurological decline and a monitored environment.
Explains to the son what findings are being looked for, why the blood thinner matters and that treatment decisions depend on the scan and specialist advice.
Closes with an admission and transfer decision, a neurosurgical callback time and a plan for observation and family updates.

model_answer: I would treat this as a high-risk head injury. Age, apixaban, vomiting and a reduced GCS all increase the chance of an intracranial bleed. I would check airway, breathing, circulation, GCS, pupils, focal neurology and the cervical spine while obtaining collateral history from her son about the mechanism, timing, loss of consciousness and her baseline thinking. She is usually independent, so the repeated questions are a real change. I would arrange immediate CT of the head and, where indicated, the cervical spine. I would not wait for another GCS observation or routine blood results before imaging. During transfer, a trained staff member should monitor consciousness, pupils, breathing and blood pressure. In parallel I would request full blood count, renal function and clotting, establish the last apixaban dose and contact haematology and the regional neurosurgical unit. Reversal should not be given blindly; it depends on the scan, bleeding severity, renal function, timing of the last dose and the local major haemorrhage protocol. If imaging shows an intracranial haemorrhage, the neurosurgical and haematology teams need an urgent joint plan and possible transfer. She needs a monitored admission and repeated neurological observations even if the first scan is reassuring. I would explain to her son what we are looking for, why the medicine matters and when the next update will come.
references_provided: Current UK head injury guidance, local major haemorrhage and anticoagulant reversal pathways, and neurosurgical transfer contact.

title: A toddler who may have swallowed a button battery
setting: Paediatric emergency department in a UK hospital with no paediatric gastroenterology service
candidate_instructions: Assess the child, arrange the immediate investigation and discuss the transfer and treatment plan with the parent.
materials_provided: A 20-month-old has been drooling and refusing food after playing with a remote control. The child is alert, has normal saturations, normal work of breathing and a temperature of 36.8 C. The parent found the battery compartment open but is not certain whether a battery is missing. Weight is 11 kg. A chest X-ray is immediately available.
sp_role_script: You are the anxious parent. Opening: 'She was only out of my sight for a minute. Could it be stuck?' Hidden information: the remote uses a shiny disc battery, the child has no breathing difficulty and no known allergies. You feel guilty and frightened. If the candidate asks about the child's swallowing, say she is refusing even water. If asked about transport, ask why the child cannot simply wait for the battery to pass. Warm to the candidate when they explain the plan honestly and include you in decisions.

checklist.item: Treats a possible button battery ingestion as a time-critical emergency and confirms the child's airway, breathing, circulation and ability to swallow.
Arranges immediate AP radiographs of the neck, chest and abdomen, with a lateral view if an oesophageal battery is suspected, to locate the battery rather than relying on history alone.
States that a battery in the oesophagus or airway requires endoscopic or specialist removal within 2 hours of presentation, even if the child appears stable.
Calls the paediatric consultant, anaesthetist, regional gastroenterology or ENT service and poisons or specialist advice immediately.

Keeps the child nil by mouth except for protocol-directed honey or sucralfate when an oesophageal battery is confirmed and the child meets the local age, timing and safety criteria; avoids inducing vomiting and uses age and weight-appropriate monitoring and comfort measures.
Explains that a stable appearance does not exclude mucosal injury and that delay can cause perforation or airway injury.
Reassures the parent without blame, explains the imaging result and includes them in the transfer decision.
Arranges urgent retrieval or transfer to a centre able to remove the battery and gives a structured handover of time, findings and fasting status.
Gives clear safety advice about batteries in the home, follow-up and returning symptoms, and confirms the parent knows who will update them.

model_answer: A possible swallowed button battery is a time-critical emergency, even when the child looks well. I would assess airway, breathing, circulation and swallowing, keep the child calm and attach monitoring as appropriate. I would ask the parent to bring the device or packaging if it is available and confirm the battery size. I would arrange immediate AP radiographs of the neck, chest and abdomen, adding a lateral view if an oesophageal battery is suspected. If the battery is in the oesophagus or airway, the child needs endoscopic or specialist removal within 2 hours of presentation, even if they look well; I would not observe or delay for fasting. I would call the paediatric consultant, anaesthetist, regional gastroenterology or ENT service and specialist poisons advice now. If imaging confirms an oesophageal battery, ingestion was less than 12 hours ago, and there is no perforation or contraindication, I would give commercial honey 10 mL every 10 minutes for up to 6 doses while arranging endoscopic removal within 2 hours. The honey must not delay removal or transfer. Otherwise, I would keep the child nil by mouth, and I would not induce vomiting or give food or drink to try to move the battery. A stable appearance does not exclude a burn or perforation risk. I would explain to the parent that the battery can cause injury quickly and that transfer is needed even if the child seems comfortable. The local team would arrange retrieval or transfer to a centre able to remove it, with a handover of time, imaging and fasting status. If the battery has already passed into the stomach, management still requires specialist advice because size, symptoms and imaging findings affect the plan. I would give prevention advice, document the discussion and confirm follow-up.
references_provided: Current UK button battery ingestion guidance, paediatric observation chart and regional retrieval contact.

title: First ten minutes of a bus collision major incident
setting: Emergency department command desk after a multi-casualty bus collision
candidate_instructions: Act as the initial emergency department commander. Set up the response, allocate resources and give the first structured briefing.
materials_provided: Ambulance control reports at least 12 casualties, including two critical adults and one child, arriving over the next 15 minutes. The department has three resuscitation bays, one paediatric resuscitation space and no free inpatient beds. The major incident plan and trust command contact list are available.
sp_role_script: You are the hospital site manager and the nurse in charge. Opening: 'Ambulance control says twelve casualties and the first vehicle is four minutes away. What do you need?' Hidden information: two operating theatres are available, radiology can provide major trauma imaging, and the executive on call is waiting for a decision. Challenge vague instructions and ask for named roles, triage location and a communication route. Follow clear task allocation and report back when tasks are complete.

checklist.item: Declares activation under the local major incident plan, states the command role and appoints named leads for triage, resuscitation, paediatrics, flow and communication.
Establishes a receiving and triage area separate from the normal walking wounded stream and protects access for emergency vehicles.
Prioritises immediate life threats and a reliable casualty count over definitive diagnosis, and uses the recognised triage system specified by the plan.
Allocates resuscitation, paediatric, radiology, theatre and inpatient capacity with a clear plan for patients already in the department.
Gives a short briefing with the incident, expected casualties, roles, communication channel and time for the next update.
Contacts the executive on call, specialty leads and blood bank, and agrees escalation triggers for mutual aid or diverting routine activity.
Assigns a scribe and tracks casualties by unique identifier, location, triage category and time without relying on memory.
Protects staff safety, security and infection control while allowing rapid assessment of contaminated or distressed casualties.
Closes with a command rhythm, a specified information update time and a plan for staff welfare, debrief and family liaison.

model_answer: I would activate the major incident plan and state clearly that I am taking the initial emergency department commander role. The first vehicle is minutes away, so the priority is to prepare a safe receiving system before patients arrive. I would appoint a triage lead, resuscitation lead, paediatric lead, flow lead and communications scribe. The walking wounded stream must be separated from priority casualties, and ambulance access must remain clear. A unique casualty log will track identifiers, arrival times, triage categories, locations and interventions. I would use the triage system specified in the plan and prioritise life threats rather than complete diagnoses. I would speak to the site manager and executive on call about freeing resuscitation space, theatre capacity, radiology and inpatient beds. The blood bank and major trauma and paediatric teams need early warning. I would brief the team using a short structure: what happened, how many casualties, where they are going, who is leading each area and how information will flow. Staff must know when the next update will occur and how to escalate. Security, staff safety and family liaison also need named leads. I would set a review interval and immediately escalate if casualty numbers or acuity exceed capacity. The response closes with controlled handovers, a shared casualty board and a structured debrief after the acute phase.
references_provided: Trust major incident plan, hospital command contact list, triage cards and casualty tracking form.

title: Reviewing a missed pulmonary embolism
setting: Emergency department governance meeting room
candidate_instructions: Lead the initial patient safety incident response discussion using the trust's current PSIRF policy and plan. Separate facts from assumptions, identify contributory factors and agree immediate, proportionate and longer-term actions.
materials_provided: A 57-year-old was discharged with pleuritic chest pain and a normal chest X-ray. They returned two days later with a cardiac arrest and died from a pulmonary embolism. The initial note recorded no leg swelling, but the patient later reported calf pain. A Wells score and D-dimer pathway were available but not used. The clinician was covering two areas during a staffing gap.
sp_role_script: You are the clinical governance lead. Opening: 'The family want answers and the junior doctor is frightened. Where do we start?' Hidden information: the electronic notes show a delayed triage time, the radiology report was available but not opened, and there is no evidence of an unsafe clinician pattern. Ask the candidate to explain how they will uphold duty of candour and just culture. Push back if the proposed actions are only teaching or only individual blame.

checklist.item: Confirms the case has been routed through the trust's current patient safety incident response policy and plan, agrees the proportionate learning response required and assigns who will contact and support the family.
Plans an honest duty-of-candour discussion with the family, including an apology for what happened and clear limits on what is not yet known.
Builds a factual timeline from triage, assessment, tests, radiology, discharge and return, and separates documented facts from recollections and assumptions.
Reviews the index presentation against the current PE pathway, including risk assessment, diagnostic testing, documentation and safety-netting.
Identifies contributory factors across staffing, workload, supervision, clinical reasoning, information technology and communication without a predetermined individual verdict.
Confirms the clinician has support and representation and applies a just-culture assessment based on systems and behaviour rather than outcome severity.
Proposes immediate actions such as a supervised review of similar recent cases, checks of unopened radiology results and an escalation plan for staffing gaps.
Sets outcome, process and balancing measures for the improvement plan and assigns named owners and review dates.
Closes with a learning-sharing plan, a scheduled family update and a defined trigger for broader regional or national learning.

model_answer: I would start by checking that the case has been reported and routed through the trust's current PSIRF patient safety incident response policy and plan, that agreement has been reached on the proportionate learning response required, and that the family has a named senior contact. The family should receive an early, honest duty-of-candour conversation: what is currently known, what remains under review, an apology for the loss and a commitment to update them. I would separate the review into a factual timeline: triage, clinical assessment, chest X-ray, radiology review, discharge and return. Only after the facts are clear would I examine clinical reasoning against the PE pathway. The missing Wells assessment, calf pain, delayed triage and unopened result all matter, but I would not decide in advance that one clinician caused the death. Contributory factors may include staffing gaps, two-area working, supervision, handover, information technology and documentation. The junior doctor needs support, representation and a just-culture assessment based on conduct and systems, not simply the severity of the outcome. Immediate safety actions should protect current patients: review comparable recent discharges, confirm how unopened results are escalated and create a plan for unsafe staffing gaps. Longer-term actions could include pathway prompts, education, a supervision standard and an audit of PE assessments. Each needs an owner, a measure and a review date. I would track process measures such as PE risk assessment and outcome measures such as missed diagnoses, while checking for unintended delays.
references_provided: Trust patient safety incident response, duty-of-candour and just-culture policies plus the current local PE diagnostic pathway.

title: Critical appraisal of a conservative oxygen trial
setting: Quiet appraisal room beside the emergency department
candidate_instructions: Discuss the internal validity, external validity and practice implications of the supplied fictional trial. Do not summarise the article and do not perform calculations.
materials_provided: A fictional practice abstract reports a multicentre randomised trial in 3,000 adults with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Participants received either titrated oxygen to a target saturation range or unrestricted oxygen when not hypoxic. The primary outcome was a composite of death, reinfarction and stroke at 30 days. The composite result had a confidence interval that crossed no effect. Oxygen use before randomisation varied, staff could not be blinded and 8% of participants were lost to follow-up for the primary outcome.
sp_role_script: You are the examiner facilitating a guided appraisal. Opening: 'Focus on the questions that determine whether this trial could change your care. I will ask you not to provide a summary.' If the candidate describes the methods in sequence without judging them, ask what specific bias or relevance problem matters. Ask about composite outcomes, non-blinding, missing outcomes and transportability to the emergency department. Later ask what local monitoring or implementation issue would still need solving if the result were convincing.

checklist.item: Identifies the primary comparison, population, intervention, target oxygen strategy and primary outcome in PICO terms.
Assesses randomisation, allocation concealment, baseline differences and whether the intervention was delivered as intended.
Explains how lack of blinding could influence co-interventions, decision-making or assessment of components of the composite outcome.
Recognises that an imprecise composite result crossing no effect cannot establish superiority or equivalence and considers the individual components.
Discusses the 8% loss to follow-up and asks whether missing patients could alter the result, particularly if missingness differs by group.
Considers whether the trial population, oxygen targets, monitors and usual emergency care match the local setting.
Separates patients who are hypoxic and require oxygen from the trial population and avoids applying the result indiscriminately.
States that guideline review, multidisciplinary discussion and audit are needed before changing oxygen practice.
Explains the strength and limits of the evidence to colleagues using clear language and identifies what additional evidence could change the decision.

model_answer: I would judge the trial against the exact question: in adults with suspected acute coronary syndrome who are not hypoxic, does titrated oxygen compared with unrestricted oxygen change important outcomes? The population and target range need checking because the result does not apply to a patient who is already hypoxic. I would inspect allocation concealment, baseline characteristics and evidence that the two oxygen strategies were actually delivered. Staff could not be blinded, which can affect co-treatment, decisions and assessment of some composite outcomes. I would examine the components of death, reinfarction and stroke rather than treating the composite as one simple result. A confidence interval crossing no effect means the study is compatible with benefit and harm. It does not prove equivalence. The 8% missing primary outcomes also needs attention, especially if missingness differs between groups. For external validity, I would ask whether the trial settings, response times and monitoring match my department. The practical question would be whether oxygen titration can be delivered consistently without causing desaturation or extra staff burden. I would not change local practice from one imprecise trial. I would compare it with systematic review evidence and current guidance, ask the oxygen and cardiology leads to review it and consider whether the local protocol clearly distinguishes hypoxic from non-hypoxic patients. If a change is considered, I would support education and audit with balancing measures.
references_provided: Fictional peer-reviewed practice article extract, critical-appraisal checklist and current oxygen prescribing standard.

title: Written research proposal for an ED syncope pathway
setting: Emergency department research office with protected writing time
candidate_instructions: Write a concise proposal for a study evaluating a new emergency department syncope assessment pathway. Include the question, design, outcomes, data plan, ethics and feasibility.
materials_provided: The department sees about 140 adult syncope presentations each month. A new structured assessment and follow-up pathway is being considered. Current practice varies between clinicians and there is concern about both unsafe discharge and unnecessary admission. No additional research funding is confirmed.
task_details: Use headings: research question, design and population, intervention and comparator, outcomes, data and analysis, ethics and safety, feasibility and governance. State one primary outcome and no more than three secondary outcomes. Do not promise a result or claim that the pathway is effective before evaluation.

checklist.item: States a focused research question naming the adult ED population, syncope pathway, usual care comparator and main outcome.
Chooses a feasible design such as a prospective implementation study, stepped rollout or interrupted time series and explains why it fits.
Defines eligibility and exclusion criteria, including whether high-risk presentations and patients unable to consent are handled separately.
Names one patient-important primary outcome and a small set of secondary outcomes covering safety, flow or resource use.
Describes data sources, definitions, missing data, confounding, sample-size or precision considerations and a statistical analysis plan.
Includes safety monitoring for missed serious diagnoses, 30-day serious outcomes and early readmission, with a prespecified stopping or review trigger.
Addresses ethics, consent, confidentiality, data protection and the role of patients or public contributors in the design.
Describes feasibility factors including staff training, information technology, research support, funding and a pilot phase.
Names governance approvals, the responsible sponsor or lead and the process for reporting and implementing findings without overclaiming.

model_answer: Research question: among adults presenting to the emergency department with syncope, does a structured assessment and follow-up pathway compared with usual care reduce a patient-important adverse outcome without increasing avoidable admission? Design and population: I would start with a prospective, two-phase implementation study covering consecutive adults with a documented syncope presentation. I would exclude patients already in an alternative critical care pathway and define how patients without capacity or repeat attenders are handled. Intervention and comparator: the pathway would include a standard risk assessment, senior review, documented safety advice and a defined follow-up route. Usual care would be the current clinician-led process during a baseline phase. Outcomes: the primary outcome would be a composite of death, serious recurrent arrhythmia, major haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism or stroke within 30 days. Secondary outcomes would be unplanned admission, readmission and pathway compliance. Data and analysis: I would use clinical records, imaging and outcome linkage, prespecify definitions and missing-data handling, and design the study with a statistician. A stepped rollout or interrupted time series could reduce contamination, but the final design depends on site capacity. I would present estimates with confidence intervals and avoid causal certainty from weak designs. Ethics and safety: approvals would cover consent, confidentiality and data protection, with an independent safety review of 30-day serious outcomes. Feasibility and governance: staff training, electronic prompts, data collection and follow-up need a lead. I would run a pilot with audit before seeking wider adoption.
references_provided: National research ethics guidance, local information-governance policy and the department's syncope audit summary.

title: Severe headache at 34 weeks
setting: Obstetric assessment bay in a district general emergency department, with a midwife present and immediate access to the maternity unit.
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient, decide whether this is a hypertensive emergency in pregnancy, begin safe initial management, and agree a clear plan with her and the maternity team.
materials_provided: Blood pressure 176/112 mmHg on two readings five minutes apart. Urine protein to creatinine ratio 52 mg/mmol. Platelets 90 x 10^9/L, ALT 136 U/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L. Fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute. The patient is 34 weeks and 2 days pregnant and has had no seizure.
sp_role_script: You are 34 weeks pregnant. Open with: 'This headache started yesterday, but now the lights are flashing and the pain is unbearable.' You also have epigastric pain and feel sick. You are frightened about being admitted because nobody can collect your six year old from school. Disclose the visual symptoms and epigastric pain if asked. Reassure readily once the candidate explains the risks, but ask who will help with childcare. You have not taken cocaine or missed antihypertensive medicines.

checklist.item: Recognises severe hypertension with neurological and hepatic features as possible severe pre-eclampsia rather than treating it as migraine.
Requests senior obstetric and anaesthetic involvement early and arranges continuous maternal and fetal monitoring.
States the need for controlled blood pressure reduction and magnesium seizure prophylaxis using the local maternity protocol.
Explains the immediate risk to mother and baby in short, plain sentences without causing unnecessary alarm.
Asks about childcare and other barriers, then activates an appropriate social or family solution.
Checks the patient's understanding and agreement before transfer to the maternity unit.
Sequences urgent blood tests, treatment, maternity review and transfer without waiting for every result.
Documents a clear disposition, monitoring plan and escalation trigger for seizure, worsening blood pressure or fetal compromise.

model_answer: This presentation suggests severe pre-eclampsia: blood pressure above 160/110 mmHg, new visual symptoms, epigastric pain, proteinuria and abnormal platelets and liver tests. I would call the obstetric registrar and anaesthetic team now, place the patient in a monitored obstetric area, continue maternal observations and obtain a ctg. I would treat the blood pressure promptly with an agent from the local obstetric protocol, avoiding a rapid uncontrolled fall, and start magnesium seizure prophylaxis if the maternity protocol indicates it. I would take blood for full blood count, renal and liver function, coagulation and group and save, monitor urine output and watch for HELLP syndrome. I would explain that the headache and flashing lights may be caused by a dangerous pregnancy complication and that admission is needed for treatment and close observation. I would ask who can care for her child and involve the emergency department social worker or maternity team if a practical plan cannot be made quickly. Treatment and assessment should continue while that is arranged. Disposition is transfer to the maternity unit for consultant obstetric review and likely delivery planning. I would document the diagnosis, treatment times, transfer handover and escalation triggers for seizure, severe hypertension, reduced consciousness or abnormal fetal trace.
references_provided: Local maternity hypertension and pre-eclampsia pathway; obstetric early warning chart; sample group and save form.

title: Fever after chemotherapy
setting: Ambulatory oncology assessment area adjacent to a UK emergency department.
candidate_instructions: Take a focused history, identify the immediate priorities, and organise treatment and referral for this unwell patient.
materials_provided: Temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius, respiratory rate 22/min, heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, oxygen saturation 96% on air, NEWS2 5. Chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma finished eight days ago. Absolute neutrophil count from this morning is 0.3 x 10^9/L.
sp_role_script: You feel shivery, sick and weak. Open with: 'I was told to come straight in if I became hot, and now I cannot stop shaking.' You have had one episode of vomiting, mild sore throat and no diarrhoea. You do not know which chemotherapy drugs you had, but you have a treatment card. Show the card when asked. Deny chest pain and rash. You become anxious when the word sepsis is used, so ask whether this is life threatening and what will happen next.

checklist.item: Establishes the chemotherapy regimen and date, recent steroids, allergies, previous reactions and current antimicrobial prophylaxis.
Asks specifically about fever timing, rigors, respiratory symptoms, mouth or skin breaches, diarrhoea and line symptoms.
Recognises neutropenic sepsis as an emergency even though the NEWS2 score is not very high.
Plans cultures, lactate, blood gas, blood count, biochemistry and imaging without delaying antibiotics.
Selects anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam therapy in line with the local neutropenic sepsis pathway and documents allergy status.
Contacts oncology or haematology and critical care outreach early enough for central access, antimicrobial advice and possible level 2 care.
Explains the urgent treatment plan honestly and checks what the patient has understood.
Sets a clear review interval and escalation plan while confirming that admission is required.

model_answer: This is suspected neutropenic sepsis. A temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.3 x 10^9/L and a recent lymphoma treatment is a time-critical emergency, even though the NEWS2 score is only moderately raised. I would place the patient in a monitored area, take blood cultures from peripheral and line sites before antibiotics when this causes no delay, and send lactate, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver tests, coagulation and a blood gas. I would give an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam recommended by the local neutropenic sepsis pathway promptly, after checking penicillin allergy, renal function and recent microbiology. I would also give fluids according to repeated assessment rather than a single fixed volume and review oxygen needs. I would contact haematology and critical care outreach immediately, request a chest radiograph if respiratory signs are present, and search for a source including skin, mouth, abdomen and the central line. I would explain that the immune system cannot currently fight infection well and that admission, intravenous treatment and observation are needed. Disposition is admission under oncology or haematology with a clear review time, sepsis reassessment, and escalation for rising oxygen requirement, hypotension, confusion or oliguria.
references_provided: Local neutropenic sepsis antimicrobial pathway; patient chemotherapy alert card; NEWS2 chart.

title: Breathless after missed dialysis
setting: Emergency department side room with access to a dialysis liaison service and critical care outreach.
candidate_instructions: Assess the cause of breathlessness, identify the immediate risks, and arrange safe treatment and destination.
materials_provided: A 59 year old haemodialysis patient missed two sessions after transport failed. Weight has risen by 4 kg. Respiratory rate 28/min, oxygen saturation 87% on air, blood pressure 188/102 mmHg, heart rate 96/min. Bibasal crackles and raised jugular venous pressure. ECG shows peaked T waves. Potassium 5.9 mmol/L, creatinine 790 micromol/L, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'I cannot get my breath lying down and my usual dialysis transport never came.' You feel exhausted and frightened. You use two pillows at home and have reduced urine output. You cannot remember all medicines and have brought a tablet bag. Disclose missed sessions and access to a fistula if asked. You ask to sit upright and become anxious when told an emergency treatment is needed.

checklist.item: Links fluid overload, hyperkalaemia and acidosis with missed dialysis rather than treating breathlessness as a new respiratory illness.
Positions the patient upright, gives titrated oxygen and uses non-invasive ventilation if clinically indicated by the local pathway.
Requests immediate ECG and repeat potassium while protecting the fistula arm from blood pressure measurement and venepuncture if avoidable.
Starts urgent hyperkalaemia treatment according to the ECG and potassium result, including calcium if ECG changes are present.
Contacts renal services for emergency dialysis and critical care outreach for possible ventilatory support.
Avoids large fluid boluses and reviews medicines for additional potassium load or nephrotoxicity.
Explains the need for emergency dialysis in plain language and allows the patient to ask questions.
States a monitored disposition with repeat observations, potassium checks and a named clinician responsible for renal transfer.

model_answer: The likely problem is severe fluid overload and hyperkalaemia after missed dialysis. I would sit the patient upright, give titrated oxygen and start CPAP or non-invasive ventilation for persistent hypoxia or severe respiratory distress if he is alert and can protect his airway. I would call critical care immediately. If he develops respiratory exhaustion, reduced consciousness, inability to protect his airway or NIV fails, I would proceed to tracheal intubation and invasive ventilation. I would attach monitoring and obtain an immediate ECG. The fistula arm should be protected from blood pressure cuffs and avoidable needle use. I would send urgent gas, potassium, renal function and full blood count, then treat hyperkalaemia promptly. Calcium is needed if there are ECG changes; insulin with glucose, nebulised salbutamol and other measures should follow the local hyperkalaemia protocol with repeated glucose and potassium checks. I would avoid large crystalloid boluses because this patient is fluid overloaded. I would call renal services immediately for emergency dialysis and critical care outreach for support with hypoxia, ventilation and monitoring. I would explain that missed dialysis has caused fluid and potassium to build up and that dialysis is the definitive treatment. If transfer is delayed, I would agree a clear holding plan and repeat observations. Disposition is a monitored critical care area or renal high dependency bed with continuous cardiac monitoring and rapid renal review. I would document treatment times, review status and escalation triggers.
references_provided: Local hyperkalaemia treatment chart; renal unit contact sheet; NEWS2 chart.

title: Overdose and a request to leave
setting: A quiet assessment room in the emergency department with access to liaison psychiatry and the local poisons service.
candidate_instructions: Assess capacity and immediate risk, explain the need for treatment, and manage the patient's request to leave safely.
materials_provided: A 19 year old presents three hours after taking an unknown number of paracetamol tablets and drinking two bottles of wine. Venous gas shows pH 7.32, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, paracetamol concentration 1480 mg/L at three hours. ALT 42 U/L, INR 1.1, blood glucose 6.1 mmol/L. The patient is drowsy but rousable, oriented to place and person, and wants to leave immediately.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'I have had enough. I do not want blood tests or an antidote, so I am going home.' You are angry and embarrassed, but your speech is mildly slurred. You deny another ingestion and say there is no one safe to call. If asked, disclose that you took tablets after an argument and have previously self-harmed, but you deny current suicidal intent. Ask what right staff have to keep you. Become less defensive when the candidate listens and explains the decision step by step.

checklist.item: Uses a calm, non-judgemental opening and explores the overdose, current distress and reasons for wanting to leave.
Assesses mental capacity using the four statutory questions, considering intoxication, fluctuating arousal and the need for treatment.
Recognises that a paracetamol concentration of 1480 mg/L at three hours after an unknown ingestion exceeds the treatment threshold and starts acetylcysteine without waiting for a repeat level.
Repeats the concentration at four hours and checks ALT and INR to guide continuation and escalation rather than to decide whether treatment should start.
Contacts the poisons service and senior clinician while ensuring continuous observation.
Requests urgent liaison psychiatry assessment and considers the least restrictive safe environment.
Explains any treatment given without consent under best interests or emergency legal powers only when the facts support it.
Maintains dignity and privacy and checks the patient's understanding of the immediate plan.
Documents capacity assessment, mental state, poison risk, treatment decision and the named senior reviewer.

model_answer: I would start by sitting down and saying I wanted to understand what had happened and why leaving felt safer than staying. I would ask about the tablets, timing, alcohol, previous self-harm and current suicidal thoughts. The drowsiness and alcohol make fluctuating capacity likely, so I would not rely only on a single conversation. I would assess understanding, retention, reasoning and communication under the Mental Capacity Act. Even without formally plotting a 3-hour sample, a concentration of 1480 mg/L at 3 hours and an unknown ingested dose are far above the UK treatment threshold, so I would start acetylcysteine immediately rather than wait for a repeat level. I would still repeat the concentration at 4 hours and check ALT and INR, but these tests guide continuation of treatment, not whether to start it. I would contact the poisons service and a senior emergency physician. Continuous observation is required. I would ask liaison psychiatry to assess suicide risk and whether the Mental Health Act is relevant. Physical treatment may proceed in best interests if the patient lacks capacity and delay would risk serious harm, using the least restrictive approach. If capacity is intact, I would discuss the risk of declining treatment, offer a safe plan and take advice about legal options. Disposition is admission to a monitored observation area with continuous observation and urgent psychiatric review. I would document the capacity assessment, treatment rationale and consultant review. I would escalate immediately to the consultant and on call mental health team if agitation, drowsiness or suicidal intent worsens.
references_provided: Local paracetamol overdose pathway; UK poisons service contact sheet; Mental Capacity Act assessment prompt.

title: Cold night on the street
setting: A busy emergency department assessment cubicle during a winter outreach handover from an ambulance crew.
candidate_instructions: Assess this patient with cold exposure and fluctuating confusion, address refusal of care, and make a safe multidisciplinary plan.
materials_provided: A 61 year old rough sleeper was found outdoors overnight. Core temperature 34.4 degrees Celsius, heart rate 48/min, respiratory rate 12/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, oxygen saturation 94% on air. Venous gas pH 7.31, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L. ECG has prominent J waves and sinus bradycardia. The patient initially says he does not want admission.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'I am fine, just cold. I do not need a hospital bed.' You give inconsistent answers about the night and cannot say where you stayed. You become suspicious when asked about medication. If asked sensitively, disclose regular alcohol use with withdrawal before, no food since yesterday and no recent head injury. You have no fixed address. If capacity or immediate safety is discussed, agree reluctantly to a short admission once staff explain the cold and confusion.

checklist.item: Obtains the exposure history and checks for trauma, alcohol or drug use, medication, falls and time spent outdoors.
Uses a low-reading thermometer, assesses conscious level and performs a structured primary survey before passive and active warming.

Recognises clinically significant hypothermia at 34.4 degrees Celsius with confusion and bradycardia, states the grading system used, and applies the appropriate local or Swiss stage rather than assigning severity from the numerical temperature alone.
Orders a 12 lead ECG, glucose, blood gas, full blood count, renal function, clotting and alcohol screening, and treats reversible contributors.
Discusses capacity and the risks of cold exposure and confusion without dismissing the patient's choice.
Uses passive warming and warmed fluids according to the local hypothermia pathway and requests senior review.
Involves outreach, housing and safeguarding or social care, and records a safe discharge plan or admission plan for each possible outcome.
Sets a monitored disposition with repeat temperature, observations and escalation for arrhythmia or further confusion.

model_answer: This patient has clinically significant hypothermia at 34.4 degrees Celsius with bradycardia and fluctuating confusion. If using Swiss clinical staging, the impaired consciousness makes this Stage II, while a temperature-based classification would place him in the mild range. I would move him gently to a warm cubicle, obtain a proper low-reading temperature and complete a primary survey while looking for falls, head injury, intoxication and infection. I would remove wet clothing, dry him, use warm blankets and keep lying down. Warmed intravenous fluids, warmed oxygen and active warming follow the local hypothermia pathway, with senior support because myocardial irritability is possible. I would obtain an ECG, blood gas, glucose, renal function, full blood count, coagulation and alcohol or drug screening. I would monitor continuously. His inconsistent answers and recent exposure mean I need to assess capacity now and repeat that assessment once warmer and more alert. If he lacks capacity, I would make a best interests decision for treatment and a safe place, using the least restrictive option. I would involve housing outreach, social care or safeguarding, and the alcohol liaison service. I would ask the emergency department consultant to review any proposed discharge into the cold. Disposition is a warm monitored area with hourly observations, active warming, alcohol withdrawal monitoring and a safe social plan. I would document capacity, temperature trend and the named clinician responsible for reassessment. I would escalate to critical care if bradycardia, arrhythmia, hypotension or the GCS worsens.
references_provided: Local hypothermia pathway; low-reading thermometer; housing and outreach contact card.

title: Teaching the first minute of a major haemorrhage call
setting: A teaching room just outside the resuscitation area, with a whiteboard and a printed scenario cue card.
candidate_instructions: Teach an ACCS trainee how to lead the first minute of a major haemorrhage call in a simulated trauma case. Assess understanding and leave them with a clear next step.
materials_provided: The trainee is in their first year and has not led a major haemorrhage call. The cue card shows an adult with a pelvic fracture, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, heart rate 134/min and active bleeding during pelvic binder application.
sp_role_script: You are an ACCS trainee who is keen but nervous. Say: 'I know what treatments might be needed, but I freeze on who to instruct when someone says the blood pressure is falling.' You can state three priorities when prompted but need prompting to assign roles and ask for closed-loop communication. Respond well to structured questions and a short rehearsal.

checklist.item: Establishes the trainee's prior experience and a single achievable learning goal before teaching.
Explains a short actionable framework for the first minute: safety, recognition, call for help, role allocation and immediate bleeding control.
Models clear closed-loop instructions and asks the trainee to repeat the critical actions.
Uses the cue card to ask the trainee to rehearse the first minute rather than only recite facts.
Checks understanding with a practical question and corrects errors without humiliating the learner.
Gives specific feedback about one strength and one change in behaviour.
Agrees a supervised next attempt and names when the learner should ask for consultant help.

model_answer: I would first ask what the trainee has led and what they find hardest. They have identified role allocation and communication as the gap, so I would set one goal: lead a clear first minute in the simulated major haemorrhage call. I would teach a simple sequence: confirm scene safety, recognise shock, call for the major haemorrhage team, allocate four audible roles, start direct pressure and pelvic binding, and request blood products through the local pathway. I would demonstrate one calm command and ask them to repeat it back. With the cue card, I would ask them to run the first minute aloud. I would prompt only when necessary and use pause, question and replay if they freeze. I would check why each action comes next, not merely the order. Feedback would name one strength, such as the clear request for help, and one change, such as using the person's name and a closed-loop response. I would then run a second short rehearsal. The trainee should call the consultant if the patient loses output, the airway is threatened, or they cannot obtain blood products. Disposition of the teaching episode is a supervised repeat attempt and a written goal for the next resus drill. I would escalate to the supervising consultant if the learner remains unsafe or misunderstands a critical action.
references_provided: Printed simulated major haemorrhage cue card; local major haemorrhage activation card.

title: Collapse after a home birth
setting: Resuscitation bay receiving an unwell patient 25 minutes after a home delivery.
candidate_instructions: Lead the resuscitation, diagnose the most likely cause of shock, and stabilise the patient with the team.
materials_provided: A woman delivered at home 25 minutes ago and has ongoing heavy vaginal bleeding. Heart rate 138/min, blood pressure 76/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, oxygen saturation 94% on 15 L/min, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius. Estimated blood loss 1.6 L. The uterus feels soft. Two large bore IV cannulas are in place.
sp_role_script: You are playing the registered nurse coordinating the room. State: 'I have activated the obstetric emergency team and major haemorrhage call.' Ask the candidate for clear medication, blood product and transfer instructions. Offer the obstetric registrar and O-negative blood after 60 seconds if the candidate has not requested them. The patient is drowsy and cannot give coherent answers. Escalate the voice and urgency as systolic pressure falls.

checklist.item: Takes control, states the working diagnosis and assigns clear roles to airway, circulation, drugs and scribe.
Recognises postpartum haemorrhage and hypovolaemic shock rather than treating the tachycardia alone.
Calls for obstetric and major haemorrhage support and initiates the local blood product pathway.
Performs uterine massage and asks for available obstetric measures without delaying resuscitation.
Gives tranexamic acid and uterotonic treatment in line with the local obstetric pathway while checking allergies.
Prioritises warmed blood products, avoids excessive crystalloid and monitors response with observations and bedside tests.
Requests repeated haemoglobin, coagulation, calcium and group and save, and anticipates deterioration.
Gives concise closed-loop instructions and asks the team for a repeat of critical actions.
Plans immediate transfer to theatre or obstetrics and names the person leading the transfer.

model_answer: This is major postpartum haemorrhage with hypovolaemic shock. I would take control and state that the priority is stopping bleeding while restoring circulation. I would allocate roles for airway, monitoring, IV access, drugs, blood and documentation. I would call the obstetric registrar, anaesthetist and major haemorrhage team if not already present. I would start direct uterine massage, obtain fundal tone regularly and ask the obstetric team to assess retained products or genital tract trauma. I would give tranexamic acid within three hours of birth according to the local obstetric pathway and use uterotonics as directed. I would activate the blood product pathway and give warmed blood products rather than repeated large crystalloid boluses. I would monitor blood pressure, heart rate, capillary refill, urine output, blood gas, calcium and coagulation and repeat full blood count. I would anaesthetise and airway plan only when required by the team. O-negative blood may be needed until crossmatched products arrive. I would use closed-loop communication and ask for a verbal summary every few minutes. Transfer to theatre or obstetrics should proceed once initial stabilisation has begun, with a named team ready on arrival. Disposition is theatre or obstetric critical care.
