I would document blood loss, treatment times, product use and a clear handover. I would escalate to the consultant obstetrician, anaesthetist and critical care team if bleeding, shock or coagulopathy continues.
references_provided: Local obstetric haemorrhage pack; major haemorrhage activation card; obstetric early warning chart.

title: Seizure after cocaine use
setting: Resuscitation bay with a simulated patient having repeated generalised seizures and a colleague acting as the bedside nurse.
candidate_instructions: Lead the immediate resuscitation of this seizure, identify dangerous contributors, and arrange safe ongoing care.
materials_provided: A 27 year old was brought in after using cocaine. He is convulsing continuously for four minutes and has had two earlier brief episodes. Oxygen saturation 91% on air, heart rate 146/min, blood pressure 168/96 mmHg, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius, blood glucose 7.4 mmol/L. No trauma witnessed.
sp_role_script: You are the nurse in the simulated room. Start with: 'He has been fitting for four minutes and the oxygen is dropping.' Provide observations and medications when asked. Prompt once if no airway position or oxygen has been addressed. Confirm no known allergy and no regular antiepileptic medicine when asked. Announce when total seizure time reaches eight minutes and call for the anaesthetic team if not requested.

checklist.item: Allocates airway, monitoring, drug and timing roles and asks for a running seizure clock.
Protects the airway, provides high flow oxygen and checks glucose without placing anything in the mouth.
Treats convulsive status epilepticus with a weight appropriate benzodiazepine from the local protocol.
Requests a second line anticonvulsant and anaesthetic support when seizures continue after the first treatment.
Looks for cocaine related complications including hyperthermia, arrhythmia, hyponatraemia, rhabdomyolysis and trauma.
Orders ECG, blood gas, electrolytes, creatine kinase, renal function, toxicology as indicated and urgent imaging if the course suggests it.

Monitors core temperature frequently and starts active cooling if severe hyperthermia develops, for example a core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius or heat-stroke physiology, without causing shivering or delaying seizure treatment.
Reassesses the patient after each intervention and states a clear escalation threshold.
Secures critical care or high dependency disposition and gives a structured handover.

model_answer: This is convulsive status epilepticus, likely precipitated by cocaine use. I would take a brief team brief, allocate roles and start the seizure clock. The patient needs left lateral positioning, suction, high flow oxygen and continuous monitoring. I would check glucose and give the local protocol benzodiazepine at the correct weight and route. If seizures continue, I would give a second dose within the protocol and call anaesthetics early for airway support and anaesthesia if needed. A second line anticonvulsant should follow the local status pathway without delay. I would look for cocaine complications, especially hyperthermia, arrhythmia, hyponatraemia, rhabdomyolysis and occult head injury. I would request an ECG, blood gas, electrolytes, renal function, creatine kinase, magnesium and pregnancy testing when relevant. Severe hyperthermia needs active cooling with close monitoring. I would avoid treating hypertension aggressively at the expense of cerebral perfusion. After seizure control, I would reassess airway, blood pressure, temperature and conscious level. Disposition is a critical care area for continued sedation assessment, cardiac monitoring and repeat biochemistry. I would call intensive care early and give a concise handover with seizure duration, drugs, airway status and outstanding risks. I would escalate to the consultant if seizures continue past the second line protocol or the airway cannot be maintained.
references_provided: Local status epilepticus pathway; weight based emergency drug chart; adult observation and ECG monitor.

title: Stridor after a house fire
setting: Resuscitation bay receiving a patient from a domestic fire, with burns and airway teams available.
candidate_instructions: Lead the initial assessment and airway plan for this patient and arrange appropriate definitive care.
materials_provided: A 44 year old was rescued from a smoke filled flat. They have soot around the mouth and nose, a hoarse voice and a faint inspiratory stridor. Respiratory rate 28/min, oxygen saturation 94% on air, heart rate 122/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, GCS 14. Carboxyhaemoglobin 22%. Superficial burns to the face and right forearm. No evidence of major trauma.
sp_role_script: You are the anaesthetic registrar arriving in the room. Say: 'I can see soot and hear stridor. Tell me your airway plan and what you need from me.' Offer video laryngoscopy, difficult airway trolley and surgical airway backup. If the candidate waits for more results before calling for senior help, state that the voice is becoming quieter. Provide set observations on request.

checklist.item: Calls the anaesthetic and burns teams early and clearly states that the airway is at immediate risk.
Sits the patient upright if tolerated, gives high flow oxygen and avoids unnecessary airway manipulation before a plan is agreed.
Recognises progressive airway oedema from inhalation injury and plans early intubation rather than waiting for complete obstruction.
Uses a shared airway plan with senior support, difficult airway equipment and a declared front of neck access plan.
Interprets pulse oximetry cautiously in suspected carbon monoxide poisoning and requests co-oximetry and blood gas testing.
Considers cyanide exposure and other combustion products while treating hypoxia and shock.
Limits non-urgent procedures and arranges monitoring, IV access and transfer logistics around the airway plan.
Explains the airway plan to the patient and gives closed loop instructions to the team.
Names the destination, transfer lead and post intubation ventilation plan.

model_answer: Soot, hoarseness and stridor after a fire indicate a high risk of rapidly progressive upper airway oedema. I would keep the patient upright, give high flow oxygen and call anaesthetics and the burns team immediately. I would prepare for early intubation before obstruction becomes complete. The airway should be managed as a shared high risk procedure with video laryngoscopy, suction, difficult airway trolley and a declared front of neck access plan. I would avoid giving a long acting muscle relaxant until the operator is ready. The carboxyhaemoglobin of 22% supports carbon monoxide exposure, and pulse oximetry does not reliably distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. I would request co-oximetry, assess for cyanide exposure and continue oxygen. I would attach monitoring, obtain IV access and address burns and pain once the airway is secured. I would explain the need for breathing support to the patient in short sentences. Disposition is a critical care bed after intubation and ventilation, with burns and critical care review. If this is a major burn or complex inhalation injury, I would discuss transfer with the regional burns service. I would document the time to intubation, difficult airway plan, ventilation settings and a clear post procedure review. I would escalate immediately to the airway lead and burns consultant if stridor worsens or a difficult airway is anticipated.
references_provided: Difficult airway trolley checklist; local inhalation injury pathway; regional burns unit contact card.

title: Open tibial fracture at the roadside
setting: Emergency department major trauma bay receiving a patient transferred from scene with an open lower leg injury.
candidate_instructions: Perform and describe the initial practical management of this open tibial fracture, including neurovascular assessment, initial dressing, splinting and escalation.
materials_provided: A 32 year old cyclist has a 4 cm open wound over the anterior tibia with visible bone, a pale foot and weak dorsalis pedis pulse. The wound is dirty. Blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, heart rate 98/min, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius. Analgesia has been started. Plain films are available after initial assessment.
task_details: Explain each action aloud while using the simulated limb and equipment. Ask for additional instruments, dressings, splints, drugs or imaging when needed. State what you would document and who you would call.

checklist.item: Checks pulses, perfusion, sensation and motor function in the foot before and after any manipulation.
Assesses gross alignment and requests gentle realignment when vascular compromise is present, with appropriate analgesia or sedation.

Removes only loose gross debris without irrigating the open long-bone fracture in the emergency department, then covers the wound with a saline-soaked sterile dressing and an occlusive layer without repeatedly lifting it.
Prescribes early appropriate intravenous antibiotics after allergy and local guideline checks.
Checks tetanus status and requests appropriate follow up or vaccination.
Applies a well fitting splint and elevates the leg while avoiding pressure over the wound.
Requests lower limb radiographs and contacts orthopaedics urgently with the wound, vascular and contamination findings.
Explains the plan to the patient and documents wound photographs, neurovascular status and treatment timings.

model_answer: I would treat this as an open fracture with possible vascular compromise. I would expose both legs, check distal pulses, capillary refill, colour, sensation and movement, and record the findings before touching the wound. If the foot remains poorly perfused after analgesia, I would discuss gentle realignment with the trauma team and use procedural sedation or regional analgesia according to the local protocol. I would photograph the wound first if doing so causes no delay, remove only visible loose gross dirt without irrigating the open long-bone fracture before wound excision. I would cover the wound once with a saline-soaked sterile dressing and an occlusive layer and avoid repeated inspection. I would take bloods, group and save, prescribe early intravenous antibiotics from the local open fracture guideline after checking allergies, and check tetanus status. I would apply a padded splint that does not press on the wound and elevate the limb. I would request radiographs of the whole tibia and fibula and call orthopaedics immediately. A weak pulse and pale foot need urgent senior trauma and vascular review. Disposition is admission under orthopaedics with planned theatre, continued antibiotics and repeat neurovascular checks. Escalate immediately if pulses are lost, pain escalates or the foot becomes cold.
references_provided: Local open fracture antibiotic guideline; tetanus status checklist; neurovascular assessment chart.

title: Electrical burn on the shop floor
setting: Emergency department assessment cubicle receiving a worker from an industrial unit.
candidate_instructions: Take a focused history, examine the injuries, identify hidden electrical injury, and arrange safe onward care.
materials_provided: A 36 year old electrician was thrown from a distribution board at work. He had a brief loss of consciousness but is now alert. Entry burn to the right palm and exit wound between the toes. Heart rate 104/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 98% on air. ECG shows sinus rhythm with no acute ST change. Creatine kinase is pending.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'There was a flash and I was on the floor. My hand hurts, but I feel okay now.' You have a headache and mild chest discomfort, but no shortness of breath. If asked, disclose a brief loss of consciousness, no tetanus in ten years and no prior heart disease. You are worried about losing pay and ask whether you really need to stay. Show the hand when asked and describe the foot wound.

checklist.item: Establishes voltage, duration of contact, scene safety, loss of consciousness, fall and current symptoms.
Examines entry and exit sites and searches for deep tenderness, compartment signs, fracture and occult injury.
Recognises that visible skin burns may understate deep tissue and cardiac injury.
Requests ECG, troponin if indicated, creatine kinase, renal function, urinalysis and appropriate imaging.
Arranges cardiac monitoring for the observation period specified by local policy and repeats the ECG after any deterioration.
Treats pain and wounds, checks tetanus status and plans hand surgery assessment for the palmar burn.
Explains why hidden injury can occur after a reassuring examination and addresses the patient's work concerns.
States a monitored disposition and explicit escalation plan for arrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis or neurovascular change.

model_answer: The visible burns are only part of the injury. Electricity can damage muscle, nerves and the heart along the current path. I would clarify the voltage, duration, whether there was a fall and whether the patient lost consciousness. I would examine the entry wound, the exit wound, all limbs, the spine if there is a fall mechanism, and the heart. I would document distal neurology and pulses. I would request an ECG, repeat it during observation, and check troponin if local policy or chest symptoms require it. Creatine kinase, renal function, urine output and urinalysis help detect muscle breakdown. The palmar burn needs a sterile dressing, elevation, tetanus review and urgent hand surgery assessment. Analgesia should be given early. I would explain that the normal rhythm now does not exclude delayed rhythm problems or deep muscle injury. Under local electrical injury policy he should be observed on a cardiac monitor for the recommended period, with admission if the ECG changes, he develops chest pain, has a significant fall or has raised muscle breakdown markers. Disposition is an observation bed or admission depending on those findings, with clear escalation for arrhythmia, dark urine, reduced urine output or worsening hand perfusion.
references_provided: Local electrical injury observation policy; ECG tracing; tetanus status form.

title: Bruising in an eight month old
setting: Paediatric assessment room in a UK emergency department with a paediatric nurse present.
candidate_instructions: Assess the infant and carer, identify safeguarding concerns, and explain the immediate safeguarding and medical plan.
materials_provided: An eight month old is brought by her parent after crying when lifted. There is a cluster of blue brown bruises on both upper thighs and a small bruise behind the right ear. The infant is alert and feeding. Respiratory rate 34/min, heart rate 138/min, oxygen saturation 98%, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. The parent says the bruises appeared after the child rolled off a sofa. A second carer gives a different time and mechanism.
sp_role_script: You are the accompanying parent. Open with: 'She rolled off the sofa yesterday. I do not know why there are marks on both legs.' Give a vague, changing timeline and avoid eye contact when details change. Say you are worried about being blamed. If the candidate uses a calm, non-accusatory approach, disclose that your partner looks after the infant overnight and you have felt unsafe at home, but do not volunteer this at the start.

checklist.item: Records separate accounts from each carer and the exact timing, position, mechanism and subsequent behaviour.
Examines the whole infant with the appropriate chaperone and looks for other injuries, oral or ear findings and signs of neglect.
Recognises that bruising in a non independently mobile infant is a serious safeguarding concern.
Uses a calm, non-accusatory approach that encourages disclosure without promising confidentiality.
Discusses the case immediately with the paediatric consultant and follows the local child safeguarding pathway.
Refers to children's social care and other agencies as required, recording what information is shared and why.
Requests a child protection medical assessment and avoids repeated unnecessary examinations or unrecorded photographs.
Explains the medical and safeguarding steps to the carer in plain language and states that the infant's safety is the priority.

model_answer: Bruising in an eight month old who is not independently mobile must be treated as a serious safeguarding concern. I would keep the infant with a named paediatric nurse and obtain a complete medical history. I would ask each carer separately for the mechanism, timing, who was present and how the infant behaved afterwards. I would examine the whole infant, with a chaperone, for other marks, tenderness, ear or mouth injury, and signs of neglect. I would not repeatedly interview the family or suggest an explanation. I would discuss the case immediately with the paediatric consultant and follow the local child safeguarding pathway. Children's social care and, where indicated, the police should receive a referral under that pathway. I would arrange a child protection medical by an appropriately trained clinician and any required imaging. I would explain that the injuries do not fit the accounts so far and that the next step is to protect the child while the facts are assessed. This is not an accusation and does not prevent support for the family. Disposition is admission or another place of safety agreed by the paediatric and safeguarding teams. I would document the exact words used, timings, visible findings and who was contacted. I would escalate to the on call paediatric consultant and named safeguarding lead if a safe placement cannot be agreed.
references_provided: Local child safeguarding flowchart; paediatric safeguarding contact list; body map.

title: Major incident while the department is full
setting: Emergency department command area during a suspected mass casualty incident at a nearby transport hub.
candidate_instructions: As the senior emergency doctor before the consultant arrives, set the initial command priorities and tell the team what you want done in the next ten minutes.
materials_provided: Twenty three casualties are expected within fifteen minutes. Six could be time critical. The emergency department has three resuscitation bays, two are occupied by deteriorating admitted patients, and the waiting room is full. Two nurses are on breaks, the blood bank has four units of O-negative blood and the trauma team has been called. Police have not yet declared a deliberate incident.
sp_role_script: You are the ED nurse in charge. Open with: 'I have six time critical casualties coming and nowhere to put them.' Ask the candidate for priorities. Report limited capacity, staff availability and the presence of a senior nurse who can act as casualty clearing officer. Push for a decision when the candidate gives vague instructions. Disclose new information after two minutes: police request a secure perimeter and there is a possible secondary device.

checklist.item: Declares or recommends a major incident under local policy and identifies command and communication roles.

Reassesses the two deteriorating admitted resuscitation patients with their admitting and critical care teams, keeps them where equivalent monitoring can continue, and uses hospital command and the local major incident plan to create additional monitored capacity or distribute time-critical casualties safely.
Allocates teams by casualty priority rather than by arrival order, using the local major incident triage method.
Requests key support: consultant, critical care, blood bank, radiology, security, portering and additional nursing staff.
States the early priorities for time critical casualties: catastrophic bleeding, airway, breathing, circulation and rapid destination decisions.
Gives a concise all team brief and uses closed loop communication for safety-critical instructions.
Sets up casualty tracking and documentation with one person responsible for patient identity and movement.
Responds to the possible secondary device by moving to a command point and following police and security direction.
Names the handover plan for the arriving consultant and the trigger for escalation to regional support.

model_answer: I would immediately recommend activation of the hospital major incident plan and tell the nurse in charge to open the incident log. My first ten minutes would focus on command, space, staff and casualty flow. I would identify a command point, a casualty clearing officer and a communications lead. The two current resuscitation patients are deteriorating, so I would not describe or move them as stable. I would ask their admitting and critical care teams to transfer them to definitive monitored care and ask hospital command to create additional monitored surge capacity under the local plan. I would also agree regional distribution or mutual aid immediately if the single free resuscitation bay cannot safely receive the predicted time-critical casualties. I would allocate named teams to red, amber and green streams and use the local triage method as casualties arrive. I would ask for the consultant, critical care, blood bank, radiology, portering, security and extra nursing staff. I would protect blood products for patients with major bleeding and tell the blood bank the likely need. I would give a short brief: safety first, treat catastrophic bleeding and airway threats, then move patients toward definitive care. When police report a possible secondary device, I would pause movement, get the command point confirmed by security and follow police direction. I would maintain closed-loop communication and document every patient movement. I would hand over to the consultant with current capacity, casualties expected, staff gaps and immediate risks, and escalate to regional support if demand exceeds capacity. Disposition of this phase is continued major incident command under the arriving consultant, with a named silver liaison and a scheduled capacity review.
references_provided: Trust major incident plan extract; local major incident triage card; ED capacity board.

title: A discharge you cannot accept
setting: Emergency department clinical decisions area during a bed shortage.
candidate_instructions: Address the senior colleague's plan to discharge a patient with suspected sepsis, protect the patient, and resolve the disagreement professionally.
materials_provided: A 76 year old care home resident has a temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius, respiratory rate 24/min, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, normal GCS and oxygen saturation 95% on air. Lactate is 3.2 mmol/L. The medical registrar says the patient can go back to the home with oral antibiotics because the department is full.
sp_role_script: You are the medical registrar. Open with: 'We need the trolley. Give oral antibiotics and send her back, she has no red flags.' You are tired and under pressure but not hostile. If the candidate describes the NEWS2, lactate, hypotension and likely source, acknowledge the concern but say the medical bed will not be available for hours. Agree to help once the candidate offers a safe interim plan and a clear escalation route.

checklist.item: Opens with shared concern for the patient and asks the colleague to review the observations and risk together.
Identifies suspected sepsis with hypotension and raised lactate as unsafe for discharge from the emergency department.
Uses clear, respectful graded assertiveness rather than personal criticism or silence.
Proposes a safe interim plan while beds are unavailable, including a monitored ED space, early antibiotics and fluids based on repeated assessment.
Contacts the emergency department consultant and critical care outreach if the colleague will not agree a safe plan.
Escalates the capacity problem to the site manager or patient flow team separately from the clinical disagreement.
Checks that the agreed plan, responsibilities and review times are clear to the whole team.
Documents the clinical concern, discussion, escalation and agreed disposition.

model_answer: I would start by agreeing that the department is under pressure and that we both want to use resources safely. I would then ask the medical registrar to review the observations with me: fever, tachycardia, hypotension, raised respiratory rate and lactate are not consistent with safe discharge to a care home. I would state clearly that I am concerned the patient may have sepsis and could deteriorate during transfer. I would use graded assertiveness, naming the specific risk and asking for a revised plan. I would offer a workable alternative: keep her in a monitored ED area, start the local sepsis treatment, take cultures and bloods, and agree a review time. I would ask critical care outreach to help while the bed is arranged. If the registrar still refused a safe plan, I would call the emergency department consultant and, if needed, the on call medical consultant. I would separately escalate the bed and crowding problem to the site manager. I would record the clinical findings, advice given, my concern and who agreed the plan. Disposition is a monitored emergency department space with sepsis treatment and rapid senior review, followed by admission when a bed is available. I would make it clear that a bed shortage changes where care is delivered, not whether the patient receives it.
references_provided: NEWS2 chart; local sepsis pathway; patient flow escalation card.

title: Learning from a wrong drug selection
setting: Emergency department governance meeting preparation, using notes from a recent medication incident review.
candidate_instructions: Review the incident summary and write a structured improvement plan that reduces the risk of selecting the wrong potassium containing medicine.
materials_provided: Over twelve months, eight order entry errors involved a potassium containing medicine being selected for a patient with severe renal impairment. Two errors reached the patient, causing temporary hyperkalaemia. Staff report that the order set displays potassium formulations on the default screen and that renal function is not visible at the point of selection. The incident review found reliance on individual vigilance and no formal training or audit.
task_details: Write findings under three headings: what happened, why it happened, and what will change. Include an implementation plan and how you will measure whether the change worked.

checklist.item: Describes the incident pattern using the supplied counts without overstating causation.
Identifies that renal impairment and a confusing order set contribute to the same high risk medication error.
Proposes a systems change such as removing potassium products from default screens or adding a renal function warning.
Allocates named owners, timescales and resources for the immediate, short term and longer term actions.
Includes staff education and a blame free feedback loop for reporting near misses.
Selects measures such as incident rate, near miss rate, order set use and audit of high risk prescriptions.
Plans a small scale test, review points and checks for unintended effects such as treatment delay.
States when to escalate to the medication safety committee or senior management.

model_answer: The pattern shows repeated selection of potassium containing medicines despite severe renal impairment. Two events reached patients, so this is more than isolated human error. The order set makes high risk products easy to choose and does not show the renal function needed to make the decision. Staff are relying on memory and individual vigilance, with no training or audit loop. I would act at the system level. Immediately, I would ask pharmacy and digital systems to remove potassium formulations from the default view and add a warning when renal function is abnormal. I would place a prompt to check the latest potassium and renal function before prescribing. Short term, I would brief prescribers, nurses and pharmacy, encourage near miss reporting and run a weekly review of high risk orders. The medication safety committee would own the change, with named leads for digital design, education and audit. I would test the change on one order set, collect feedback and watch for delayed treatment from excessive warnings. Measures would include wrong product selection, near misses, warning overrides and a sample audit of potassium prescriptions in renal impairment. I would review after four weeks and again after three months, using run charts rather than a single snapshot. Escalate early if another patient is harmed or if staff bypass the new safety controls. Disposition of the plan is a medication safety committee decision on scale, adaptation or pause, supported by the measured data.
references_provided: Anonymised medication incident summary; order set screenshot; local quality improvement template.

title: Appraising a prehospital plasma trial
setting: Academic discussion room following the reading period for a fictional released trial paper.
candidate_instructions: Discuss the paper with the examiner. Do not summarise the whole paper or perform calculations. Focus on whether the methods support the result and whether the result should change UK practice.
materials_provided: A multicentre randomised trial compared prehospital freeze dried plasma with crystalloid in adults with suspected major trauma and hypotension. The primary outcome was 28 day mortality: 12.7% versus 13.5%, absolute difference 0.8 percentage points, 95% confidence interval 2.9 percentage points lower to 1.4 percentage points higher. Mortality at 24 hours favoured plasma, but the confidence interval crossed no difference. Protocol adherence was 71%. Treatment began a median of nine minutes earlier in the plasma group. Serious transfusion reactions were similar.
sp_role_script: You are the examiner. Open with: 'Was this trial internally valid enough for the mortality result to be used in practice?' Ask follow up questions about allocation, missing data, adherence and applicability to a UK major trauma centre. Correct an answer only if it relies on the abstract alone. Keep the discussion focused on validity and practice, not arithmetic.

checklist.item: States the main causal question and recognises that the 28 day mortality confidence interval includes no difference.
Assesses randomisation, allocation concealment and whether groups were balanced for injury severity and time to treatment.
Discusses the effect of 71% protocol adherence and how it may dilute or complicate interpretation.
Explains why a secondary 24 hour mortality finding should be treated cautiously.
Considers missing outcome data, adverse events and the plausibility of the proposed mechanism.
Balances the result against current prehospital trauma pathways, blood availability, cost and system effects.
Gives a clear conclusion that distinguishes evidence of no benefit from proof of harm, while identifying what future data are needed.

model_answer: The trial asks whether early prehospital plasma improves survival in suspected major trauma with hypotension. The primary result is imprecise: the confidence interval includes both a meaningful benefit and a small harm, so it does not establish a mortality benefit. Internal validity depends on the randomisation system, allocation concealment and balance of injury severity and transport time. A trial opening before hospital arrival can still be vulnerable to unblinded co-interventions. The 71% adherence is important because contamination or non receipt can dilute an early treatment effect and makes per protocol analysis harder to interpret. The 24 hour mortality signal is secondary, has more testing risk and should be hypothesis generating. Missing outcomes and adverse event details must be checked. External validity is also limited because prehospital systems, distances, blood availability and trauma centre access differ. I would not recommend a UK service change from this single trial. I would consider the result supportive of further research, particularly with adherence and 24 hour outcomes prespecified. For practice, I would continue the local major haemorrhage pathway and focus on the interventions already supported, such as rapid bleeding control, damage control resuscitation and early transfer. The paper should be discussed in the major haemorrhage governance group with a clear research question for any future UK study. I would escalate any proposed pathway change to that group, and the disposition of this appraisal is no immediate service change with further review when stronger evidence is available.
references_provided: Fictional practice trial scenario and abstract table; critical appraisal prompt; local major trauma guideline summary.

title: New confusion in a care home resident
setting: Emergency department frailty assessment bay with access to a bladder scanner and the care home notes.
candidate_instructions: Assess the likely cause of this older adult's acute confusion, identify immediate risks, and make a safe care and disposition plan.
materials_provided: An 82 year old care home resident has been confused since yesterday. Temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius, respiratory rate 18/min, heart rate 88/min, blood pressure 142/76 mmHg, oxygen saturation 96% on air, NEWS2 1. The patient has a palpable lower abdominal mass and has not passed urine for twelve hours. Medicines include oxybutynin, codeine and ramipril. Baseline is independent walking and conversation; now the patient is disoriented to place and pulling at clothing.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'I just want to go back to my room. Who are all these people?' You are restless and occasionally repeat the same question. If the examiner asks, say you have pain in your lower tummy. You deny breathlessness and chest pain. You become calmer when staff introduce themselves and explain each step. You cannot reliably describe your medicines or usual routine.

checklist.item: Contacts the care home and establishes the baseline cognition, onset, recent falls, medication changes and bowel and bladder function.
Completes a focused examination including hydration, abdomen, bladder scan, skin, neurology and signs of infection.
Recognises acute urinary retention as a reversible cause of delirium instead of attributing confusion to dementia.
Reviews anticholinergic and opioid medicines and requests relevant blood tests, urine testing and an ECG.
Relieves retention using the local catheterisation policy and records post drainage output and symptoms.
Uses reorientation, short sentences, familiar objects and involvement of a known carer to reduce distress.
Arranges prompt senior or geriatric review and avoids routine antipsychotic prescribing for simple agitation.
States a disposition with a clear function and medication review plan and a safe escalation route if confusion worsens.

model_answer: This is acute delirium in an older adult with a clear possible trigger: painful urinary retention. I would first introduce myself, use a calm voice and keep a familiar carer with the patient. I would contact the care home to establish the baseline, the exact onset, medicines, recent falls, bowel function and any infection symptoms. I would assess hydration and examine the abdomen, bladder, skin, chest and nervous system. A bladder scan and catheterisation under the local policy should relieve the retention. I would send blood count, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, infection markers and an ECG, and test urine if a urinary source is plausible. I would review oxybutynin, codeine and ramipril with pharmacy and stop medicines that are contributing. I would avoid a sedative or antipsychotic for mild agitation because these can worsen delirium and falls. I would reorient the patient, manage pain and maintain sleep and mobility. Geriatric review should happen promptly. Disposition will depend on the response and care home support. If the patient returns to baseline and the cause is corrected, shared care planning may allow discharge with a medication review and follow up. Otherwise I would admit for monitoring and further assessment. I would escalate to the geriatric or medical consultant if confusion worsens, the patient cannot drink or there is no return to baseline.
references_provided: 4AT delirium screen; bladder scanner; local catheterisation policy; care home medication list.

title: Nausea, weakness and a calcium emergency
setting: Emergency department assessment cubicle with access to urgent oncology and renal advice.
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient, identify the emergency metabolic problem, and arrange safe initial treatment and specialist care.
materials_provided: A 63 year old presents with two weeks of back pain, nausea, constipation and increasing confusion. Heart rate 102/min, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Corrected calcium 3.72 mmol/L, creatinine 286 micromol/L, haemoglobin 79 g/L, ECG shows shortened QT interval. The patient is drowsy but rousable.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'I keep being sick and I cannot think straight. My back has been hurting for weeks.' You are thirsty and constipated. You have not taken calcium or vitamin D supplements. You have no known cancer, but you have lost weight. If asked, disclose no recent falls and no chest pain. You become frightened when told the calcium is high and ask what it means.

checklist.item: Recognises severe hypercalcaemia with neurological and renal effects as a medical emergency.
Asks about malignancy, bone pain, weight loss, supplement use, immobility, falls and medicines that affect calcium.
Requests parathyroid hormone, phosphate, magnesium, protein electrophoresis, vitamin D, renal function and relevant imaging after initial stabilisation.
Starts careful intravenous fluid resuscitation and monitors for fluid overload in the context of renal impairment.
Discusses a bone resorption inhibitor with senior or specialist teams and does not use one without considering renal function and volume status.
Identifies that the anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and back pain make myeloma a leading possibility.
Contacts oncology or haematology and renal services early and arranges a monitored bed.
Explains the calcium emergency and the need for tests and admission in plain language.

model_answer: This is severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia at 3.72 mmol/L, with confusion, nausea, dehydration and renal impairment. I would place the patient in a monitored area and check airway, breathing and circulation. I would give intravenous sodium chloride cautiously, monitoring urine output, heart rate, blood pressure and signs of fluid overload because renal function is abnormal. I would send calcium, albumin, phosphate, magnesium, parathyroid hormone, renal function, full blood count and protein studies. The combination of back pain, anaemia, renal impairment and hypercalcaemia makes myeloma likely, so I would discuss imaging and haematology review early. I would ask the senior clinician or specialist about a bone resorption inhibitor, taking renal function and volume status into account. I would stop any medicine that raises calcium and review diuretics or nephrotoxins. An ECG and cardiac monitor help identify QT and rhythm effects. I would explain that the calcium is dangerously high and that treatment aims to protect the kidneys and brain while the cause is found. Disposition is admission under medicine or haematology with renal input and repeated calcium, renal function and neurological checks. I would escalate immediately if there is seizure, worsening drowsiness, arrhythmia or inadequate urine output.
references_provided: Corrected calcium result; ECG trace; local hypercalcaemia and oncology pathway.

title: Cold, slow and barely responsive
setting: Emergency department high observation area during winter, with endocrine and critical care advice available.
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient with bradycardia and hypothermia, form a differential diagnosis, and arrange safe care.
materials_provided: A 67 year old was found at home by a neighbour. Core temperature 33.9 degrees Celsius, heart rate 42/min, respiratory rate 10/min, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, oxygen saturation 92% on air and GCS 13. Skin is dry and pale. ECG shows sinus bradycardia and low voltage complexes. Blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L. The patient has a visible neck scar.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'My neighbour found me on the floor. I have been sleeping all day.' You answer slowly and have difficulty staying awake. If asked, disclose no heating for two days, long standing neck surgery and poor appetite. You do not know your medicines. Your neighbour reports no seizure and no clear head injury. You are less responsive when left cold and improve slightly when covered.

checklist.item: Gathers collateral history about the home environment, medicines, neck surgery and duration of reduced consciousness.
Uses a low reading thermometer, performs a primary survey and examines for goitre, infection, trauma and peripheral perfusion.
Considers myxoedema coma alongside exposure, sepsis, stroke, medication and hypoglycaemia.
Requests thyroid function, cortisol, blood gas, electrolytes, glucose, full blood count, renal and liver function and an ECG.
Institutes gentle passive rewarming and warmed fluids without unnecessary rough movement.

Starts the local myxoedema coma protocol without waiting for confirmation or specialist approval, giving intravenous hydrocortisone before or with intravenous levothyroxine using current local doses and routes.
Calls critical care outreach and endocrine specialties and determines the ventilatory and monitoring needs.
Explains the risk of slow breathing and low temperature to the patient and neighbour and states the admission plan.
States a high dependency disposition and escalation triggers for apnoea, hypotension or worsening conscious level.

model_answer: This patient has hypothermia, marked bradycardia, reduced consciousness and evidence of previous thyroid surgery. I would consider myxoedema coma, while keeping exposure, sepsis, medication, stroke and head injury in the differential. I would move the patient gently to a warm area, use a low reading thermometer and perform a primary survey. I would provide airway support as needed, titrated oxygen and continuous monitoring. Warm blankets and warmed intravenous fluids should begin without rough handling. I would send thyroid function, cortisol, glucose, full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, blood gas and infection tests, and obtain an ECG and chest radiograph. I would call critical care and endocrinology immediately but would start the local myxoedema coma protocol without waiting for laboratory confirmation or specialist approval. I would give intravenous hydrocortisone before or with intravenous levothyroxine, using the local dose and route, while providing airway, ventilation and haemodynamic support. Hypoventilation may worsen during rewarming, so ventilation and blood gases need repeated review. I would explain to the neighbour and patient that a thyroid and temperature problem may have caused the collapse. Disposition is a critical care or high dependency bed with repeated gases, neurological observations and temperature monitoring. I would escalate for apnoea, rising carbon dioxide, hypotension or declining conscious level.
references_provided: Low reading thermometer; local hypothermia pathway; endocrine emergency contact sheet; ECG tracing.

title: Home is the priority with a suspected clot
setting: Emergency department side room with oncology and palliative care colleagues available by telephone.
candidate_instructions: Discuss the suspicion of pulmonary embolism with a patient who wants to go home, negotiate a safe plan, and make appropriate escalation arrangements.
materials_provided: A 61 year old with metastatic pancreatic cancer has sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain. Respiratory rate 24/min, heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, oxygen saturation 90% on air. The patient is alert, has capacity and says they want to die at home. A recent oncology letter documents active treatment and a prognosis of months.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'I know what a clot could mean, but I do not want to spend my last weeks in hospital.' You value comfort and being with your family. You understand the risk of sudden deterioration and can explain the options back. You have a supportive partner and community palliative team. Become upset if staff say you must be admitted without exploring what can safely be done at home.

checklist.item: Explores the patient's understanding, priorities and fear and confirms the wish to remain at home.
Recognises possible pulmonary embolism and assesses immediate stability, contraindications and bleeding risk.
Uses the pregnancy appropriate or non pregnancy PE diagnostic pathway and arranges urgent imaging or specialist review without delaying treatment.
Explains uncertainty, likely diagnosis, treatment options and the risk of sudden deterioration in plain language.
Contacts oncology and the community palliative team to test whether an early supported discharge is feasible.
Plans oxygen, symptom control, anticoagulation if appropriate and explicit deterioration advice.
Checks the patient's understanding and records their informed preference and agreed limits of treatment.
States a named disposition, a safe transfer plan and a clear escalation route if the patient becomes unstable.

model_answer: I would acknowledge that staying at home is a legitimate and important goal. I would ask what the patient understands about the possible clot, what they fear most and who is at home. I would take a focused history for haemoptysis, syncope, bleeding risk and previous clot, then assess oxygenation, perfusion and cardiac strain. This presentation has a high clinical probability of pulmonary embolism because of active metastatic cancer, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia. I would arrange immediate CT pulmonary angiography. Unless she has active bleeding or another absolute contraindication, I would start the locally approved weight-based therapeutic anticoagulant now while arranging imaging, and I would not defer treatment pending confirmation. I would call oncology and the community palliative team to discuss an early supported plan. Oxygen and symptom treatment can start here. Her active cancer and oxygen requirement rule out discharge based on stable blood pressure alone. Any home palliative plan would need validated low-risk criteria, a confirmed treatment plan and a named rapid-response team. I would explain that a large clot can cause sudden collapse and that a home plan depends on support and a rapid response route. I would agree a clear ceiling of treatment, anticipatory medicines and when to call 999 or the palliative team. If imaging cannot safely be arranged and the risk is high, I would recommend admission for treatment and reassessment of a home plan. Disposition is a shared decision recorded with named responsibilities and a specific review time. The patient should not be sent home without a confirmed diagnostic and treatment plan. I would escalate to the consultant and critical care outreach if oxygen needs rise, blood pressure falls or the patient becomes confused.
references_provided: Suspected pulmonary embolism pathway; oncology letter; community palliative care contact card.

title: Needlestick injury and a source who declines testing
setting: Emergency department quiet room with occupational health and infection prevention advice available.
candidate_instructions: Manage the exposed healthcare worker's concern and discuss source testing with the patient in a way that respects consent while protecting staff.
materials_provided: A nurse sustained a hollow needle injury while taking blood. The source patient has a history of injecting drug use and says they do not want blood taken. The nurse is tearful and asks whether they will catch HIV. The source patient is alert and has capacity. The nurse has completed first aid and is waiting for risk assessment.
sp_role_script: You are the source patient. Open with: 'I said no blood tests. Why should my blood be taken because someone had an accident?' You are wary because of past judgemental care. If staff explain the reason, confidentiality and the limited tests requested, you become willing to discuss consent. You should not be pressured or threatened. Reveal previous hepatitis C treatment only if asked about blood borne infection and confidentiality is clearly explained.

checklist.item: Acknowledges the nurse's fear without making promises about the outcome and confirms immediate first aid.
Establishes the exposure type, needle type, depth, blood exposure and immune status of the exposed worker.
Explains to the source patient the purpose, limits and confidentiality of HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C testing without coercion.
Contacts occupational health or the local urgent exposure service immediately and starts the agreed risk assessment pathway.
Discusses timely HIV post exposure prophylaxis when indicated, including the 72 hour treatment window and current local guidance.
Checks hepatitis B vaccination status and arranges immunoglobulin or vaccination as advised.
If consent is refused, seeks senior and infection control advice instead of testing the source without a lawful basis.
Records the exposure, advice, consent discussion and follow up and gives the nurse written contact details.

model_answer: I would first check that the nurse has washed the wound, encouraged bleeding and covered it, then acknowledge how frightening the event feels without promising that infection cannot occur. I would take details of the needle, depth, visible blood, vaccination status and any immunosuppression. I would contact occupational health or the local urgent exposure service at once. I would speak with the source patient privately and explain that testing is limited to blood borne viruses, remains confidential and helps decide preventive treatment. I would not threaten or pressure them. If consent is given, urgent HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C tests can inform care. If consent is refused, I would ask senior infection control or occupational health about lawful options and would not test without a proper basis. The exposed nurse should receive a risk assessment, advice about HIV post exposure prophylaxis, and hepatitis B vaccination or immunoglobulin if indicated. Any HIV prophylaxis should start as soon as possible, ideally within hours, and no later than 72 hours if the local pathway supports it. Follow up must be booked before leaving. Disposition is occupational health follow up for the nurse and usual clinical care for the source patient, with clear documentation of consent and advice. I would escalate to the infection control consultant and occupational health physician if consent remains unresolved or prophylaxis cannot be started promptly.
references_provided: Local blood borne virus exposure pathway; occupational health contact sheet; HIV post exposure prophylaxis information leaflet.

title: Reading a capnography trace
setting: Emergency department teaching bay with a simulated monitor and a junior registrar learner.
candidate_instructions: Teach the learner to use a capnography trace during and after advanced airway management. Focus on interpretation and one safe action for each pattern.
materials_provided: The learner has passed an airway course six months ago but has not independently interpreted a sudden loss of waveform during resuscitation. You are given three printed traces: a normal square waveform, a sudden flat trace and a gradually rising baseline with a falling peak.
sp_role_script: You are an emergency medicine registrar. Open with: 'I know the number should be around 5, but when the trace disappears I look at the chest instead of thinking through a sequence.' You can identify a normal waveform but confuse tube displacement with loss of cardiac output. Ask for a framework rather than a list of facts. Repeat back the plan when asked.

checklist.item: Checks the learner's current understanding and agrees a focused learning objective for the station.
Explains what the waveform represents and why both the trace shape and trend matter.
Teaches a safe sequence for sudden loss of waveform, including confirmation of patient state, circuit and tube position.
Uses the printed traces to ask the learner to interpret each one and state the next action.
Distinguishes a likely disconnection or obstruction from a low or absent cardiac output without relying on a single trace.
Checks understanding with a new scenario and corrects unsafe assumptions.
Gives specific feedback and agrees when the learner should call the airway lead.

model_answer: I would ask the learner to explain what they already look for and agree a goal: use capnography to make a safe decision when the trace changes. I would explain that the trace confirms ventilation and shows trends, while the number alone can mislead. A normal square shaped trace with a stable peak suggests airway and circuit continuity. A sudden flat trace requires instant reassessment of the patient, oxygen delivery, circuit connection and tube position. The learner should call for help while confirming whether the patient has output and whether the tube is still in the trachea. A gradually rising baseline with a falling peak may suggest obstruction, circuit problems or a change in ventilation and perfusion, so they need to inspect the whole system and the patient. I would use the three traces as pauses for interpretation, asking for the action before revealing my answer. I would correct the assumption that a flat trace always means oesophageal intubation. I would give feedback on one clear strength and one change, then ask the learner to repeat the sequence in a short scenario. They should call the airway lead for uncertainty, loss of trace with deterioration, difficult ventilation or suspected obstruction. Teaching disposition is supervised use of the framework on the next resuscitation, with a brief review afterward. I would escalate to the airway lead if the learner cannot state a safe response to loss of trace or suspected tube displacement.
references_provided: Three printed capnography traces; difficult airway escalation card; local airway checklist.

title: Asthma that is becoming quiet
setting: Resuscitation bay with a tired patient sitting forward, a nurse and respiratory therapist available.
candidate_instructions: Lead the resuscitation of this severe asthma attack, identify impending respiratory failure, and arrange definitive care.
materials_provided: A 25 year old with known asthma is drowsy, using accessory muscles and speaking in single words. Respiratory rate 8/min, oxygen saturation 88% on air, heart rate 142/min, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg. Chest auscultation shows minimal air entry. Blood gas on high flow oxygen shows pH 7.21, PaCO2 8.4 kPa and lactate 3.2 mmol/L. The patient has had no response to repeated nebulised treatment.
sp_role_script: You are the emergency nurse. Open with: 'The chest is almost silent and she is getting harder to rouse.' Report medication doses and times when asked. Offer high flow oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators, steroids, magnesium and anaesthetic support. If the candidate waits for the blood gas to repeat before escalating, say that the patient is becoming more drowsy and the respiratory rate is falling.

checklist.item: Takes control, states impending respiratory failure and calls anaesthetics, critical care and a senior emergency clinician.
Recognises drowsiness, exhaustion, poor air entry and rising carbon dioxide as signs of a peri arrest state.
Provides high flow oxygen, continuous bronchodilator therapy and early systemic corticosteroid treatment according to the local pathway.
Gives intravenous magnesium when indicated and avoids sedatives or drugs that worsen respiratory depression.
Plans airway management with a senior operator and uses ventilation strategies that avoid dynamic hyperinflation.
Prepares for hypotension after intubation, including IV fluid and vasopressor planning with critical care.
Requests a chest radiograph and tests for alternative or complicating diagnoses after initial stabilisation.
Gives closed loop instructions and asks the team to verbalise oxygen, drug and airway plans.
Secures critical care disposition and sets explicit post intubation ventilation and reassessment triggers.

model_answer: This is a peri arrest severe asthma attack. The quiet chest, exhaustion, falling respiratory rate, rising carbon dioxide and drowsiness indicate that respiratory failure is close. I would call anaesthetics, critical care and the consultant immediately, then take control of the room. I would sit the patient upright, give high flow oxygen and continue continuous nebulised bronchodilators. I would give systemic corticosteroid and intravenous magnesium as directed by the local asthma pathway. I would monitor ECG, oxygen saturation and blood pressure and avoid sedating medicines. Because she is drowsy, exhausted, hypercapnic and close to respiratory arrest, I would proceed now to urgent controlled intubation by an anaesthetist or intensive care consultant rather than waiting for another blood gas or further deterioration. I would optimise oxygen, intravenous magnesium, corticosteroid and nebulised bronchodilator treatment during immediate preparation and plan low-rate, long-expiratory-time ventilation to limit dynamic hyperinflation. I would prepare for post intubation hypotension. Oxygen delivery, IV access and drug roles should be allocated aloud. I would request a chest radiograph after stabilisation to look for pneumothorax or consolidation. I would explain to the team that the main immediate risk is cardiac arrest during airway management. Disposition is a critical care bed with ventilation, repeated blood gases and bronchospasm treatment. If the patient arrests, I would follow current resuscitation guidance and consider reversible causes such as tension pneumothorax. I would hand over the timing of drugs, airway plan and recent blood gas. I would escalate to the consultant if dynamic hyperinflation, hypotension or rising carbon dioxide persists after initial treatment.
references_provided: Local acute asthma pathway; status asthmaticus drug chart; difficult airway trolley; critical care referral card.

title: Penetrating wound to the groin
setting: Major trauma resuscitation bay receiving a patient with active bleeding after an assault.
candidate_instructions: Lead the initial trauma resuscitation and control this junctional haemorrhage while arranging definitive care.
materials_provided: A 31 year old has a stab wound to the left groin with pulsatile bleeding. Heart rate 142/min, blood pressure 72/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, oxygen saturation 94% on 15 L/min. The patient is pale, agitated and has cold peripheries. The trauma team and massive transfusion protocol are available.
sp_role_script: You are the trauma nurse. Open with: 'Direct pressure is not controlling the bleeding and he is becoming more confused.' Ask for clear instructions about pressure, blood products, drugs and theatre. State that the trauma surgeon and anaesthetist are present. If the candidate only asks for imaging before controlling the bleeding, say that blood is pooling under the dressing and the systolic pressure is falling.

checklist.item: Takes command, states catastrophic junctional haemorrhage and allocates airway, circulation and documentation roles.
Applies sustained direct pressure or wound packing as appropriate and requests additional haemostatic measures from the trauma team.
Activates the major haemorrhage pathway and requests warmed blood products early.
Gives tranexamic acid within three hours of injury when indicated by the local major trauma pathway.
Prioritises prevention of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy while limiting crystalloid.
Arranges immediate surgical or interventional radiology destination and contacts the major trauma centre if required.
Requests crossmatch, coagulation, calcium and blood gas, and monitors response to resuscitation.
Uses closed loop communication and gives the patient brief reassurance while the team works.
Names the transfer lead and states the plan if bleeding cannot be controlled in the emergency department.

model_answer: This patient has catastrophic junctional haemorrhage from a groin wound. I would take control and state that bleeding control comes before imaging. One team member should maintain direct pressure or pack the wound, with the trauma surgeon deciding whether a junctional device or operative control is needed. I would activate the major haemorrhage pathway and request warmed red cells, plasma and platelets according to the local protocol. I would give tranexamic acid promptly if within the treatment window and not contraindicated. Airway and breathing need rapid assessment, but I would not allow procedures to delay transfer to theatre. I would give only small, repeated fluid boluses while blood products arrive and actively warm the patient. I would send crossmatch, full blood count, coagulation, calcium and blood gas and ask for repeated measurements of perfusion. The priority destination is theatre or interventional radiology with the trauma surgeon leading. If the patient is at a non specialist hospital, I would contact the major trauma centre early and agree whether to transfer immediately or after initial control. I would use closed loop communication and name one person to track blood products and one to record times. Disposition is immediate theatre, followed by critical care. I would hand over the wound findings, product totals, drug times and response. I would escalate to the consultant trauma surgeon and major trauma centre if bleeding remains uncontrolled or physiology continues to worsen.
references_provided: Major haemorrhage activation card; trauma team roles sheet; massive transfusion pack; major trauma centre contact list.

title: Pulled unconscious from cold water
setting: Resuscitation bay receiving a patient after a cold water immersion and bystander rescue.
candidate_instructions: Lead the initial resuscitation, prioritise oxygenation and warming, and arrange post immersion critical care.
materials_provided: A 34 year old was pulled from a river after approximately eight minutes. Bystander CPR was started. On arrival there is a weak pulse, GCS 3, agonal breathing, oxygen saturation 76%, heart rate 38/min and blood pressure 84/48 mmHg. Core temperature 28.6 degrees Celsius. There is water and vomit around the mouth. No obvious major trauma.
sp_role_script: You are the resuscitation nurse. Open with: 'She has a weak pulse and is barely breathing. Suction is ready and the warming blanket is on.' Give observations and support when asked. If the candidate gives chest compressions in the presence of a weak pulse, ask them to confirm the rhythm first. Prompt once if airway suction has not been considered.

checklist.item: Allocates airway, ventilation, suction, warming, monitoring and documentation roles and calls critical care.
Clears the airway, provides high concentration oxygen and supports ventilation as the immediate breathing priority.
Recognises severe hypothermia and altered breathing and avoids chest compressions when a clear pulse is present.
Assesses for trauma, cervical injury and other reasons for collapse without delaying oxygenation or warming.
Starts active external and internal warming with warmed oxygen and fluids and minimises heat loss.
Requests blood gas, glucose, potassium, renal function, toxicology and imaging as appropriate after stabilisation.

Recognises the heart rate below 45/min, systolic pressure below 90 mmHg and temperature below 30 degrees Celsius as criteria for imminent cardiac arrest and arranges direct transfer to an extracorporeal rewarming centre.
Communicates briefly with the resuscitation team and keeps the patient's dignity protected.
Names a critical care disposition and transfer plan with clear ventilation and temperature goals.

model_answer: This patient has severe hypothermia after immersion, with a weak pulse and inadequate breathing. The priority is airway suction, high flow oxygen and assisted ventilation. I would check the rhythm and avoid chest compressions while a clear pulse is present. I would call critical care, anaesthetics and the regional extracorporeal CPR centre early. The team should minimise movement and heat loss, remove wet clothing and start active warming with warmed oxygen and warmed intravenous fluids. Core temperature must be monitored with an appropriate device. Because the temperature is below 30 degrees Celsius, the heart rate is below 45/min and the systolic pressure is below 90 mmHg, she meets Resuscitation Council UK criteria for imminent cardiac arrest. I would arrange direct transfer for extracorporeal rewarming after immediate stabilisation and heat-loss measures, rather than waiting for cardiac arrest or refractory instability. I would look for trauma, spinal injury, aspiration and another cause of collapse without delaying oxygenation. I would obtain blood gas, glucose, potassium, renal function and toxicology, and arrange imaging only if it will not delay definitive transfer. I would explain to the team that rewarming may cause arrhythmia and haemodynamic instability. I would hand over immersion time, temperature, airway findings and treatments. I would escalate immediately if breathing becomes inadequate, the rhythm changes or perfusion worsens.
references_provided: Local immersion and hypothermia pathway; warming equipment checklist; critical care and extracorporeal support contact card.

title: Cyclist with a pulseless hand
setting: Emergency department procedure room with orthopaedic equipment and a simulated patient arm.
candidate_instructions: Demonstrate the assessment and simulated reduction of a posterior elbow dislocation with vascular compromise, then state the aftercare and referral plan.
materials_provided: A 24 year old fell from a bicycle. The elbow is grossly deformed and held in 30 degrees of flexion. The radial pulse is absent, the hand is pale and cool, and the patient has patchy numbness in the median nerve distribution. Circulation and neurology were normal before the injury. Analgesia and procedural sedation are available under local protocol.
task_details: Use the simulated arm to describe the reduction, including positioning, traction and the reassessment you would perform immediately afterward. State all necessary drugs and monitoring aloud. Ask for any equipment or specialist help you would need.

checklist.item: Documents deformity, radial pulse, capillary refill, colour, sensation and motor function before intervention.
Provides effective analgesia and procedural sedation using the local protocol, with fasting and airway considerations.
Performs or describes longitudinal traction with gentle correction of displacement while avoiding forceful leverage.
Rechecks pulses, capillary refill, sensation and motor function immediately after reduction.
Applies an appropriate posterior splint and sling without compressing the antecubital fossa.

Documents the neurovascular findings, then urgently reduces and splints the pulseless deformed elbow; requests post-reduction radiographs and obtains pre-reduction films only if they will not delay reduction.
Contacts orthopaedics and vascular surgery urgently when perfusion does not return after reduction.
Explains the risk of nerve or artery injury and gives aftercare and follow up instructions.

model_answer: The absent radial pulse and pale hand make this an urgent vascular emergency. I would document the radial pulse, capillary refill, colour, median nerve sensation and motor function before moving the arm. I would provide prompt analgesia and use procedural sedation under the local policy with continuous monitoring and airway support available. I would position the arm for gentle longitudinal traction, correct the displacement gradually and avoid levering the joint. I would immediately recheck the pulse, perfusion and neurology. If circulation returns, I would immobilise the elbow in a posterior splint and sling, avoiding pressure in the antecubital fossa, and arrange post reduction imaging. I would check the limb again after splinting. If the pulse does not return or the arm is still poorly perfused, I would contact orthopaedics and vascular surgery immediately and arrange operative reduction or vascular assessment. I would give analgesia and antiemetic treatment as needed and document every attempt, not just that reduction occurred. Before discharge I would explain the risk of missed nerve or artery injury and provide warning symptoms, an early fracture clinic or specialist follow up and a clear emergency return plan. Disposition is usually observation after successful reduction, but persistent vascular compromise requires urgent theatre. I would escalate for increasing pain, pallor, numbness or a compartment syndrome pattern.
references_provided: Elbow reduction and procedural sedation checklist; neurovascular observation chart; splint sizing guide.

title: A tiny wound and severe hand pain
setting: Emergency department cubicle with access to hand surgery and occupational health advice.
candidate_instructions: Assess this hand injury, identify the hidden risk, and arrange urgent specialist care.
materials_provided: A 29 year old mechanic has a puncture wound at the base of the right index finger after using a high pressure grease gun. The wound is 2 mm with little bleeding. The hand is swollen, tense and extremely painful. The patient has normal sensation and no obvious fracture on a preliminary radiograph. Blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, heart rate 102/min and temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'It was just a tiny squirt of grease. It barely bled. Can I just have antibiotics and go home?' You are in severe pain and worried about missing work. If asked, describe a working pressure of 3000 psi and state that the pain began immediately. Ask whether the small wound means the injury is minor. You become more accepting of admission when the risk to the finger is explained.

checklist.item: Establishes the pressure, substance, equipment, depth and mechanism and records time of injury and work details.
Performs a full hand examination including perfusion, sensation, tendon function, swelling and compartment signs.
Recognises that a high pressure injection injury is a surgical emergency despite a small skin wound.
Provides early analgesia, removes rings, elevates the hand and applies a clean dressing without probing or exploring.
Requests relevant imaging and blood tests while stating that normal plain films do not exclude deep tissue injury.
Contacts hand surgery immediately and arranges urgent assessment or transfer.
Starts appropriate intravenous antibiotics and checks tetanus status under local guidance.
Explains why the small wound is misleading and why admission is needed for possible tissue necrosis or infection.

model_answer: A high pressure injection injury can force grease deep into the tissues through a tiny puncture. The visible wound is not a reliable measure of severity. I would ask about the pressure, material and tool, examine the whole hand and document pulses, capillary refill, sensation, tendon function and swelling. I would remove rings, elevate the hand and provide early analgesia. I would not probe or explore the wound in the emergency department. I would request relevant imaging and blood tests, but I would explain that a normal radiograph does not exclude deep injection injury. I would call hand surgery immediately and arrange urgent operative exploration, debridement and possible fasciotomy. I would give intravenous antibiotics according to local policy and review tetanus status. The patient should be nil by mouth and prepared for theatre. I would explain that grease can cause severe inflammation and tissue death, and that admission is needed to save function. Disposition is urgent hand surgery through a local department or transfer to a specialist centre, with limb elevation and neurovascular observations. I would escalate immediately if pain increases, the digits become pale or insensate, or swelling threatens the skin. I would document the mechanism, pressure, examination and contact time with hand surgery.
references_provided: Hand surgery contact card; local limb injury antibiotic guideline; hand neurovascular chart.

title: Coughing after a handful of peanuts
setting: Paediatric emergency department assessment room with a parent and child actor, and urgent respiratory support available.
candidate_instructions: Assess the child, identify the likely foreign body, and arrange safe immediate transfer for definitive care while managing the parent's anxiety.
materials_provided: A two year old was eating peanuts when they began coughing and wheezing. The coughing has settled, but there is reduced air entry on the right and an expiratory wheeze. Respiratory rate 30/min, oxygen saturation 95% on air, heart rate 132/min, alert and able to speak. Chest radiograph is initially reported as normal. A small sibling has a peanut allergy.
sp_role_script: You are the parent. Open with: 'The cough stopped, so does that mean it is gone? I am terrified because my older child has a peanut allergy.' You are protective and ask whether the child needs a camera. If the candidate listens and explains the airway risk, calm down and help keep the child still. Ask when food can be given again.

checklist.item: Establishes the choking event, food type, timing, symptoms and whether the child has normal breathing and speech.
Performs a calm paediatric airway and respiratory assessment and identifies focal signs despite the quiet interval.
Recognises suspected lower airway foreign body and treats the normal radiograph as non reassuring.
Keeps the child calm and upright, gives oxygen if needed and avoids blind finger sweeps or unnecessary airway manipulation.
Calls paediatric respiratory or ENT teams and arranges urgent rigid bronchoscopy at the appropriate centre.
Distinguishes this stable presentation from complete obstruction where current paediatric choking first aid is needed.
Explains that a quiet period can occur and why the child needs specialist removal rather than discharge.
Keeps the child nil by mouth and plans a monitored transfer with a named team.

model_answer: The choking event followed by focal reduced air entry and wheeze suggests a peanut in the airway. The child is currently breathing and speaking, so I would keep them calm and upright, avoid blind finger sweeps and avoid forcing examination that could provoke deterioration. I would give oxygen if saturations fall and monitor respiratory rate, effort and oxygen saturation continuously. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude a peanut because many organic foreign bodies are not clearly seen. I would ask the parent to keep the child still and nil by mouth. I would call the paediatric respiratory or ENT team immediately and arrange urgent rigid bronchoscopy at the correct specialist centre. If complete obstruction develops in this two-year-old, I would give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating while the child remains conscious. If the child becomes unresponsive, I would call for help if this has not already been done, place the child on a firm surface, give 5 rescue breaths and start paediatric CPR. I would explain to the parent that symptoms can quieten while an object remains and that removal is needed to prevent obstruction, infection or lung damage. Disposition is urgent transfer under paediatric or anaesthetic supervision with airway equipment, oxygen and staff ready. I would document the event, focal findings, imaging result and referral time. I would not send the child home even if the cough has stopped. I would escalate immediately to the paediatric consultant and anaesthetist if stridor, tiredness or complete obstruction develops.
references_provided: Paediatric choking guidance card; paediatric observations chart; respiratory and ENT referral contact sheet.

title: Six boarded patients and one deteriorating
setting: Emergency department clinical coordination desk during a period of high occupancy.
candidate_instructions: Set priorities for the next twenty minutes, protect the deteriorating patient, and create a safe flow plan with the nurse in charge.
materials_provided: There are six admitted patients occupying assessment spaces, three ambulance handovers waiting, two resus bays occupied by patients who could move to a ward, and one patient in the waiting room with new confusion. One CT scanner is available, one porter is on shift and the site manager reports no ward beds until 16:00. The current time is 13:40.
sp_role_script: You are the nurse in charge. Open with: 'I have ambulances outside, no beds, and the waiting room is getting unsafe. What do you want changed first?' Provide capacity and staff details on request. Push back if the candidate tries to address every problem without prioritising. Reveal that the confused waiting room patient has a NEWS2 of 7 after two minutes.

checklist.item: Identifies the deteriorating waiting room patient as the first clinical priority and arranges immediate assessment and a monitored space.
Moves clinically stable resuscitation boarders to a suitable alternative area only after assessing their monitoring needs.
Triages ambulance handovers by clinical risk and ensures off loading does not leave patients unobserved.
Allocates named staff to the waiting room, resus, flow and handover tasks and uses the site manager effectively.
Gives a short team brief with one safety message and a shared trigger for escalation.
Escalates bed capacity and corridor risk to the hospital operational team with specific needs and a deadline.
Plans a second capacity review time and asks for a named clinician to own each high risk patient.
Documents the decisions, risks and outstanding capacity concerns without blaming individual teams.

model_answer: The first priority is the patient in the waiting room with new confusion and a rapidly rising NEWS2. I would ask the nurse in charge to move them straight into a monitored space and allocate a clinician to assess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose and possible sepsis or stroke. I would not wait for a ward bed. Next, I would review the two resuscitation patients and move one only if their ongoing monitoring and treatment can continue safely elsewhere. That creates space for the most urgent ambulance handovers. I would ask the site manager to find any safe bed, discharge lounge or escalation area and give a specific deadline. I would allocate a senior nurse to the waiting room, a team to handover and one person to track patient movement. I would hold a thirty second huddle: the risk is unobserved deterioration, the plan is to move the deteriorating patient and create one resus space, and any NEWS2 rise should be escalated immediately. I would review again at a set time or sooner if capacity changes. I would document decisions and unresolved risk. Disposition is a monitored department with defined ownership for every high risk patient.
