If safe care cannot be maintained, I would escalate to the emergency department consultant and hospital silver command.
references_provided: Department capacity board; NEWS2 chart; hospital patient flow escalation card; ambulance handover log.

title: Two nurses down at midnight
setting: Emergency department coordination office at the start of a night shift.
candidate_instructions: Respond to an unexpected staffing gap, set safe priorities, and agree a plan with the nurse in charge and the wider hospital team.
materials_provided: Two registered nurses have called in sick. The department has four resuscitation patients, twenty four assessment patients, a busy waiting room and two newly qualified nurses on shift. Agency cover is unlikely before 05:00. The nurse in charge is visibly stressed and one doctor is already managing two unstable patients.
sp_role_script: You are the nurse in charge. Open with: 'Two nurses are gone, I have four resus patients and the juniors are frightened. I do not think we are safe.' You are tearful and tired. If the candidate listens and makes concrete choices, you help identify staff who can move from lower acuity areas. If the candidate only says 'work harder' or 'be careful', you challenge them to state what will actually change.

checklist.item: Acknowledges the staffing concern and treats it as a patient safety problem rather than a personal failing.
Maps staff and skills to resus, assessment and waiting areas and identifies one safe minimum staffing model.
Escalates to the duty manager, consultant and site team with specific gaps and asks for concrete support.
Pauses or defers lower risk activity and creates a protected review process for waiting room patients.
Holds a clear huddle that names roles, break cover and the escalation trigger for deteriorating patients.
Supports the newly qualified nurses with supervision, specific tasks and permission to ask for help.
Sets a review time and documents the staffing risk and agreed mitigations.
Plans a post shift incident report and welfare follow up without assigning blame.

model_answer: I would tell the nurse in charge that I share the concern and that we will make the safest possible plan together. I would ask for a quick skills and location map, then protect one resus team and one clinician for the waiting room. I would move the most capable available nurse away from lower acuity work, ask the doctor covering two unstable patients to hand one to the consultant, and identify which non-urgent activities can pause. I would call the duty manager and consultant with specific requests: one nurse, one healthcare assistant and senior support for the novice staff. I would ask the site team to check nearby wards or the discharge lounge for safe help. I would hold a short huddle so every person knows their area, who to call and when to escalate. I would tell the newly qualified nurses which patients they should not manage alone. Breaks and hydration need a named cover plan, because tired staff make more mistakes. I would agree a review time and document the gap, decisions and unresolved risk. Disposition is a reduced but safe service with escalation to hospital command if the minimum staffing cannot be met. I would arrange an incident report and welfare follow up after the shift.
references_provided: Local escalation and safe staffing policy; department skills board; incident reporting form.

title: A run chart that changed after triage
setting: Quality improvement meeting preparation, with a twelve week run chart of time from arrival to first antibiotic for suspected sepsis.
candidate_instructions: Interpret the chart and write a balanced improvement plan. Do not assume that the change was effective or that every variation is a signal.
materials_provided: Median time to first antibiotic was stable at 54 minutes for the first eight weeks. A new triage prompt was introduced. Over the next four weeks the median fell to 39 minutes, with two weeks below the control limits. Missed antibiotic doses and staff-reported alert fatigue were not measured until week eleven. The data system changed in week ten and the triage prompt was later found to remain open when patients left the department.
task_details: Write four short sections: what the chart shows, what cannot be concluded, what data quality issues matter, and a safe next improvement step. The examiner will mark your written answer.

checklist.item: Describes the shift in the run chart without claiming that the intervention alone caused it.
Identifies the mid series data system change as a possible source of artifactual variation.
Recognises that the open prompt for departed patients may distort the measured time.
Balances speed with correct patient identification, allergy checks and antibiotic selection.
Adds balancing measures such as alert burden, inappropriate antibiotic use and missed treatments.
Plans a small test using PDSA cycles with a named owner and predefined review dates.
Includes frontline staff feedback and avoids blaming individuals for variation.
States a decision rule for scale, adaptation or stop based on both process and balancing measures.

model_answer: The run chart shows a stable median for eight weeks and a lower median after the triage prompt was introduced, with two points outside the previous variation. This is encouraging, but it does not prove that the prompt alone caused the change. The data system changed during the period, and the prompt could remain open after a patient left, which could make the measured time shorter without faster treatment. The missing balancing data are important because a prompt that speeds antibiotic administration may also create alert fatigue, wrong patient selection or unnecessary treatment. I would first validate the data by matching a sample of records to the antibiotic administration times and checking how the prompt closes. I would then ask staff and pharmacy what changed in practice. A safe improvement test would compare a revised prompt, with clear patient identification and an easy stop rule, against the current process for a limited period. The team would measure median time, severe sepsis treatment, wrong patient alerts, antibiotic appropriateness and staff workload. A named owner would review the chart every two weeks and use predefined PDSA cycles. I would not scale the prompt across the department until both the intended benefit and the balancing measures are stable. If the data remain unreliable, I would pause expansion and fix the information system first. I would escalate data quality concerns to the information governance lead, and disposition of the project is a controlled local test with a scheduled scale, adapt or stop decision.
references_provided: Anonymised twelve week run chart; data dictionary; local quality improvement project template.

title: An accelerated troponin pathway paper
setting: Critical appraisal discussion room with the examiner and a fictional released journal paper.
candidate_instructions: Discuss the validity and applicability of the study. Do not summarise it or perform calculations. Decide whether it is enough to change the local chest pain pathway.
materials_provided: A single centre non-inferiority study tested an accelerated high sensitivity troponin pathway against serial testing in adults with suspected acute coronary syndrome. At 30 days, major adverse cardiac events occurred in 3.1% with the accelerated pathway and 3.4% with standard care, with a non-inferiority margin of 1.0 percentage point. Thirty eight percent of eligible patients were excluded because they had renal impairment or an abnormal ECG. Follow up was by record review and complete for 94% of participants.
sp_role_script: You are the examiner. Open with: 'Why might the reported 30 day safety result be fragile?' Ask about selection, missing data and how you would judge transferability to a UK emergency department. If the candidate gives a broad research lecture, bring them back to this study and ask for a decision.

checklist.item: Identifies the primary safety question and explains that non-inferiority cannot be concluded unless the upper confidence bound for the treatment difference lies below the prespecified margin, without calculating the risk difference.
Assesses whether allocation, blinding and group comparability in a single centre study support the conclusion.
Explains how excluding a large group with renal impairment or ECG changes limits applicability.
Discusses incomplete follow up and record based outcome ascertainment as potential bias.
Considers whether the downstream care and event rates match the local population and guideline pathway.
Recognises that a safety trial cannot by itself establish the organisational or resource consequences of a faster pathway.
Gives a clear recommendation with conditions, uncertainty and a plan for local review.

model_answer: The study asks whether an accelerated high sensitivity troponin pathway is no worse than serial testing for 30 day major adverse cardiac events. The event percentages are numerically close and lower with the accelerated pathway, but I cannot conclude non-inferiority from these point estimates alone. I would confirm that the upper bound of the prespecified confidence interval for the between-group difference lies below the 1.0 percentage point margin and that the intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses support the same conclusion. I would inspect allocation concealment, standardised care and whether the groups had similar risk at baseline. In a single centre study, local processes may help produce the result. The finding is less transferable because 38% of eligible patients were excluded for renal impairment or abnormal ECG, exactly the patients in whom a rapid pathway can be hardest to apply. I would ask whether these exclusions were prespecified and whether the remaining group represents our undifferentiated chest pain population. Follow up by record review and 94% completeness can miss events treated elsewhere, so the safety estimate may be optimistic. I would check how patients with defaulting or unclear results were managed. A 30 day outcome is useful but does not cover longer term missed diagnoses. Non-inferiority also depends on reliable implementation, serial sampling and a clear action threshold. My conclusion is cautious support for a local pilot, not immediate replacement of the current pathway. I would test it with an explicit eligibility list, a stop rule for excluded patients, follow up checks and balancing measures such as overcrowding and repeat testing. I would escalate a proposed pathway change to the local acute coronary syndrome guideline group, and disposition of this appraisal is a guarded pilot with a formal safety review.
references_provided: Fictional practice trial abstract and eligibility table; local suspected acute coronary syndrome pathway; critical appraisal prompt.

title: Pleuritic pain at 28 weeks
setting: Emergency department obstetric assessment bay with access to maternity and acute medicine review.
candidate_instructions: Assess this pregnant patient with chest pain and breathlessness, arrange urgent investigation and treatment, and plan safe ongoing care.
materials_provided: A 28 week pregnant patient has sudden right sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after resting at home. Respiratory rate 24/min, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, oxygen saturation 94% on air. Left calf is tender and swollen. ECG is sinus tachycardia. No vaginal bleeding and fetal movements are normal.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'It came on suddenly when I stood up and now I cannot take a deep breath.' You feel frightened about the baby and ask whether tests will harm the pregnancy. You have no haemoptysis and no syncope. If asked, disclose recent long car travel and a swollen calf. You can give informed consent for imaging once the risk and benefit are explained clearly.

checklist.item: Takes a focused history for pulmonary embolism, bleeding risk, recent travel or immobility, pregnancy complications and fetal wellbeing.
Assesses respiratory effort, perfusion, chest and leg findings and fetal movement while noting maternal observations.
Uses the pregnancy specific suspected pulmonary embolism pathway and does not rely on D-dimer to exclude the diagnosis.
Starts treatment dose low molecular weight heparin before imaging when risk is high, after checking bleeding contraindications and local guidance.
Arranges urgent appropriate chest imaging with maternity and radiology input rather than allowing fetal concern to delay diagnosis.
Explains the balance of maternal and fetal risk from untreated clot and from imaging in clear language.
Contacts obstetric, acute medicine and haematology teams and arranges fetal assessment when appropriate.
States a monitored admission plan with repeat observations and explicit deterioration triggers.

model_answer: This presentation makes pulmonary embolism the leading diagnosis. I would place the patient in a monitored area, give oxygen to maintain normal saturations and assess airway, breathing and circulation. I would request an ECG, chest radiograph, blood gas, full blood count, renal and liver function, clotting and group and save. I would not rely on D-dimer, because it is not useful for excluding pulmonary embolism in pregnancy. I would use the pregnancy specific suspected pulmonary embolism pathway and discuss urgent imaging with radiology and obstetrics. CTPA or ventilation perfusion imaging can be performed with a pregnancy adapted protocol, and treatment should not be delayed by concern about fetal radiation. If the clinical probability is high and there is no major bleeding risk, I would start treatment dose low molecular weight heparin before the scan under local guidance. I would explain why an untreated clot is more dangerous than the carefully controlled imaging dose. I would also assess the tender calf and arrange fetal monitoring according to obstetric advice. Disposition is admission for anticoagulation, imaging, oxygen and repeated maternal observations. Escalate immediately for syncope, worsening hypoxia, hypotension or chest pain. I would hand over the imaging result and anticoagulation timing to the obstetric and medical teams.
references_provided: Local pregnancy pulmonary embolism pathway; maternal early warning chart; radiology pregnancy imaging information.

title: Fever in a transplanted kidney
setting: Emergency department side room for an immunosuppressed patient, with transplant and renal services available.
candidate_instructions: Assess the patient with a renal transplant, identify the urgent risks, and arrange treatment and specialist review.
materials_provided: A 48 year old with a renal transplant has one day of fever, graft pain and nausea. Temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 96% on air, NEWS2 6. Creatinine has risen from 145 to 236 micromol/L since yesterday. Tacrolimus trough is not yet available.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'My transplant kidney is sore and I feel awful. Please do not let me lose it.' You have reduced urine output. You take tacrolimus and mycophenolate. If asked, disclose no recent travel, no diarrhoea and a missed routine blood test last week. You ask whether immunosuppression should be stopped and become anxious when admission is mentioned.

checklist.item: Establishes transplant history, immunosuppressive medicines, rejection episodes, urine output, adherence and exposure history.
Assesses graft tenderness, volume status, skin, chest and perfusion and records infection signs.
Recognises possible graft infection, rejection, obstruction or drug toxicity and does not focus on one cause.
Orders cultures, lactate, blood count, biochemistry, drug levels, urine tests and transplant ultrasound without delaying treatment.
Starts antibiotics from the local immunosuppressed patient pathway after checking allergies and recent microbiology.
Contacts the transplant service and renal team early for immunosuppression advice and definitive treatment.
Explains that immunosuppression should not be stopped or changed without specialist advice and answers the patient's concerns.
States a monitored speciality disposition with clear sepsis and urine output review triggers.

model_answer: A transplant patient with fever, graft pain, hypotension and rising creatinine is at high risk of graft infection and sepsis, but rejection or obstruction may also be present. I would move the patient to a monitored room, take cultures before antibiotics when that causes no delay, and request lactate, full blood count, renal and liver function, blood gas, urine testing, cytomegalovirus testing if indicated and a tacrolimus level. I would prescribe antibiotics from the local immunosuppressed patient pathway after checking allergies and previous cultures. I would give careful fluids guided by perfusion and urine output. I would contact the transplant and renal teams immediately to discuss immunosuppression and the need for graft ultrasound. I would not stop mycophenolate or tacrolimus without specialist advice because that could precipitate rejection. I would explain that admission is needed to treat infection and protect both the patient and the transplant. Disposition is admission under the renal or transplant team with sepsis observations, strict fluid balance and a named review time. Escalation is required for worsening hypotension, confusion, anuria or a deterioration in the ultrasound findings. I would document medicine times and speak directly to the transplant team.
references_provided: Local immunosuppressed sepsis pathway; renal transplant alert card; NEWS2 chart; transplant unit contact sheet.

title: Weak legs that are moving upward
setting: Emergency department high observation area with access to neurology and critical care.
candidate_instructions: Assess this progressive weakness, identify respiratory and autonomic risk, and arrange safe monitoring and treatment.
materials_provided: A 39 year old has had two days of ascending leg weakness and now cannot climb stairs. Reflexes are absent and vibration sensation is reduced at the toes. Vital capacity is 18 mL/kg and falling. Heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 96% on air. The patient has had no recent diarrhoea but had a flu-like illness three weeks ago.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'My legs have been getting weaker since yesterday and now my hands feel clumsy.' You are frightened about becoming unable to breathe. You have no chest pain and no head injury. If asked, disclose that swallowing is becoming harder and you feel breathless when lying flat. You want to know whether you will be paralysed and what can be done.

checklist.item: Establishes the rate and pattern of weakness, sensory change, swallowing or speech symptoms, infection history and exposure history.
Assesses limb power, reflexes, sensory pattern, cranial nerves, breathing effort and vital capacity at repeated intervals.
Recognises probable Guillain Barre syndrome and identifies respiratory failure and bulbar weakness as immediate risks.
Requests cerebrospinal fluid assessment, blood gas, electrolytes, glucose, infection tests and relevant imaging according to the differential.
Calls neurology and critical care early and arranges high dependency monitoring with serial vital capacity.
Considers intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange with neurology and checks contraindications such as immunoglobulin A deficiency.
Avoids corticosteroids for this presentation unless another diagnosis and specialist plan supports them.
Explains the likely diagnosis, uncertainty and risk of breathing support while checking the patient's understanding.
Names an intensive care or neurology disposition and states specific escalation triggers.

model_answer: Ascending weakness, absent reflexes and recent viral illness suggest Guillain Barre syndrome. The falling vital capacity, bulbar symptoms and breathlessness when lying flat make respiratory failure likely. I would move the patient to a monitored high dependency area and involve neurology and critical care now. I would perform serial vital capacity, respiratory rate and single breath count, examine swallowing and speech, and monitor ECG because autonomic instability can occur. I would request blood gases, electrolytes, renal function, glucose, liver tests, infection screening and cerebrospinal fluid examination if neurology agrees. Nerve conduction studies may be needed later. I would not give corticosteroids for suspected Guillain Barre syndrome. Neurology should advise on intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange and check contraindications, including immunoglobulin A deficiency. I would avoid unnecessary movement and provide thromboprophylaxis and pressure care according to the local plan. I would explain that weakness may progress for a time and that breathing support can be provided if needed. Disposition is a critical care or neurology high dependency bed with repeated respiratory measurements. I would escalate immediately for a further fall in vital capacity, difficulty swallowing, choking, aspiration or rising carbon dioxide.
references_provided: Local neuromuscular weakness pathway; vital capacity and respiratory observation chart; neurology and critical care contact sheet.

title: Bleeding and pregnancy loss
setting: Emergency department obstetric assessment room with a midwife and the obstetric team available.
candidate_instructions: Assess the bleeding, give immediate care, and discuss the likely pregnancy loss with sensitivity while agreeing the next steps.
materials_provided: A 15 week pregnant patient has heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping. On arrival, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on air and temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Haemoglobin is 98 g/L. On bedside ultrasound by the treating clinician no fetal heart is visible, but a full assessment is pending. The patient is tearful and accompanied by her partner.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'Please tell me the baby is still there.' Speak quietly and cry if the candidate gives bad news without warning. If asked, say you have had pain at home, passed a large clot and filled two pads in an hour six hours ago. You want your partner with you. Once the candidate explains the findings and uncertainty, ask what will happen next and whether you can have a funeral or religious ceremony.

checklist.item: Establishes blood loss, pain, passage of tissue, gestation, prior pregnancies, blood group and relevant medical history.
Assesses circulation, abdominal and pelvic tenderness and ongoing bleeding while maintaining privacy and dignity.
Requests IV access, group and save, full blood count and crossmatch as indicated and contacts the obstetric team.
Recognises that bedside ultrasound alone cannot establish the final diagnosis and arranges urgent obstetric ultrasound review.
Gives a clear warning and uses the patient's preferred terms when explaining the likely loss and uncertainty.
Asks about cultural, religious and burial needs and offers a suitable staff member or bereavement support.
Plans anti D immunoglobulin if indicated by blood group and local guidance and discusses management options with obstetrics.
States a monitored obstetric disposition with ongoing observation, clear return triggers and follow up by the obstetric or second-trimester pregnancy loss service.

model_answer: I would first check the patient's circulation and ongoing blood loss, place her on a monitoring bed and gain intravenous access. I would provide pain relief and privacy with her partner present. I would take a focused history of gestation, bleeding, clots and tissue passage, then arrange full blood count, group and save and crossmatch if needed. I would ask the obstetric team and second-trimester pregnancy loss service for urgent review. I would explain that the bedside scan does not show a heartbeat and that a full assessment is needed, using clear language and pausing after the news. I would not imply certainty before the formal scan. I would involve the midwife and ask about cultural, religious or burial needs, and I would offer bereavement information and support. I would check the blood group and arrange anti D immunoglobulin if the local pathway indicates it. If bleeding continues or she becomes unstable, I would discuss urgent obstetric or surgical management. If she is stable after assessment and the process is complete, the obstetric team can arrange follow up. Disposition is either monitored admission or supported obstetric review depending on bleeding and results. I would document the exact information given and the support provided. I would escalate to the consultant obstetrician and critical care team if bleeding remains heavy, pain worsens or the observations become abnormal.
references_provided: Local second-trimester bleeding and pregnancy loss pathway; anti D immunoglobulin checklist; bereavement and pregnancy loss leaflet.

title: Breathlessness, family pressure and a preferred plan
setting: Emergency department side room with oncology, palliative care and critical care outreach available.
candidate_instructions: Relieve the patient's distress, explore their goals, and manage a disagreement with the relative about escalation.
materials_provided: A 65 year old with metastatic lung cancer has worsening breathlessness. Respiratory rate 28/min, oxygen saturation 88% on air, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, heart rate 106/min and GCS 15. There is a small right pleural effusion and no evidence of a large pneumothorax. The patient says they do not want a breathing tube. The relative insists that everything must be done.
sp_role_script: You are the patient. Open with: 'I am not afraid of dying, but I am frightened of suffocating. Please do not put a tube down my throat.' You can explain that comfort and time with family matter most. If asked, disclose that the palliative team knows you and that you want treatment for breathlessness that can help quickly. Your relative is not in the room during the first part of the conversation.

checklist.item: Assesses and treats reversible contributors to breathlessness while avoiding interventions that conflict with the patient's informed values.
Explores the patient's understanding, fears and goals before discussing specific treatments.
Plans oxygen, careful fluid or drainage decisions and titrated symptom treatment in line with palliative guidance.
Confirms capacity and records the patient's own refusal or acceptance of intubation without seeking relative consent.
Invites the relative to a separate conversation and explores their fear and reason for demanding full escalation.
Explains that the relative's role is to support the patient's wishes and does not attack or dismiss the family.
Involves oncology, palliative care and critical care outreach in a shared treatment plan.
Documents the ceiling of treatment, symptom plan, review time and named escalation route.

model_answer: I would focus first on the patient's breathlessness and fear. I would sit at eye level, use a calm voice and ask what the symptom feels like and what matters most. I would give oxygen to a target range and assess for reversible problems such as pleural effusion, infection or pulmonary embolism. I would discuss small volume drainage or other treatment only if it fits the patient's goals. I would use opioids and other symptom treatments in a titrated palliative plan with senior or palliative advice. The patient has capacity and has clearly said no to intubation, so that decision belongs to them. I would record their own goals and ceiling of treatment. I would speak with the relative separately and ask what they fear will happen. I would explain that we will treat breathlessness and distress fully, but that intubation may not achieve the outcome they hope for and may not fit the patient's wishes. I would not ask the relative to consent to treatment. Oncology and palliative care should be involved. Disposition may be a monitored bed, a palliative care bed or a supported home plan depending on symptom control and the patient's informed choice. I would state clear triggers for symptom review and escalation while respecting the agreed plan.
references_provided: Local palliative breathlessness pathway; oncology summary; capacity and treatment escalation form.

title: Teaching a sixty second safety huddle
setting: Emergency department team room with an emergency medicine specialty registrar learner and a printed example of a crowded shift.
candidate_instructions: Teach the learner to lead a short safety huddle before a difficult shift. Focus on useful structure, shared risk and clear ownership.
materials_provided: The learner will coordinate the next shift. The printed brief lists four resuscitation patients, two patients waiting for beds, a new nurse on her first shift, and a planned CT transfer.
sp_role_script: You are an emergency medicine specialty registrar who has been asked to learn how to run the huddle. Open with: 'I usually read out the bed numbers and then everyone disappears. It feels like a list, not a plan.' You can identify the high risk patients but are not sure how to make the team speak up. Ask for a repeatable structure you can use in eight minutes or less.

checklist.item: Asks what the learner currently does and agrees a specific teaching goal for the huddle.
Teaches a short structure: safety, highest risks, plan, ownership and escalation.
Models how to ask every team member for a concern without turning the huddle into a long meeting.
Uses the printed shift to have the learner rehearse a real huddle aloud.

Identifies the resuscitation cohort as the highest-risk group and gives named ownership for active review of any unstable patient, supervision of the novice nurse, and the timing and escort for the CT transfer.
Gives feedback on clarity, brevity and whether another person could repeat the plan.
Leaves the learner with a written prompt and a supervised next attempt.

model_answer: I would ask the learner what happens now and what they want the huddle to achieve. Their goal is to move from reading a list to creating shared ownership. I would teach a five part structure: a one sentence safety moment, the highest clinical risks, the plan for each, a named person for each action, and the trigger for escalation. I would remind them that the huddle should be short enough to repeat later. I would demonstrate by asking the team, 'What could hurt a patient in the next hour?' Then I would ask the learner to run the printed shift aloud. They should identify the resuscitation cohort as the highest-risk group, name who owns active review of any patient who becomes unstable, protect the novice nurse with supervision and give the CT transfer a clear timing and escort. I would ask them to stop after each section and ask one team member to repeat back the plan. Feedback would name one clear strength and one change. I would correct any vague phrase such as 'keep an eye' by asking for a person, an action and a time. The learning is complete when the learner can give a short huddle another staff member can repeat. Disposition is a supervised huddle at the start of the next shift with a written prompt.
references_provided: Printed shift brief; one page safety huddle prompt; local escalation card.

title: Cord prolapse in the emergency department
setting: Resuscitation bay with a patient in advanced pregnancy and the obstetric team called from the labour ward.
candidate_instructions: Lead the immediate response to a suspected umbilical cord prolapse and prepare for emergency delivery.
materials_provided: A 34 week pregnant patient arrived after spontaneous rupture of membranes and felt something in the vagina. A loop of pulsating cord is visible at the introitus. There is no active pushing, no heavy bleeding and the fetal heart is 90 beats per minute. Maternal observations are respiratory rate 22/min, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% on air.
sp_role_script: You are the obstetric registrar on the phone. Say: 'Keep her off the cord and prepare for immediate caesarean delivery. Tell me the fetal heart and whether you can elevate the presenting part.' Give clear instructions for knee chest positioning and bladder filling if transfer will be delayed. Ask the candidate to repeat the plan and call back with the fetal heart every two minutes.

checklist.item: Calls the obstetric emergency team and states that this is a time critical fetal emergency.
Positions the patient knee chest or in a left lateral head down position according to the local obstetric guideline.
Avoids handling or replacing the cord and uses a gloved hand to elevate the presenting part if trained and instructed.
Provides oxygen and continuous fetal heart monitoring and records the times of each change.
Prepares for category 1 caesarean delivery in the obstetric theatre with the aim of birth within 30 minutes, unless an immediate competent examination shows that vaginal birth is imminent.
Discusses bladder filling or tocolysis with obstetrics when transfer will be delayed, without delaying definitive care.
Explains the emergency to the patient in short sentences and obtains enough cooperation without delaying treatment.
Names a transfer lead, prepares airway and neonatal support, and gives a structured handover.

model_answer: This is an obstetric emergency because cord compression can rapidly cause fetal hypoxia. I would call the obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams immediately and tell them there is a visible pulsating cord. I would put the patient into a knee chest position or the position specified by the local obstetric guideline and keep her there. I would avoid touching the cord and record the fetal heart continuously. If trained and instructed, I would use a gloved hand to elevate the presenting part, but I would not attempt to replace the cord. I would give oxygen and monitor maternal observations. Because vaginal birth is not imminent at 34 weeks and the fetal heart rate is 90 beats per minute, the obstetric team should prepare for category 1 caesarean delivery aiming for birth within 30 minutes; bladder filling or tocolysis may be used only as a bridge and must not delay delivery. The patient should be transferred on a trolley in the correct position, with a named person maintaining positioning and handover. I would explain that the cord is being compressed and that delivery is needed urgently. I would prepare for a collapsed baby and ensure neonatal support. Disposition is immediate transfer to the obstetric theatre for category 1 caesarean delivery. I would document the fetal heart, times, position changes and team instructions. Delay in definitive obstetric care is the main risk. I would escalate immediately to the consultant obstetrician and anaesthetist if delivery cannot proceed promptly or the fetal heart remains abnormal.
references_provided: Local cord prolapse pathway; obstetric emergency contact card; fetal monitoring record.

title: Wide complexes after a tricyclic overdose
setting: Resuscitation bay with a patient who has taken an unidentified overdose and is becoming drowsy.
candidate_instructions: Lead the immediate resuscitation, recognise dangerous poisoning features, and arrange safe ongoing care.
materials_provided: A 24 year old has taken an unknown number of antidepressant tablets. Heart rate 132/min, blood pressure 86/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 96% on air. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 148 ms. The patient has had one brief seizure and now has a GCS of 12. Venous pH is 7.28 and potassium is 4.2 mmol/L.
sp_role_script: You are the emergency nurse. Open with: 'The ECG is wide and she has already seized once. What do you want drawn up?' Provide medication history and results when asked. Ask the candidate to confirm the treatment before administration. Announce that the blood pressure is falling and the patient is becoming harder to rouse if airway and circulation are not addressed.

checklist.item: Allocates airway, monitoring, drug, ECG and documentation roles and calls the poisons service and critical care.
Provides airway support, oxygen, suction and continuous cardiac monitoring without inducing vomiting.
Recognises a sodium channel blocking toxidrome and treats the wide QRS with sodium bicarbonate according to the local toxicology pathway.
Treats seizures with benzodiazepines and avoids giving flumazenil.
Monitors and treats hypotension, acidosis and electrolyte disturbance while avoiding harmful antiarrhythmic choices.
Requests repeated blood gases, ECG, glucose, electrolytes and renal function and checks the poison history with collateral sources.
Checks drug, dose and route aloud before administration and asks for closed loop confirmation.
Secures critical care disposition and states the triggers for intubation or cardiovascular collapse.

model_answer: A tricyclic overdose can cause sodium channel blockade, seizures, hypotension and fatal arrhythmia. I would take control, allocate roles and call the poisons service and critical care. I would support the airway, give oxygen, attach continuous cardiac monitoring and keep IV access. The wide QRS and seizure after a suspected tricyclic overdose indicate serious toxicity, so I would give sodium bicarbonate according to the local toxicology protocol. I would treat further seizures with a benzodiazepine and avoid flumazenil because it can precipitate seizures and arrhythmia. I would monitor blood pressure and use fluid cautiously, with early vasopressor support if shock persists. Repeated blood gases, ECG, electrolytes, glucose and renal function are needed. I would not give class IA or class IC antiarrhythmics. I would speak with the poisons service before unusual treatments. The patient needs a critical care bed with continuous ECG monitoring and a clear plan for intubation if conscious level or ventilation worsens. Disposition is critical care for observation and treatment of arrhythmia, seizures and aspiration risk. I would hand over the exact ECG changes, seizure duration, drugs given and time of ingestion. Any sudden collapse requires immediate resuscitation. I would escalate to the consultant and critical care team if the QRS widens further, shock persists or the airway is lost.
references_provided: Local tricyclic overdose pathway; poisons service contact card; ECG tracing; critical care referral form.

title: Swollen tongue after a new blood pressure tablet
setting: Resuscitation bay with a patient developing facial swelling and noisy breathing after starting ramipril.
candidate_instructions: Lead the immediate airway assessment and resuscitation, identify the likely medicine related cause, and arrange definitive care.
materials_provided: A 58 year old started ramipril six days ago. The tongue and lips are swollen, the voice is muffled and there is inspiratory stridor. Respiratory rate 26/min, oxygen saturation 93% on air, heart rate 116/min and blood pressure 146/82 mmHg. There is no urticaria, wheeze or recent food or insect exposure.
sp_role_script: You are the anaesthetic registrar. Open with: 'The tongue is enlarging and the stridor is louder. What is your airway plan?' Report that there is no rash or wheeze and that the patient is on an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. Offer a difficult airway trolley, video laryngoscopy and a front of neck access plan. State that the voice is deteriorating if the candidate delays calling for senior airway support.

checklist.item: Recognises a threatened airway and calls anaesthetics, the airway lead and critical care immediately.
Identifies angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor related angioedema and distinguishes it from anaphylaxis by the history and examination.
Sits the patient upright if safe, gives high flow oxygen and minimises examination that could provoke further swelling.
Prepares for early senior airway management with difficult airway equipment and surgical access backup.
Stops the suspected medicine and avoids giving anaphylaxis treatment automatically when the picture is isolated drug related angioedema.
Seeks specialist advice about targeted treatments and supportive care, recognising that antihistamines and steroids may not reverse this mechanism.
Gives concise closed loop instructions and explains the airway risk to the patient without prolonged discussion.
Names a critical care disposition and a post airway observation plan for recurrent swelling.

model_answer: This is likely angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor related angioedema. Tongue swelling and stridor indicate a threatened airway. I would call anaesthetics, critical care and the airway lead immediately and take control of the room. I would keep the patient upright, give high flow oxygen and avoid unnecessary airway stimulation. I would not assume this is anaphylaxis when there is no rash, wheeze or exposure history, although deterioration must always prompt reassessment. I would stop ramipril and prepare for early intubation by the most experienced operator, with video laryngoscopy, suction, difficult airway equipment and a declared front of neck access plan. The team must be ready for rapid loss of view. I would seek specialist advice about targeted treatments and supportive measures, and I would not rely on antihistamines or steroids as definitive treatment. I would avoid giving intramuscular adrenaline unless the patient develops a true anaphylactic picture. Disposition is a critical care bed after airway control, with monitoring for recurrent swelling after extubation. I would document the medicine, onset, airway findings and treatment times. If intubation is not possible, the team must move immediately to the planned surgical airway. I would escalate to the airway lead and intensive care consultant if stridor worsens or recurrent swelling develops.
references_provided: Difficult airway trolley checklist; local angioedema pathway; current allergy and anaesthetic contact cards.

title: A low fall with a blood thinner
setting: Emergency department major trauma assessment area for an older adult after a care home fall.
candidate_instructions: Assess the injuries, identify the risks of anticoagulation and frailty, and arrange a safe multidisciplinary plan.
materials_provided: An 88 year old fell from standing, struck their head and has right hip pain. GCS 15, respiratory rate 18/min, heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 136/78 mmHg. They take apixaban, last dose five hours ago. CT head shows a small acute subdural haematoma without midline shift. There is a displaced right neck of femur fracture. The patient is usually mobile with a frame and has capacity.
sp_role_script: You are the patient. Open with: 'I banged my head and now my hip is agony. I want to go back to my home.' You are orientated and can make decisions. If asked, disclose that you take apixaban for atrial fibrillation and that a neighbour usually visits. You become anxious when told you need admission and ask whether the head bleed will get worse.

checklist.item: Establishes the fall mechanism, head strike, anticoagulant dose and timing, baseline mobility, cognition and home support.
Completes a trauma primary survey, neurological examination and hip assessment and records serial GCS and pupils.
Recognises that a small subdural haematoma in an anticoagulated older adult can deteriorate and needs senior review.
Contacts the major trauma, neurosurgical and orthopaedic teams and seeks local anticoagulation reversal guidance.
Plans early analgesia, pressure area care and timely hip fracture surgery while balancing the head injury risk.
Explains the uncertainty and need for observation and checks the patient's goals and understanding.
States a monitored admission disposition with neurological observation and escalation triggers.
Involves orthogeriatrics, nursing and therapy teams in a plan for mobility, nutrition and discharge.

model_answer: This is a major injury in an older adult because a small intracranial bleed can expand and the femoral fracture requires surgery. I would complete a primary survey, record serial GCS and pupils, examine the hip and look for other injuries. I would contact the major trauma, neurosurgical and orthopaedic teams early. I would seek immediate local haematology or major haemorrhage advice about reversal of apixaban and timing of surgery. I would avoid assuming that a small bleed is safe. I would give effective analgesia, protect pressure areas and arrange urgent orthopaedic planning while maintaining neurological observations. Blood tests, crossmatch and repeat imaging should follow the trauma and local anticoagulation guidelines. I would explain that the head injury and hip fracture both need admission and that the patient will be monitored closely. I would ask about home arrangements and involve orthogeriatrics, therapy and social care. The patient should not go back to the care home from the emergency department because the head injury needs observation and the fracture needs definitive treatment. Disposition is a monitored trauma or orthopaedic bed with a clear plan for repeat neuro observations and surgery. I would escalate immediately for a falling GCS, new weakness, severe headache or vomiting.
references_provided: Local anticoagulation reversal guideline; major trauma obs chart; orthogeriatric referral form.

title: Crushed hand in an industrial press
setting: Emergency department procedure room with a simulated crushed hand and access to hand surgery.
candidate_instructions: Assess and describe the initial management of this crushed hand, including pain control, neurovascular checks, wound care, splinting and escalation.
materials_provided: A 42 year old factory worker trapped their dominant right hand in a press for two minutes. The hand is swollen, bruised and deformed across the metacarpals with a bleeding laceration over the dorsum. Capillary refill is two seconds and sensation is reduced in the index finger. There are no other injuries. The patient is alert with heart rate 106/min and blood pressure 128/82 mmHg.
task_details: Explain every step aloud while working on the simulated hand. State the analgesia, imaging, wound dressing, splint and referral you would arrange. Describe the neurovascular checks you would repeat and the signs that require urgent theatre.

checklist.item: Checks radial and digital pulses, capillary refill, colour, sensation and tendon function and documents deficits.
Provides multimodal analgesia and considers regional anaesthesia or procedural sedation under the local protocol.
Covers the wound with a sterile dressing, elevates the hand and removes rings or tight items.
Requests appropriate hand radiographs and blood tests, including creatine kinase when significant muscle crushing is present.
Looks for compartment syndrome and crush syndrome risks rather than focusing only on the visible wound.
Contacts hand surgery urgently and arranges admission or transfer for exploration and fixation.
Explains the risk of loss of function and the plan for theatre and gives simple neurovascular warning advice.
Sets a monitored disposition with repeat neurovascular observations and a clear escalation trigger.

model_answer: I would treat this as a significant crush injury with possible fracture, tendon injury and compartment syndrome. I would first check the radial and digital pulses, capillary refill, colour, sensation and movement in every finger. I would document the reduced index sensation before analgesia. I would give prompt multimodal analgesia and consider a regional block or procedural sedation under the local protocol. I would remove rings, cover the open wound with a sterile dressing, elevate the hand and provide tetanus and antibiotic treatment if indicated by the wound and local policy. I would request hand radiographs and blood tests, including creatine kinase because muscle crushing can cause rhabdomyolysis. I would look repeatedly for severe pain, tense swelling and worsening passive stretch. I would call hand surgery immediately and explain the site, deformity, wound and neurovascular findings. The patient should be nil by mouth and prepared for urgent exploration, washout and fixation. I would explain that the visible injury may hide deeper damage and that hand function is at risk. Disposition is admission under hand surgery with elevation, neurovascular checks and pain control. I would escalate immediately if perfusion worsens or signs of compartment syndrome develop.
references_provided: Hand injury observation chart; local analgesia and sedation protocol; hand surgery contact card; tetanus form.

title: Lower abdominal pain in a fifteen year old
setting: Paediatric emergency department bay with a confidential adolescent consultation space and access to gynaecology.
candidate_instructions: Assess the pain and bleeding safely, arrange urgent gynaecological review, and manage confidentiality and safeguarding with the adolescent.
materials_provided: A 15 year old has eight hours of worsening right iliac fossa pain and a small amount of vaginal bleeding. Urine pregnancy test is positive. Heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min and temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. The patient says she does not want her parents told.
sp_role_script: Open with: 'Please do not tell my mum. I only told the receptionist because I was scared.' You are frightened and embarrassed. If asked, confirm that you are sexually active and that your boyfriend is also 15. You can explain that you want confidential care, but ask who will be told if something is seriously wrong. Respond to a calm, private explanation and agree to supported contact if the clinical situation becomes urgent.

checklist.item: Takes a private adolescent history and separately assesses Gillick competence for the specific examination, investigation and treatment decisions, checking whether she can understand, retain, use and weigh the relevant information and communicate a choice.

If she is Gillick competent, seeks her own consent to examination, investigation and treatment and shares confidential information only where a lawful and proportionate safeguarding justification exists; if she is not competent, involves someone with parental responsibility unless treatment is immediately necessary to prevent serious harm.
Assesses circulation, abdominal tenderness and pregnancy signs while preserving privacy and offering a chaperone.
Recognises possible ectopic pregnancy and arranges urgent senior and gynaecology assessment.
Requests blood group, full blood count, hCG and urgent pelvic ultrasound while continuing observations.
Explains confidentiality, its limits and the safeguarding concern for a sexual relationship involving a minor.
Supports the patient to involve a trusted adult and does not promise absolute secrecy.
Considers anti D immunoglobulin and the local early pregnancy and safeguarding pathways with specialist advice.
States a monitored disposition with safeguarding referral and a named senior clinician.

model_answer: A positive pregnancy test with pain and bleeding in a 15 year old raises the possibility of ectopic pregnancy and requires urgent assessment. I would speak with her privately, use an appropriate chaperone and take a sensitive sexual history. I would assess Gillick competence for each proposed examination, investigation and treatment decision. If she is competent, I would seek her own consent and explain what information must be shared for safeguarding and why. If she is not competent, I would involve someone with parental responsibility unless urgent treatment is immediately necessary to prevent serious harm, and I would document the legal basis. I would explain the limits of confidentiality at the start and reassure her that treatment would not be delayed. I would place her in a monitored cubicle, check circulation and abdominal signs and send blood group, full blood count, hCG and urgent pelvic ultrasound. I would contact the paediatric or gynaecology consultant immediately. If she is unstable, I would follow the local early pregnancy emergency pathway and arrange anti D if indicated. The relationship with another 15 year old is still a safeguarding matter under the local pathway, so I would make a timely referral and discuss the case with the named safeguarding team. I would support her to tell a trusted adult and explain why staff need to share limited information. I would not promise that no one else will be told. Disposition is a monitored paediatric or gynaecology bed with safeguarding documentation and a named senior lead. I would escalate for worsening pain, syncope, hypotension or increasing bleeding.
references_provided: Early pregnancy assessment pathway; paediatric safeguarding flowchart; adolescent confidentiality guidance; anti D checklist.

title: Violence in the waiting room
setting: Emergency department waiting area after a patient becomes agitated, throws a chair and moves toward the clinical desk.
candidate_instructions: Lead a safe response to the immediate threat, coordinate the team and protect patients while continuing care for a collapsing patient.
materials_provided: The person is pacing, shouting and repeatedly clenching their fists. Staff are behind the desk, several patients are nearby, and one child is crying. Security is two minutes away and police have been called. Another patient in the waiting room has become pale and slumped in a chair.
sp_role_script: You are the senior nurse. Open with: 'He has thrown a chair and is blocking the corridor. At the same time an older man has slumped in the waiting room.' Ask the candidate for clear instructions. Report that security is coming and police are on route. If the candidate approaches alone, warn that the person may be carrying something and staff are not trained to physically restrain him.

checklist.item: Takes control and prioritises staff, patient and environmental safety before trying to calm or examine the agitated person.
Uses calm de-escalation from a safe distance, with an exit route and a clear boundary rather than confrontation.

Moves other patients and staff away and names one person to liaise with the security response already en route and the police who have already been called, giving a clear location, keeping the line open and providing updates.
Separates the immediate threat response from the medical response and allocates a team to the collapsed patient.
Considers agitation from hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, intoxication, head injury or mental illness without approaching unsafely.
Avoids threatening language, crowding, sudden movements and physical restraint unless there is an immediate unavoidable risk.
Plans a clinical assessment and least restrictive management once security has made the area safe.
Documents the incident, handover, injury checks and support for affected staff and patients.

model_answer: I would treat the safety of patients and staff as the first priority. I would create distance, keep an exit route behind me and ask the team not to crowd or restrain the person unless there is an unavoidable immediate risk. I would assign one named staff member to liaise with the security team already en route and the police who have already been called, give a clear location, keep the line open and provide updates. Another team would move nearby patients, especially the crying child and the collapsed patient, away from the threat. I would use a calm voice and short statements, acknowledge that the person is distressed and set a clear boundary without arguing. I would not approach alone. Once security has established safety, I would check whether the agitation may be caused by hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, intoxication, head injury or mental illness. The collapsed patient needs an independent airway and circulation assessment immediately. I would keep the two responses separate so neither is neglected. Restraint and sedation would only be used under the local policy, with legal advice and the least restrictive option. Afterward I would document events, injuries, police and security involvement, and arrange staff debrief and support. Disposition depends on the medical cause, mental health assessment and whether a safe environment can be maintained. I would escalate to police, security and the senior clinical manager immediately if the threat cannot be contained or another patient deteriorates.
references_provided: Local violence and security policy; security incident card; de-escalation prompt; incident reporting form.

title: Explaining a delayed diagnosis to a family
setting: Emergency department family room after an older patient with a missed infection has deteriorated and moved to intensive care.
candidate_instructions: Lead an initial open disclosure conversation with the daughter, explain what is known and unknown, and agree the next steps.
materials_provided: A 72 year old attended yesterday with leg pain and was discharged with a suspected muscle strain. They returned today with severe pain, confusion and shock. Necrotising fasciitis is now suspected and they are in theatre. The daughter wants to know why the diagnosis was missed. The case review has started but the full timeline is not yet complete.
sp_role_script: You are the patient's daughter. Open with: 'I told the doctor something was badly wrong. Why did you send my dad home?' You are angry and frightened but willing to listen. If the candidate acknowledges the harm, apologises and explains what is known and unknown, you calm slightly. Ask what will happen now, who will keep you updated and how to make a complaint without losing access to information.

checklist.item: Introduces the team, confirms the relationship and gives the conversation privacy and enough uninterrupted time.
Acknowledges distress and answers the question about the previous visit without defensiveness.
Gives a clear factual summary, states uncertainty and avoids blaming an individual or speculating.
Offers a sincere apology for the harm and distress without claiming the full causal review is complete.
Explains the current clinical situation, theatre and intensive care plan and when the next update will occur.
Starts the local incident review and duty of candour process and identifies who will be the family's contact.
Offers patient advice and liaison service or complaint information without making it a condition of care.
Checks what the daughter has understood and records the discussion and promised follow up.

model_answer: I would meet the daughter in a private room with a senior nurse and introduce everyone. I would start by acknowledging how frightening this is and invite her to tell me what she understands. I would not become defensive. I would explain that her father attended yesterday with severe leg pain and was thought to have a strain, and that he has returned with a much more serious condition. I would say that the review is ongoing and that I cannot yet give the full explanation. I would offer a sincere apology for the harm and distress, without saying the review has already found a specific error. I would explain that he is in theatre and that the immediate priority is stabilisation and treatment. I would agree a named person, a time and a method for the next update. I would open the local incident and duty of candour process and explain that the family will receive the findings as they emerge. I would give information about patient advice and liaison services and complaints, and make clear this will not affect care. I would check what she has understood and record the discussion. Disposition is intensive care with a family communication plan, not an immediate discharge discussion. I would escalate to the responsible consultant and medical director if information is missing, the review is delayed or the family's concerns are not being addressed.
references_provided: Trust duty of candour guidance; family communication record; patient advice and liaison contact leaflet.

title: Reducing low value head scans
setting: Emergency department quality improvement planning desk with a local audit summary.
candidate_instructions: Use the audit summary to write a small improvement plan for emergency department head injury imaging. Include outcome, balance and process measures.
materials_provided: A retrospective audit found 120 CT head requests over three months in patients who did not meet any indication in the current local head injury policy. Eight scans showed an incidental finding and two led to specialist follow up. The median time from arrival to CT was 52 minutes. Staff say the electronic request form asks about anticoagulation but does not show the decision rule. Radiology reports increasing requests during peak hours.
task_details: Write four sections: the problem, the change to test, the measures, and the review plan. Include one potential unintended harm of the change.

checklist.item: Recognises that the audit identifies variation without assuming that every scan was unjustified.
Chooses a specific and measurable aim, such as improving documented use of the local head injury rule.
Selects a practical intervention such as an embedded decision prompt and targeted teaching rather than a memo alone.
Includes an outcome measure, a process measure and at least one balancing measure.
Identifies the risk of missing a clinically important injury, especially with anticoagulation, frailty or unclear history.
Plans a small test with a named owner, timescale and frontline feedback.
States a review rule for adapting, scaling or stopping the change and checks for data quality.

model_answer: The audit shows 120 CT requests outside the local policy, but the two follow up findings mean I should not label every scan as harmful. The improvement aim is to increase documented use of the current head injury rule and reduce requests without a policy indication over three months. I would test an electronic prompt that displays the indications, asks for the decision and makes anticoagulation and frailty fields visible. I would add a short teaching session and gather examples from staff about why the prompt is bypassed. The outcome measure would be the proportion of CT requests meeting a documented indication and the number of clinically important missed injuries. The process measure would be prompt completion and staff use. Balancing measures would include time to first clinician review, repeat attendance, radiation from repeat scans and delays for genuinely urgent patients. I would run the change for two weeks, review the run chart and ask staff and radiology whether the prompt creates unnecessary clicks. I would adapt the wording, then test again before scaling. A named clinical lead and data analyst would own the project. The review would stop the change if a patient with a policy indication is delayed or if clinicians bypass the prompt without an alternative safety check. I would escalate any safety signal to the clinical governance committee, and disposition of the project is a controlled test with a scheduled adapt, scale or stop decision.
references_provided: Local head injury policy; anonymised CT audit spreadsheet; quality improvement plan template.

title: Appraising bedside aortic ultrasound
setting: Critical appraisal discussion room with the examiner and a fictional released diagnostic accuracy paper.
candidate_instructions: Discuss what this study can and cannot tell you about using bedside aortic ultrasound in suspected acute aortic syndrome. Do not summarise the paper or calculate test statistics.
materials_provided: In a study of 820 patients with suspected acute aortic syndrome, emergency clinicians measured the aortic root after brief training. The scan was interpretable in 82% of patients. For an aortic root above the prespecified threshold, sensitivity was 92% and specificity was 96% against specialist imaging. Fifteen percent of patients had poor image quality. Agreement between clinicians was moderate, and the study excluded patients with known aneurysm and recent cardiac surgery.
sp_role_script: You are the examiner. Open with: 'Could this test safely rule out aortic dissection in your department?' Ask about selection, the reference standard, image quality and the difference between diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes. Ask for a practical conclusion for a senior emergency physician.

checklist.item: States the diagnostic question and recognises that an uninterpretable scan must be counted as a failure of the pathway.
Assesses whether consecutive, representative patients were included and how suspected cases were selected.
Interrogates the reference standard, blinding and whether all participants received the same definitive imaging.
Discusses spectrum bias, disease prevalence, interobserver agreement and the 15% poor image rate.
Explains why diagnostic accuracy does not prove improved patient outcomes or a safe discharge strategy.
Considers the exclusions and whether the findings apply to patients with previous aortic surgery or known aneurysm.
Gives a cautious conclusion and a pathway for using the scan only as an adjunct with senior review and definitive imaging when indicated.

model_answer: The study asks whether bedside aortic root measurement can identify patients with suspected acute aortic syndrome and support rule out. The 82% interpretable rate is central because a scan that cannot be obtained is not a negative test. The 15% poor image quality and moderate interobserver agreement also weaken a rule out claim. Sensitivity of 92% means most patients with the target finding tested positive, while specificity of 96% means most without it tested negative. Those figures support rule in better than rule out and cannot be translated directly into predictive values because those depend on prevalence. I would examine whether consecutive patients were enrolled, how the reference standard was applied and whether the sonographer was blinded to it. If not all patients received the same definitive imaging, some cases may be missed. The study excluded known aneurysm and recent cardiac surgery, so the result should not be applied to those groups. Test accuracy also depends on prevalence and spectrum. A high sensitivity in a selected group does not prove that discharging patients on the basis of a bedside scan is safe. I would want outcome data, follow up for missed dissection and a clear pathway for indeterminate scans. My conclusion is that this scan may be a useful early adjunct for an experienced clinician, but it cannot replace definitive imaging under the current pathway. I would use it to speed escalation when positive and never reassure solely on a poor quality or non diagnostic view. Local governance should track image quality, missed cases and specialist imaging access. Disposition of this appraisal is no immediate rule out policy, with ongoing review and audit of any adjunctive use.
references_provided: Fictional practice diagnostic study table; local suspected acute aortic syndrome pathway; critical appraisal prompt.
